News.title: UK trains cancelled: Avanti and Northern Rail services hit by power outage
News.content:
Avanti West Coast services are affected by the disruption

National Rail warned of 'major rail disruption' in the Greater Manchester area and the north-west of England, with trains cancelled, rescheduled or delayed by up to two hours

UK trains cancelled: Avanti and Northern Rail services hit by power outage

There is "major rail disruption" in the Greater Manchester area and the north-west of England, National Rail has warned.

An electrical failure at a Manchester Rail Operating Centre has led to trains being cancelled, rescheduled or delayed since Thursday afternoon.

Services operated by Avanti West Coast, CrossCountry, East Midlands Railway, London Northwestern Railway, Northern, TransPennine Express and Transport for Wales are affected.

The disruption is expected to last until the end of Thursday, National Rail added.

News.title: Man arrested over wildfire says 'this is going to destroy my life' as body found
News.content:
Man arrested over wildfire says 'this is going to destroy my life' as body found

A 65-year-old man was arrested on Wednesday in connection with the fire - he is suspected of "recklessly causing" the blaze on Monday that is believed to have been sparked by a chain saw

View 3 Images A wildfire in Calaveras County, California (Image: Getty)

A burned body has been found inside a home after a wildfire scorched parts of central California, with the authorities believing a chainsaw started the fatal blaze.

Authorities said on Thursday, August 6, that the fire is believed to have been started by sparks from a chainsaw - one man has been arrested in connection to the blaze.

65-year-old Herbert Wayne Smith was arrested on Wednesday in connection with the fire. Herbert Wayne Smith is suspected of "recklessly causing" the blaze on Monday.

View 3 Images Firefighter fights blaze in California (Image: Getty)

Mr Smith told KCRA-TV that he was using a chain saw to cut some scrap wood when it ignited.

"I'm so sorry for everything that's happened," he said.

"This is going to destroy my life, one way or another."

The wildfire has destroyed seven structures and scorched more than 15 square miles (39 square km) of forest in the Sierra Nevada foothills of Calaveras County.

It is believed that the fire was cause while "operating equipment capable of producing sparks" without clearing flammable vegetation as required, according to the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection.

Article continues below

View 3 Images Wildfire scorched an area in California (Image: Getty)

Prosecutors will determine whether to file criminal charges.

Investigators will determine whether the fire contributed to the death of the person found in a burned home in the area.

News.title: Saudi Arabia 'braced for attacks from north and south' as Middle East tensions rise
News.content:
Saudi Arabia 'braced for attacks from north and south' as Middle East tensions rise

Officials believe important economic sites will be hit in a series of attacks overseen by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps in the days after Saudi Arabia teamed up with the US for air strikes

View 2 Images Houthi soldiers stand guard during a rally marking the 11th anniversary of the Saudi military intervention in Yemen's war earlier this year (Image: YAHYA ARHAB/EPA/Shutterstock)

Officials in Saudi Arabia are reportedly bracing for 'co-ordinated' attacks ‘from the north and south’ as tensions in the Middle East rise once again.

‌



It's thought attacks could come from Iraqi militias and Yemeni Houthis in the coming days, both overseen by the Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). The latest development in a year of uncertainty in the Middle East means the oil-rich nation is on red alert for attacks on important infrastructure.

‌



Saudi Arabia has close ties to the US, as the pair teamed up to carry out air strikes in Iraq on Iranian-supported groups on July 29.

‌



US President Donald Trump said on Friday morning (August 7) he believed his country’s war on Iran will ‘end pretty soon’ after pausing military action to allow peace talks to continue. It also emerged this week that American army officials believe they have used the majority of their highly accurate long-range missiles.

“I think they want to co-ordinate attacks from both north and south,” the official told CNN .

View 2 Images Donald Trump said on Thursday he believes the Iran war will end soon (Image: AP Photo/Alex Brandon)

‌



The potential targets were “mostly civilian and economic installations,” they added, namely energy facilities, ports and airports.

Tensions between Saudi Arabia and its neighbour Yemen have risen again in recent weeks after Yemeni Houthis claimed responsibility for a range of attacks on Saudi shipping and military targets. Eleven civilians, including a four-year-old child, were injured in Saudi Arabia on Thursday after a series of attacks by Yemen’s Houthi rebels, according to the Saudi military.

The attacks, which took place in the southern region of Najran, near the Yemeni border, came hours after the Iran-backed rebels claimed responsibility for another series of strikes in central and eastern Yemen that killed at least 30 government troops and wounded at least 50 others.

‌



A Houthi leader said Saudi-backed troops were targeted in the attacks and that “hundreds” were either killed or injured. The assaults hit camps for forces of the internationally recognized government in the provinces of Marib and Hadramout, the Yemeni officials said. They spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak to the media.

Saudi Arabia has also hit military targets in Yemen in recent days. It led a military coalition against the Houthis in northern Yemen in 2015, with the conflict coming to an end in 2022 amid a humanitarian crisis.

It comes as Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan are to sign a joint defense agreement in Saudi Arabia, according to Reuters.

Article continues below

Meanwhile, the New York Times reports that a Saudi-led military coalition backing Yemen’s official government blamed a separate shelling attack in Saudi territory on the Houthis, saying 11 civilians had been injured in the Najran border region.

News.title: Thetford anti-immigration protests: Further arrests after two nights of disorder
News.content:
Thetford anti-immigration protests: Further arrests after two nights of disorder

Two men were arrested on Thursday following two nights of disorder in Thetford, Norfolk, after people attempted to storm homes linked to asylum seekers and police officers were assaulted

View 4 Images Police have said they will remain on the scene overnight tonight (Image: Scott Hussey / SWNS)

Further arrests have been made in Thetford after crowds attempted to storm homes linked to asylum seekers and police officers were attacked.

Two men were arrested on Thursday, Norfolk Police confirmed, following two consecutive nights of unrest in the market town. One was arrested on suspicion of inciting racial hatred in connection with events on Wednesday. The other was held on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly and failing to provide his details to officers when requested.

Police powers were stepped up on Thursday evening in the aftermath of the earlier disorder. This followed officers being "subjected to significant aggression" on Wednesday, with one struck by a rock, one bitten and another spat at

View 4 Images Damage caused to a house on Bracken Road following disorder in the village of Thetford (Image: © 2026 PA Media, All Rights Reserved)

Two officers were taken to hospital after responding to the scene at Clover Way that evening, which police described as "fast-moving and volatile" with tensions mounting as a crowd advanced towards a residential property.

On Tuesday night, windows were smashed, fences broken and attempts were made to force entry into a residential property, police said.

The protesters' attempts to break into homes were fuelled by fears that the properties were being used to house asylum seekers.

Video footage circulating on social media appeared to show police escorting a number of asylum seekers away from properties in the area.

View 4 Images Police in Clover Way (Image: Scott Hussey / SWNS)

Eyewitnesses and social media users had condemned the police response, with reports suggesting that a woman in a mobility scooter was pepper-sprayed on Wednesday. The force defended their actions as proportionate and appropriate, including the deployment of Pava spray.

They stated that Pava, a handheld incapacitating substance similar to pepper spray, was deployed in response to an individual's behaviour within the crowd.

A police spokeswoman added: "We understand that concerns have been raised about a woman using a mobility scooter who was affected during the incident.

"It was not the intention for any bystander to be impacted; however, where people remain within an area of active disorder and do not follow police instructions to move away, there is a risk they may be affected by tactics deployed to protect public safety."

A resident of Clover Way, who wished to remain anonymous, revealed that at around 9.30pm on Wednesday "lots of young boys... came up on bikes and chucked eggs at the house". The largely seated demonstration began "peaceful" until additional officers arrived and formed a line, she said.

Subsequently, "it started to get a little bit rowdy" and "people took a step forward towards the police".

Nobody attempted to enter the property, she said, noting that police "started pepper-spraying people", including "a lady in a wheelchair".

View 4 Images (Image: © 2026 PA Media, All Rights Reserved)

There were "a few young idiots picking up stones, lobbing them at a police car".

"They brought a riot van down and blocked the front of the house," she said, adding that officers brandished batons, made arrests and instructed people to disperse. Norfolk Police confirmed that two arrests were made on Wednesday night on charges including public order offences, harassment and possession of an offensive weapon.

One man in his 40s remains in police custody.

Brian Thompson, 68, of Fairfields, Thetford, has been charged with possession of an offensive weapon, namely a wooden bat. He has been released on bail and is due to appear before Norwich Magistrates' Court on August 25.

Article continues below

A man in his 30s, who was arrested on Wednesday in connection with Tuesday's incidents on suspicion of a public order offence, has since been released and issued with a conditional caution.

News.title: Dublin fire: Inferno near airport as smoke seen for miles and 999 crews swarm
News.content:
The huge fire is at an industrial site in Wimbletown, Ballyboughal, and is visible from Dublin Airport. Dublin Fire Brigade have sent five engines including a water tanker

Dublin fire: Inferno near airport as smoke seen for miles and 999 crews swarm

A huge fire broke out at an industrial site near Dublin Airport with multiple fire crews rushing to the scene.

Dublin Fire Brigade warned people in the Wimbletown area of Ballyboughal to close all windows and doors as the blaze sent a massive plume of smoke into the area which was visible for miles around.

They said at the time: "We're aware of the industrial fire in Wimbletown, Ballyboughal and have five fire engines including a water tanker on the way. Thanks for all the 999 calls, firefighters are already on scene dealing with the fire."

Another blaze was also reported in Ashtown to the North West of the city. LiveDrive in Dublin said: "Emergency services are attending a fire near Navan Road (Ashtown). Smoke is visible across the area. Take care."

News.title: 'Grotesque' abuse of migrant care workers laid bare in damning report
News.content:
'Grotesque' abuse of migrant care workers laid bare in damning report

Andy Burnham faces calls to overhaul the visa system as the Royal College of Nursing warned of harrowing cases of bullying, racism and financial exploitation in the care sector

View 3 Images A damning report by the Royal College of Nursing lifts the lid on the treatment of migrant care workers (Image: Getty Images)

Harrowing cases of bullying, racism and financial exploitation have been uncovered as Andy Burnham faces calls to end "grotesque" abuse of migrant care workers.

‌



Nursing chiefs warn unscrupulous employers are taking advantage of a power imbalance in the visa system to demand huge repayments, withhold earnings and allow toxic treatment of staff. The Prime Minister faces calls to act as part of his social care shake-up.

‌



A damning report by the Royal College of Nursing (RCN) called for an overhaul of the visa system, making it easier for workers to escape employers without facing threats. It also demanded proper investigations of exploitation cases. In one case, it said, a care worker was told they would have to pay £25,000 to leave their job before their contract expired.

‌



Former neo-Nazi withdraws as Tory council election candidate after Kemi Badenoch offers him job READ MORE :

Terrorism referrals rocket as children account for one in three cases READ MORE :

View 3 Images Professor Nicola Ranger said the government must tackle 'grotesque' exploitation (Image: Adam Gerrard / Daily Mirror)

RCN General Secretary Professor Nicola Ranger said: “Just the week after the Prime Minister laid out his plans for social care in England, this report exposes the scale of grotesque exploitation taking place in the sector.

"A National Care Service meeting the needs of an ageing population, with complex conditions will need to be registered nurse led. We’re the ones with the skill and expertise to make it work, but not while so many of our migrant colleagues are being exploited.

‌



"Fixing social care and changing the system that allows this exploitation, bullying and discrimination must come hand in hand."

Under existing rules, people in the UK on a health and social care visa must be sponsored by an employer. Those who change jobs require a new sponsor and an updated visa.

In one of his first acts as PM, Mr Burnham announced he wants to speed up plans to deliver a new National Care Service. Prof Ranger warned: "One of the major causes (of migrant worker abuse) is a visa sponsorship system which creates a dangerous power imbalance, allowing unscrupulous employers to use withdrawal of sponsorship as leverage to extort money, alter contracts, reduce pay or bully and harass with impunity. It’s a shocking scenario which hands individual employers all the power. It has no place in a National Care Service.

‌



“For years, our members have bravely spoken out and sought support against these appalling practices, but we know these cases are just the tip of the iceberg. Migrant workers are routinely intimidated and left fearful of speaking out."

View 3 Images Andy Burnham has promised an overhaul of the social care system (Image: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PA Wire)

The report was based on analysis of 383 cases where migrant health and social care workers sought help from the RCN between 2023 and 2025.

‌



Of these 197 related to repayment clauses - to recover costs from staff wishing to leave their jobs before the end of their contract. More than half of these clauses were over £3,000, with one as high as £25,000.

One in five raised issues about pay, with many saying they were paid less than their contracted hourly wage. And it unearthed 35 cases where contracts were changed after a worker started - often to reduce pay or force longer hours.

And there were 68 cases of severe bullying and harassment, with some cases involving racist discrimination, the RCN said.

‌



It is estimated that 30% of staff in the adult care sector are non-British nationals. The RCN called for a new umbrella organisation to administer visas, to make it easier to tackle threats from employers. It also said the new Fair Work Agency must properly monitor the way staff are treated and go after unethical businesses.

It also said staff must be given 180 days - rather than the current 60 - to find a new employer when they move jobs to eliminate the risk of deportation.

In a speech last week, Mr Burnham praised overseas care workers, saying: "Many people from other countries have been caring for my dad [who has Alzheimer’s].

Article continues below

“I want those carers to know: we appreciate you, we appreciate what you are doing to support people here.” There is growing speculation that he plans to exclude care workers from controversial migration reforms that would see people forced to wait up to 15 years to claim indefinite leave to remain (ILR). At the moment people become eligible after five years.

A government spokesperson said: “This government stands firm on our zero-tolerance approach to labour exploitation and abuse of our immigration system by unscrupulous employers. We are taking action against rogue care providers who have used their sponsor license to exploit workers, and we’ve ended overseas recruitment for care workers after unacceptable levels of abuse and exploitation.”

News.title: Most teenagers to switch off optional overnight curfews on social media, study shows
News.content:
Most teenagers to switch off optional overnight curfews on social media, study shows

Youngsters aged 16- and 17-years-old will face an automatic block from accessing platforms from midnight to 6am - but research shows they plan to switch the curfew off next spring

View 3 Images More than a third (35%) of 16 to 18-year-olds continue scrolling on social media between 11pm and 1am, the study showed (Image: Getty Images)

Most teenagers plan to switch off a voluntary overnight curfew on social media which is due to come into effect next spring, polling suggests.

‌



Youngsters aged 16 and 17 will face an automatic block from accessing platforms from midnight to 6am under online safety plans unveiled last month.

‌



But polling by Censuswide has found 84.6% of 16- to 18-year-olds said they would opt out of the proposed curfews. Almost half of kids (45.2%) said they’d switch off the curfew to allow them to speak to family or friends, while more than a third (37.2%) said they’d do so to watch online content.

‌



More than a third of 16- to 18-year-olds (38%) are already using VPNs in daily life, with one in four (24%) expecting to use them to bypass curfew. VPNs (Virtual Private Networks) obscures a user's location or details allowing them to get around UK online safety laws.

Teenagers face block on overnight access and addictive social media features READ MORE :

Teenager severely injured after plunging 20 storeys in horror lift fall READ MORE :

View 3 Images Keir Starmer announced a social media ban for under 16s as one of his last acts as Prime Minister (Image: Sky News)

Keir Starmer introduced online curfews and restrictions on addictive design features, such as infinite scrolling, to help prevent a cliff edge when kids hit their 16th birthday and an upcoming social media ban lifts.

‌



But ministers said the measures would be voluntary to strike a balance between giving older teenagers greater safeguards online while still allowing them to control their settings.

Then-Education Secretary Bridget Phillipson suggested the voluntary element to curfews could be changed if it was found many teenagers were switching off the default settings.

Asked about their social media habits, almost four in ten (39%) teens aged 16 to 18 said they use social media between 9pm and 11pm, while more than a third (35%) continue scrolling between 11pm and 1am, the study found.

‌



Leanne Proctor, regulatory lead at the Online Responsibility Network, which organised the polling, said the research suggests a curfew is “unlikely to be enough on its own to prevent online harms”.

“This research suggests the proposed social media curfew is unlikely to be enough on its own to prevent online harms," she said. "The findings show that many young people expect to opt out of the restrictions or find ways around them, raising questions about how effective the policy will be in practice.

"There is no single solution to protecting children online. Rather than relying on broad service-level restrictions, greater focus should be placed on design feature-level protections and robust age assurance, helping to ensure young people have age-appropriate experiences without unnecessarily restricting access."

‌



Last month, then-Technology Secretary Liz Kendall, who lost her job when Andy Burnham became PM, said infinite scrolling - where a user's feed continuously loads - will be switched off for 16 and 17-year-old, while overnight curfews from midnight to 6am will be in place.

Autoplay videos, which are clips that automatically play one after another, and recommender feeds that push a personalised stream of content will also be switched off by default.

View 3 Images The package is due to come into force next spring, alongside a social media ban for under 16s. (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

‌



Some campaigners and bereaved families were fiercely in favour of a social media ban as the solution to a spiralling online harms crisis. But other experts believe a blanket ban creates a false sense of security, warning that kids will bypass the ban or be pushed into darker spaces online.

A Government spokesman said: “Young people will have a choice in how they navigate social media as they grow into adulthood.

“In our national poll, 64% of young people aged 16 to 21 supported restricting children from certain apps at night and our trials found overnight curfews quickly became part of daily routines and helped improve sleep and concentration.

Article continues below

“We are providing strong protections by default while giving 16- and 17-year-olds the ability to decide whether those protections fit their circumstances, recognising they are capable of making informed decisions.”

::: Censuswide polled 1,000 16- to 18-year-olds on behalf of Online Responsibility Network between July 21-27.

News.title: Woman misdiagnosed with aggressive cancer had hysterectomy after lab mix-up
News.content:
Woman misdiagnosed with aggressive cancer had hysterectomy after lab mix-up

Cassandra Barksdale was informed that a DNA analysis found the tissue sample showing an aggressive form of cancer belonged to a different patient and not to her, the lawsuit says

View 3 Images Cassandra Barksdale lived for months believing she had an aggressive type of cancer (Image: AP Photo/Emilie Megnien)

A woman lived for months believing she had an aggressive type of cancer, sending her and her sons into a deep depression.

‌



Cassandra Barksdale alleges that she was wrongly diagnosed with cancer and underwent an unneeded hysterectomy because of a lab error. Her attorneys filed a lawsuit Tuesday against Kaiser Permanente alleging the mix-up led to the surgery and months of physical and emotional pain.

‌



According to the lawsuit, another patient's tissue sample was mistakenly labeled as belonging to Barksdale, who at age 43 then underwent a full hysterectomy on May 15, 2025, and was told she would get instructions about chemotherapy.

‌



View 3 Images Cassandra Barksdale filed a lawsuit after her test results were swapped with another patient’s (Image: Courtesy of The Edmond Firm)

British fugitive on most-wanted list arrested in Spain READ MORE :

It's unclear how the mix-up occurred. In September, Barksdale was informed that a DNA analysis found the tissue sample showing an aggressive form of endometrial uterine cancer belonged to a different patient and not to her, the lawsuit says.

“She came into Kaiser Permanente looking for answers, and she left with a diagnosis that did not belong to her. And every step that was taken after that was based off of misinformation,” her attorney Shannan Young said.

‌



Barksdale went to Kaiser Permanente Southwood Medical Center in Jonesboro, Georgia, in early 2025 to seek treatment for heavy bleeding and fibroids, which are noncancerous growths in and around the uterus. She underwent a biopsy on March 10, 2025.

Barksdale said that after she got the biopsy results on March 17, 2025, she lived for months believing she had an aggressive type of cancer, sending her and her sons into a deep depression.

View 3 Images Cassandra Barksdale with her two sons (Image: Courtesy of The Edmond Firm)

‌



“I even started making funeral plans with them to let them know, you know, if I don’t make it out, this is what I want done,” Barksdale said.

Representatives for Kaiser Permanente wrote in a statement that, “Ms. Barksdale should not have experienced this.”

“We have highly trained staff and very thorough processes in place to prevent errors like this from taking place. After this occurred last year, we took immediate steps to ensure it could not happen again. We realize the impact of this incident and are committed to working with Ms. Barksdale and her counsel to resolve this in the most fair and accountable way we can.”

Article continues below

Because of privacy laws, information about the other patient — including what happened to her and whether cancer treatment was delayed — isn’t publicly available.

Labs have turned to a number of best practices to try and prevent errors, including barcode systems for specimen labeling and point-of-care testing.

The Georgia lawsuit asks for unspecified damages. Shannan Young said: “There’s no amount of money that’s going to return back to her, her healthy organs, or erase the experiences and the pain that she’s had. But our justice system recognizes that when somebody’s negligence harms another person, accountability requires more than ‘I’m sorry."

News.title: Thousands of rail passengers hit by power failure disruption
News.content:
Thousands of rail passengers have described "nightmare" journeys, after being hit by delays and cancellations following a power failure at a signalling centre that caused major disruption across northern England.

A 90-second power outage occurred in the area covering Network Rail's Manchester Rail Operating Centre just before 14:00 BST on Thursday. The BBC understands there was then a delay to back-up systems kicking in, meaning affected trains had to stop while signalling was down.

Network Rail said "engineers are making good progress fixing the signalling issues" but warned that major disruption was expected until the end of the day on Friday.

At least eight rail operators remained affected on Thursday evening.

"We've got to really understand what's gone wrong here, because clearly something has and we've got to make sure we investigate that thoroughly to understand why things haven't restored as we would have expected," said Chris Wright, Route Director NW at Network Rail.

Network Rail said services may continue to be disrupted "because many trains and crews are not where they would normally be after this unexpected incident".

It has advised passengers hoping to travel on Friday to continue to check online for information on any further disruption, external: "As soon as we have information, we will keep you updated."

Manchester Rail Operating Centre was opened in July 2014 and houses all the controls to safely operate the railway in the region, including signalling.

According to Network Rail, its operational control boundary spans from Crewe in the south to Carlisle in the north, and from Todmorden in the east to the Welsh border in the west.

The initial power outage on Thursday afternoon was part of a wider power supply outage in the Ardwick area, but the BBC understands there was a delay to the back-up supply kicking in - which exacerbated the problem.

News.content:
Appearing in court earlier, Ahmadzai asked for an English translator but did not respond to the charges.

His lawyer, Christos Erdas, said his client had exercised his right to remain silent, and that his rights had been "violated" through leaks of evidence and documents from the case file - including his right to the presumption of innocence.

The lawyer said that when Ross was found, she had no injuries and any apparent cause of death was "entirely absent".

He said his client wanted the forensic medical report and the "toxicological and histological examinations of the deceased" to be included in the case file.

Erdas added: "His [Ahmadzai's] stance towards the prosecuting and investigating authorities did not constitute a stance of denial but, on the contrary, one of reservation, so that he may present his defence in full once the case file has been completed with the above essential documents â which were not sought by the preliminary investigating authorities â with the sole aim of establishing the substantive truth for both sides."

Ahmadzai was remanded in custody until his trial, which could take up to 18 months.

News.title: Arrests in Norfolk town as disorder continues for third night
News.content:
More arrests have been made in Thetford as disorder linked to anti-immigration protests continued for a third night in the Norfolk market town.

A further two men in their 40s were arrested on Thursday evening, Norfolk Police said, taking the total number of people arrested in relation to the disorder to five.

One of the pair was arrested on suspicion of racial hatred, relating to offences on Wednesday, the force said. The other man was arrested on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly and failing to give his details to police when asked.

Policing powers were stepped up in Thetford on Thursday evening following the disorder earlier in the week.

It came after police officers were "subjected to significant aggression" on Wednesday, including a female police officer who was "seriously bitten".

Crowds also attempted to storm homes linked to alleged asylum seekers on Tuesday and Wednesday evenings.

Police removed some people from a property on Thursday evening.

Amid the disorder, pictures appeared to show a heavy police presence in the residential area of Canterbury Way on Thursday night.

A Home Office spokesperson condemned the behaviour, warning that "anyone taking part in this criminal activity will face the full force of the law".

Norfolk Police has imposed public safety measures in the town, including requiring people to remove face coverings if asked to do so or face arrest.

They will also be permitted to direct anyone committing, or who they suspect may commit, anti-social behaviour, to leave the area.

The measures were put in place from 18:00 BST on Thursday and remain until 07:00 on Friday.

News.title: Artificial Intelligence used to design brand new viruses
News.content:
Artificial Intelligence has been used to design brand new viruses that are fully functional and can replicate in the laboratory, say US researchers.

It is the first time whole genomes have been successfully designed by AI.

The resulting 16 novel viruses were created to infect bacteria and pose no threat to people.

The breakthrough has been labelled a "very significant turning point" in science that could unlock a new era for treating disease. But experts have also warned AI-designed viruses raise "urgent" safety and security concerns.

AI tools are rapidly advancing and have already been used to design new antibiotics.

But that is relatively simple compared with designing a new viable virus from scratch.

"This is a next step in the complexity that's designable by generative AI, this is the first time generative AI has been used to design a complete genome, it's something that can replicate and have other functions inside cellsâ¦ this was new territory for us," Brian Hie, assistant professor at Stanford University, told the BBC.

News.title: Trump again tries to limit US birthright citizenship with new executive orders
News.content:
Donald Trump is trying again to scale back birthright citizenship in the US, weeks after the Supreme Court shot down his previous attempt to eliminate the right.

The president signed two executive orders on Thursday, including one that expands the existing definitions of non-citizens whose children are not eligible for birthright citizenship.

The second order bans so-called birth tourism, the practice of pregnant mothers coming to the US to give birth so that their babies will be citizens.

"This should have happened years ago, but we're taking care of it now," Trump said from the Oval Office, criticising the Supreme Court's rejection of his previous bid to end the 150-year-old policy.

"My Administration has guarded against the risks posed by malign foreign actors who attempt to swindle American citizens by taking advantage of the generosity of our Nation," the first executive order says.

That order prohibits the automatic citizenship of babies born in the United States to two non-citizen parents where one of the parents is: a member of a foreign terrorist group, a foreign government employee, has attempted to gain citizenship through fraudulent means, or is living in US territories where citizenship is not conferred by federal statute.

Birthright citizenship for people born in US territories such as Puerto Rico is codified by federal statute.

Trump and members of his administration have repeatedly railed against birth tourism, including accusing Russian and Chinese adversaries of taking advantage of birthright citizenship to infiltrate the US.

While announcing the executive orders from the Oval Office on Thursday, Trump said that hundreds of thousands of babies have been born through birth tourism in the US.

News.title: Met Police boss admits mistake over Cambridge professor plagiarism row
News.content:
Times Higher Education (THE) reporter Grove said he had been investigating allegations Arday had plagiarised parts of his PhD, and contacted him in 2025 to offer him the right of reply.

"In early February I received a call from a Met police officer saying that a complaint had been raised against me by someone and Professor Arday was very distressed and I shouldn't contact him again," Grove told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

"It was a complete shock. Apparently it was for harassment but I hadn't contacted him for four months and then maybe I think I've only sent three or four emails to him in total."

The Met closed its inquiries into the case.

Sir Mark told LBC: "We dropped the ball on that one, let's not beat around the bush.

"A report came in of harassment or some crime like that, it should have been screened out as not requiring investigation...

"We shouldn't have made that call to him [Grove] and said that."

The University of Cambridge said on Tuesday it had begun an investigation into Arday, who became the institution's youngest black professor in 2023, following "new information" about his "academic qualifications and honorary appointments".

In a statement published by campaign group Good Law Project on Wednesday, Arday said the "relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love".

"I no longer wish to feel as though I am living under a constant spotlight, where every aspect of my life is subject to public examination and judgement," he said.

Speaking of his decision to step down he added it should not "be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me".

His resignation followed a series of media reports alleging he plagiarised parts of his PhD thesis completed at Liverpool John Moores University (LJMU) and other research.

LJMU - which awarded his PhD in 2015 - had investigated the allegations that were made last year, but did not uphold the charges.

The Times reported Arday defended himself by arguing that he had not received adequate supervision during his PhD given his autism and "learning disabilities".

In an interview with the Times, Arday said that he could not afford a proofreader to catch mistakes when he started out in academia.

Further questions were raised in the press about the truth of other claims, including Arday saying he ran 600 miles in six days and that he raised Â£5.5m for charity.

News.title: Amanda Knox defends Fringe comedy show after claims it will 'trivialise violence'
News.content:
Amanda Knox, who was convicted and later acquitted of murdering British student Meredith Kercher in Italy in 2007, has defended her solo comedy show following calls for it to be cancelled.

The sold-out show called Cartwheel, which Knox will perform at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe, discusses motherhood and how she will explain the case to her daughter.

Knox told the BBC she is not the first person to use comedy to talk about traumatic events and said her material focuses on "how the world is unsafe and unfair towards women".

But Stephanie Kercher, the victim's sister, said she is concerned it will "normalise and trivialise" violence against women, and Meredith, in particular.

Speaking on BBC Breakfast, Stephanie Kercher, said: "What I would say [to Knox] is to think about the family here, think about her friends and to turn the tables if it was your sister that this had happened to, because I know you have a sister as well."

Responding to the comments, Knox said: "The interesting irony of that is that my daughter is a huge motivation for me doing this show.

"It's about how the world is unsafe and unfair towards women and what it means to raise a daughter in that world, knowing how bad it can be.

"If they [Kercher's family] saw my show, they would recognise that."

A petition against the show, set up by a friend of Meredith, has been signed by nearly 5,000 people.

It states the show disrespects her memory and risks making light of such a harrowing event.

News.title: Village sees 50 days without rain during summer heatwave
News.content:
As the extremely dry spell continues across much of England and Wales, a small village in Surrey has notched up 50 consecutive days without rain this summer.

Wisley, most famous for being the site of the 240-acre garden owned by the Royal Horticultural Society, saw 36 continuous dry days back in the hot summer of 1976 - but has comfortably exceeded that number so far this year, with no rainfall since mid-June.

It comes after the driest July for England and Wales since Met Office records began 190 years ago, external.

Meanwhile, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has issued further yellow heat health alerts, external for most of England this weekend as the temperatures start to build again. The alerts cover the Humber, West and East Midlands, east of England, London, and the South East and South West from 09:00 BST on Saturday until 21:00 on Tuesday 11 August.

News.title: Calls for inquiry into Army teen college after reports of rape and abuse
News.content:
The women, whose names have been changed to protect their identities, all attended AFC over the last five years.

One woman, Tilly, told the BBC she was 17 when she was raped at AFC by several fellow soldiers who invited her into their room.

"They started taking my clothes off and then this led to them doing stuff I didn't consent to.

"And then I was rapedâ¦ by multiple junior soldiers, same age as me. It went on for hours. I felt like a piece of meat."

Another woman's story was shared with the BBC by her mother, who said her daughter Amy was sexually assaulted and subjected to almost daily sexual harassment during her training.

Because the lock to Amy's room was not working, her mother said "she found herself sleeping across the door to stop male soldiers coming in".

Another woman, who said she was sexually assaulted and harassed at AFC, described how misogynistic attitudes and behaviour of AFC staff rubbed off on some of the male teenagers.

She recalled one of the instructors saying: "It's all about the pussy and how much of it you can get."

The MoD told the BBC that the college "welcomes external scrutiny and challenge".

It said that AFC had in the last year "hosted the safeguarding bodies, parliamentarians, the Children's Commissioner's office and the Armed Forces Commissioner, as well as receiving an outstanding report from Ofsted".

Ashleigh Percival-Borley, a veteran who served for 13 years in the British Army as a sergeant and multi-disciplinary instructor, said "incidents like this have "really taken my confidence out of the institution and that makes me really sad".

She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme there was a "level of frustration" from women who wanted to serve in the army.

She said hearing the allegations "sickened" her as a female veteran as well as a former instructor who knew "the embodiment of the army's values and standards" needed for the role.

The Children's Commissioner for England Dame Rachel de Souza said she would ensure the "appalling attacks" were investigated and "those responsible, including for failing to safeguard these girls, are held to account".

She said all children living away from home had a right to contact her team for support, and that she would make sure all girls at AFC could do so.

News.title: Man wrongly jailed for murdering man wants to restore his 'forgotten' grave
News.content:
A man who was wrongly jailed for 11 years for murder is raising money to restore the grave of the man he was accused of killing.

Michael O'Brien was one of three men wrongly convicted of the 1987 murder of Cardiff newsagent Philip Saunders.

O'Brien, along with Darren Hall and Ellis Sherwood, became known as the Cardiff Newsagent Three. They were eventually cleared in 1999, in what became one of Wales' worst miscarriages of justice.

He said he recently visited Saunders' grave and was "sad" to see there was no longer a headstone there and the area was "unkempt."

"It just sort of hit home that one, the killer was still at large, and two, this man has largely been forgotten about," O'Brien said.

Saunders was killed with a shovel in his backyard. It seemed the ambush and brutal attack was an attempt to steal his day's takings.

In June, nearly 40 years on from the original crime, South Wales Police said they were launching a review of the evidence in the case, "in the hope advances in forensic science will provide the breakthrough needed".

News.title: Burnham orders review of grooming gang early releases
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has ordered an "urgent" review to identify any grooming gang members who may be eligible to be freed from jail under the government's early release scheme.

The announcement comes after Tory leader Kemi Badenoch raised concerns that child sex offenders could leave jail well before the end of their sentences.

She pointed out that indecent assault was not included in the list of offences that the government said would be excluded, external from the early release scheme.

Five men convicted of indecent assault as part of a historical grooming-gang case in Bradford are among the prisoners whose offences were not included in the list of exclusions.

The prime minister's spokesperson said Burnham had asked the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) to "conduct an in-depth review of cases to ensure that grooming cases were identified".

"This work is happening urgently," Burnham's spokesperson said.

"This is extremely important to the PM and he has personally intervened to ensure everything possible is being done so that vile groomers are dealt with in the way their victims deserve."

It is understood that at this stage the review will only seek to identify offenders who might be released early.

The government has not confirmed whether the review will lead to the prevention of any early releases of offenders convicted of grooming-related crimes.

Badenoch described the intervention as "another U-turn secured" and "another review from Burnham following my letter".

The government is planning to release about 5,000 offenders in England and Wales early in an effort to make space in overcrowded jails.

Burnham launched a review of the scheme after he became prime minister and this week he announced that some prisoners convicted of rape, serious child sex and other grooming offences would barred from early release.

But in a letter, external, Badenoch said many more types of offenders - including those convicted of sexually assaulting children - could be freed early.

"On Tuesday, you told the country that those convicted of grooming offences would be excluded," she wrote. "Your own government has now put in writing that some of these men will be released early anyway."

Highlighting that indecent assault was not excluded from the early release scheme, Badenoch said "many cases of child sex abuse committed before 2004 were charged this way, including Rotherham and Rochdale".

Badenoch branded this a "betrayal of victims", and urged Burnham to publish the full list of offences that remain eligible for early release.

Under changes made by Burnham, external, people sentenced for rape, serious child sex and grooming offences will now not be eligible for early release from October.

But some prisoners who are not excluded could be freed after serving a third of their total custodial sentence rather than after 40% or 50% of their term.

Burnham said he had wanted to exclude more offenders, but prison overcrowding prevented this.

The prime minister said making more prisoners exempt was not possible without the prison system collapsing and putting the public "at much greater risk".

The prison population in England and Wales on 3 August was 86,495, which was 97% of useable capacity.

The number of places in jails in England and Wales has not kept pace with the significant rise in the prison population in recent decades under successive governments.

There are cases of offenders who were convicted of indecent assault under section 14 and 15 of the Sexual Offences Act 1956.

These sections of the 1956 Act were not included in the government's list of exclusions, suggesting prisoners convicted of these crimes could qualify for the early release scheme.

Five men who were jailed in October 2005, external, after being convicted of indecent assault for abusing a teenage girl in Bradford in the early 2000s, could be eligible for early release under the scheme.

In December 2024, Ajaz Karim was jailed for 21 months after he was convicted of indecent assault for sexually abusing a 13-year-old girl at the school where he was a sports coach.

In another case, Shahid Hussain was jailed for eight years in September 2024, after he was convicted of indecently assaulting a 14-year-old girl in Rotherham in 2003.

The government has not yet confirmed exactly which offenders will be released.

The mother of PC Andrew Harper also said she was "devastated" to learn two men jailed after her son was killed will still be eligible for early release.

PC Harper, 28, was killed in 2019 when he was dragged by a car down a country road as three teenagers fled the scene of a quad bike theft in Berkshire.

His family previously said they had received a letter from the Ministry of Justice confirming that two of the offenders could be included in the early release scheme.

Earlier this week, Justice Secretary Alex Norris apologised to families affected by the early release scheme, saying they were "carrying the can from previous failures".

The justice secretary said about 5,000 extra releases will take place in 10 batches from October - down from about 6,000 before the revision.

The changes are due to be phased in, beginning with prisoners serving sentences of fewer than 575 days, going up to inmates jailed for 12 years or more being eligible for early release in June 2027.

The number of individuals released each time will depend on the prison population, which the government says will evolve between now and implementation.

News.title: Conservatives pledge to ban foreign nationals from social housing
News.content:
The Conservatives have said they would end the provision of social housing for foreign nationals in England if they win power at the next election.

The party said ending new tenancies for all foreign nationals, as well as current tenancies for couples where neither person is a UK, Irish or EU citizen, would free up an estimated 228,144 homes for British families.

The Conservatives said Labour had "lost control of immigration" and British families had been left sitting on housing waiting lists as a result.

But Labour said the policy was an "unserious, unworkable proposal, copied from Reform, that does nothing to tackle the housing crisis the Tories themselves created".

In June, Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said he would make it a requirement for foreign national tenants to find private accommodation within three months or face possible deportation if his party won power.

Under the Tory proposals, ineligible tenants would be expected to move out of their homes within six months.

Any single person currently living in social housing who is not a UK, Irish or EU citizen would lose their social home. This includes those with or without children.

Couples, where neither of them are UK or EU citizens, and they do not have EU settled status, will also lose their entitlement.

Anyone with EU settled status would not be evicted.

For future tenancies, UK nationals and those with EU settled status would be eligible but any new EU citizens without settled status would not be.

Foreign nationals with settled status, refugee status, or specific humanitarian protections can currently qualify for social housing.

Asylum seekers are not eligible for social housing, unless in exceptional circumstances such as domestic abuse cases.

Social housing, usually provided by housing associations or local councils, is typically cheaper and more secure than privately rented homes.

When they were last in government in 2024, the Conservatives were considering plans to make it a requirement for foreign nationals to have to live in the UK for 10 years before qualifying for social housing.

There are 1.34 million households on social housing waiting lists, as of March 2025, the latest government figures.

The vast majority of social housing lettings are given to single people.

In 2024-25, most lead tenants of new social lettings, the person in whose name the social home is rented, were UK nationals - 89% or 233,000 tenants.

In the same period, 2.3% of new lettings were given to refugees - 800 refugees were UK nationals, while the remaining 3,900 were non-UK nationals.

The most common nationality of refugees in a new social letting was Afghanistan with the second most common being Ukraine.

News.title: All schools in England to get pupil attendance targets, government says
News.content:
Every mainstream state school in England will be given their own target to improve pupil attendance, the government has confirmed.

Schools will also be encouraged to offer more clubs and activities on Fridays, to improve attendance at the end of the week.

It comes as official attendance data, published on Thursday, suggested school absence rates in England remained above pre-pandemic levels, with nearly one in five pupils missing at least 10% of school in the 2025/26 academic year.

Education minister Paul Waugh said the new attendance targets would take each school's local challenges into account, but that "every school has a role to play to improve attendance".

Before the Covid pandemic, when many schools closed to pupils for significant periods of time, attendance rates at English mainstream state schools regularly stayed above 95%, but schools have struggled to get back to those rates in the years since.

Thursday's figures, external suggested an overall attendance rate of 93% for 2025/26, a slight decrease on the previous year. That includes both authorised absences, such as illness, and unauthorised absences, which is when pupils miss school without permission or a valid reason.

The rates of persistent absence have doubled since the pandemic. A pupil is described as persistently absent if they miss at least 10% of school sessions.

In 2018/19, persistent absence rates for England state schools were around 10%, while the most recent data showed it was at 19% in 2025/26.

Pupils on free school meals and those with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) were also still more likely to be absent from school than their peers.

News.title: Farmer jailed for lodger's 'body in barrel' murder
News.content:
A farmer who shot his lodger and dismembered his body has been jailed for 35 years.

Richard Dyson, 55, disappeared in November 2019, but his remains, kept inside a concrete-filled barrel in a trailer on a farm near Barnsley, were not discovered for nearly six years.

A trial at Sheffield Crown Court heard how Christopher Wright killed Dyson when he tried to steal a gun from him before disposing of the body with the help of his childhood friend Karl Schwalbe.

Last month, Wright, 73, was convicted of murder and Schwalbe, 72, was found guilty of perverting the course of justice.

Wright, a former butcher, was also found guilty of conspiracy to pervert the justice, preventing a lawful burial and six firearms offences.

Jailing him, Mr Justice Cotter said: "You had worked as a butcher and were skilled enough to do such a terrible thing, something few ordinary people would have the stomach for."

Schwalbe was given a three-year sentence for perverting the course of justice.

Bethany Dainty, Dyson's daughter, said her life had become a "living nightmare".

She had issued numerous appeals for help tracing her father in the years he was missing.

In a victim impact statement read to the court, she said: "Someone watched me suffering for years and said nothing. That level of cruelty is impossible for me to understand."

News.title: Woman charged after four stabbed near Covent Garden
News.content:
A 47-year-old woman has appeared in court after four men were stabbed near Covent Garden in central London.

Stella Gollovena, of no fixed address, has been charged with four counts of wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm and one count of possession of an offensive weapon in a public place.

Police were called to Endell Street at about 12:30 BST on Wednesday after four men, aged 34, 39, 42 and 56, were found with stab wounds. They were taken to hospital with injuries that were not life-threatening or life-changing and have all since been discharged.

Gollovena appeared at Highbury Corner Magistrates' Court on Thursday afternoon where she spoke only to confirm her identity.

The incident took place in the capital's busy tourist area filled with bars, theatres and restaurants.

Police were "flagged down" by one of the injured men, the court heard.

London's Air Ambulance landed at nearby Trafalgar Square following the incident, although those wounded were taken to hospital by paramedics via road.

Four men provided statements to police, while a fifth person at the scene said they had also been stabbed but did not want to speak to officers.

Gollovena did not enter any pleas to the charges during the hearing.

She was remanded in custody and will next appear at Snaresbrook Crown Court on 3 September.

News.title: All of England's rivers and lakes polluted with chemicals, officials say
News.content:
Data from the EA shows that while 15% of rivers are classed as good, fewer than 7% of lakes reached that level.

The biggest individual problem is phosphate - a nutrient from sewage and farm runoff - with around half of rivers still exceeding safe levels.

Despite a record Â£22bn earmarked for water company environmental improvements by 2030, the overall picture has changed little since 2019.

The government is on course to miss its legally binding target of restoring 77% of England's waters to good ecological status by 2027 - a goal the environmental watchdog, the Office for Environmental Protection, has warned will be missed by a "considerable margin".

It's now investigating both the government and the Environment Agency over possible rule breaches.

Environment Secretary Angela Eagle said the figures "underline the need for wholesale change across the water sector".

She pointed to new laws the government has introduced to hold water companies to account and record investment. "We will drive forward a system that puts the public interest first," she said.

Water UK, which represents the water companies, said it was spending record amounts of money on improving the country's waterways.

"Water companies are investing Â£22bn in environmental improvements by 2030. This will help to secure our water supplies, support economic growth and end sewage entering our rivers and seas."

A New Mexico court has ordered Instagram and Facebook parent company Meta to pay $567 million to address harms to young people from its platforms in the second phase of a landmark trial the social media giant lost in March.

In a ruling late Thursday, Judge Bryan Biedcheid said the bulk of the money — $420 million — will be used for treatment services for young people. The rest will go toward awareness and prevention, screening services and other costs over the next five years.

In the first phase, jurors had ordered $375 million in civil penalties against Meta, determining that it knowingly harmed children’s mental health and concealed what it knew about child sexual exploitation on its platforms.

In the second phase, prosecutors had asked the judge to impose fundamental changes at Meta aimed at reining in addictive features, improving age verification and preventing child sexual exploitation through default privacy settings and closer oversight.

The court said federal children’s privacy laws prevent Meta from applying age-verification tools to children under 13. The Children’s Online Privacy Act, or COPPA, means it cannot order Meta to request children to submit personal data or be passively tracked online, even for age verification purposes.

The court also noted that ordering Meta to verify children’s ages for only Meta and not other social media companies would be “inequitable and unduly injurious” to the company.

The Associated Press has reached out to New Mexico’s Department of Justice and Meta for comment on the decision.

News.title: Lindsay Clancy breaks down during trial as jurors view 8-month-old’s autopsy photos
News.content:
The latest headlines from our reporters across the US sent straight to your inbox each weekday Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

Lindsay Clancy sobbed uncontrollably Thursday as jurors were shown autopsy photos of her youngest child, whom prosecutors say she strangled in 2023, prompting the court to take an unscheduled break.

During the second week of her Massachusetts murder trial, prosecutors called additional witnesses, including friends, a former colleague and her former father-in-law, to testify about Clancy’s mental and emotional state. Many described her as open about her struggles with postpartum mental health issues while portraying her as a devoted mother who cared for her children.

Prosecutors are seeking to prove that the 35-year-old former labor and delivery nurse acted deliberately and should be held criminally responsible. Clancy’s defense argues she was experiencing postpartum psychosis, a rare and severe psychiatric condition that can cause a loss of connection with reality after childbirth.

Clancy has pleaded not guilty to charges in the deaths of Cora, 5, Dawson, 3 and Callan, 8 months, who were killed on Jan. 24, 2023, after she sent her husband out on errands. Prosecutors allege the trip was a plan to remove him from the home before the killings. Clancy remains paralyzed from the waist down after jumping from a second-story window of the family’s home that night.

open image in gallery CORRECCIÓN Juicio de Lindsay Clancy ( David L Ryan/The Boston Globe via AP )

A friend recalls a difficult reunion after the killings

None of the witnesses Thursday testified they heard Clancy express suicidal or homicidal thoughts. However, after the birth of her third child, she told them of trouble sleeping and harmful side effects from medications. She text-messaged one childhood friend to say medication had “caused her to have some dark thoughts.”

Amy Bevins visited Clancy in a rehabilitation facility after the killings. The two made small talk, she said, and played a game. When asked by prosecutors if Clancy brought up her children or cried about them, she said she had not.

But on cross-examination by Clancy's defense attorney, Bevins acknowledged the meeting was “awkward” and that Clancy's sister had said not to bring up the kids.

Lindsay Clancy's former father-in-law takes the stand

Christopher Clancy testified that he knew his then-daughter-in-law was having issues. At one point, he suggested the grandchildren stay with him and his wife, but his son declined.

“I knew she was having a hard time sleeping,” Christopher Clancy said. “I knew she just didn’t feel well. I knew she went to the emergency room where my wife was working. Those types of struggles.”

Clancy’s lawyers don’t dispute that she killed the children. But in the criminal trial and a medical malpractice lawsuit, her attorneys say she had bipolar disorder that wasn’t fully diagnosed until after the killings. Her attorneys say her condition seemed to worsen on the psychiatric medications, some of them problematic for bipolar patients.

If convicted of murder, Lindsay Clancy faces life in prison without parole. If found not guilty due to a lack of criminal responsibility, she would be committed to a state mental health facility.

open image in gallery If convicted of murder, Lindsay Clancy faces life in prison without parole ( CJ Gunther/The Boston Herald via AP )

Another case that echoes Clancy’s is going back to court

Meanwhile, the judge and the district attorney learned Thursday that they face a retrial in another case involving a mother’s mental state when she killed her two school-age children in 2018.

Massachusetts’ top court threw out Latarsha Sanders’ murder conviction in the stabbings of sons Edson “Marlon” Brito, 8, and La’son Brito, 5.

Sanders told police in a recorded interview that she stabbed the boys because “bad people” text-messaged her commands to carry out a “ritual” connected to “Voodoo stuff” and the Illuminati. The latter is a purported powerful secret society at the center of various conspiracy theories, and Sanders’ family said she had become obsessively fearful of it.

Like Clancy’s lawyers, Sanders’ defense argued she was mentally ill and shouldn’t be held criminally responsible, while prosecutors said she acted deliberately. Prosecutors noted that Sanders tried to clean up the bloody crime scene, initially denied killing the children, and had written, in a disjointed personal notebook, about wanting to write books and become famous.

A defense neuropsychologist diagnosed Sanders with schizophrenia spectrum disorder, among other conditions, and testified that she was “grossly psychotic” when she killed the children.

The appeal turns on psychiatric evidence

The neuropsychologist was allowed to mention that he’d reviewed her medical records. But the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court faulted the judge for not letting jurors hear many specifics from the records, in which clinicians at a prison and a psychiatric hospital suggested similar diagnoses after Sanders’ arrest.

The doctors also noted that Sanders said she’d heard voices for decades, reported ongoing delusional and paranoid thoughts, and displayed odd behavior, such as licking windows.

Withholding the records from jurors “impermissibly stripped” the defense of its medical foundation, Justice Frank M. Gaziano wrote in a unanimous decision.

A message seeking comment was sent to a spokesperson for Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz, and messages were left for the judge, Superior Court Justice William Sullivan, through the court system.

Sanders’ lawyer, Robert F. Shaw Jr., welcomed the opinion and said he looked forward to retrying the case.

“The hope is that those records and that evidence will be able to be viewed by a jury with fresh eyes,” he said by phone. Sanders is in prison, and he hadn’t yet been able to meet with her to discuss the court ruling.

Her relatives told the Boston Globe last year that they hoped Clancy’s trial would generate more public scrutiny of Sanders’ case.

If you are based in the USA, and you or someone you know needs mental health assistance right now, call or text 988, or visit 988lifeline.org to access online chat from the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. This is a free, confidential crisis hotline that is available to everyone 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

If you are experiencing feelings of distress, or are struggling to cope, you can speak to the Samaritans, in confidence, on 116 123 (UK and ROI) or visit the Samaritans website to find details of your nearest branch.

If you are in another country, you can go to www.befrienders.org to find a helpline near you.

A woman who was hospitalized with sepsis has sued Chipotle after eating a burrito bowl she claims had salmonella-linked jalapeño peppers.

Kristen Behne got sick after eating at a Chipotle restaurant in Roseville, Minnesota, on June 24, her lawsuit claims.

“Three days later she was in a hospital bed, febrile, tachycardic, and septic—a life-threatening complication of the Salmonella infection caused by Chipotle’s grossly contaminated food,” read a lawsuit filed on Behne’s behalf against the Mexican food chain Wednesday.

Federal health officials have linked a recent Salmonella outbreak to jalapeño peppers from Mexico that were distributed to Mexican restaurants in the US, including Chipotle and Qdoba.

As of Wednesday, 345 people from 27 states have been infected with the outbreak strain of Salmonella, and there have been 36 hospitalizations, according to data collected by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Minnesota and Colorado have been hit the hardest, with more than 100 cases each. There have been no outbreak-related deaths reported.

open image in gallery A woman who was hospitalized with sepsis has sued Chipotle after eating a burrito bowl she claims had salmonella-linked jalapeño peppers ( Getty Images )

The Food and Drug Administration says people were infected with the foodborne bacteria for about a month starting on June 19. Of the nearly 200 people that officials interviewed, 93 percent reported eating at a Mexican restaurant before getting sick, including Chipotle and Qdoba, according to officials.

Behne’s lawsuit claims that she was one of the people “poisoned” by Chipotle. Her lawyers argue that the Salmonella sample recovered from her body matched the strain that caused the outbreak.

“Ms. Behne did nothing wrong. She could not have inspected her food for Salmonella; the pathogen is invisible, odorless, and tasteless,” the lawsuit read. “She was entitled to rely—and did rely—on Chipotle’s representations that the food it prepared and sold was safe to eat. Those representations were false.”

Chipotle switched its jalapeño supplier for the stores that were impacted by the outbreak starting on July 20, and Qdoba also stopped serving the peppers about a week later.

“The health and safety of our guests and employees is our highest priority,” Chipotle said in a statement Wednesday.

The company said it has a “robust ingredient traceability system and, upon learning of a potential Salmonella outbreak in the supply chain impacting wholesalers and restaurants,” it identified the affected jalapeños, “proactively removed them from the restaurants where they had been distributed, and replaced them with product from different growers.”

The FDA says it does not believe there is an ongoing risk from Chipotle and Qdoba because they removed the affected jalapeños. The Independent has reached out to Chipotle and a lawyer representing Behne for comment.

open image in gallery Over 300 people have been infected with Salmonella from jalapeño peppers sourced from Mexico, according to federal health officials ( Getty Images )

Common symptoms of salmonella infection are watery diarrhea, stomach cramps and fever. But there are also more severe symptoms, and patients could have long-term complications.

On June 27, Behne started getting symptoms such as fever, chills and vomiting, according to the lawsuit. She lost consciousness at one point and had a temperature of 102 degrees, her lawyers said.

The next day, Behne “experienced more than ten episodes of diarrhea in a twenty-four-hour period,” the lawsuit said.

She was admitted to the hospital on June 28 and discharged two days later.

But Behne “continues to experience the effects of her acute Salmonella infection and her septic episode,” and she is “at increased risk” of complications, including reactive arthritis and post-infectious irritable bowel syndrome, according to the lawsuit.

The lawsuit seeks more than $75,000 in compensatory damages.

People are also seeking legal action against Taco Bell amid the cyclospora outbreak that has infected more than 10,000 people across the country this summer.

More than 500 infected people have been hospitalized, and two patients with underlying medical conditions have died, according to officials. Federal health officials have linked the outbreak to Taylor Farms’ iceberg lettuce sourced from Mexico and sold at Taco Bell.

The Justice Department has accused Duke University's law school of illegally considering race in its admissions process, marking the latest action by the administration against higher education institutions.

In a findings letter sent to the school, the department alleged that while administrators publicly claimed to be race-neutral in admissions, they utilized other factors as proxies for race. These included personal essays and whether an applicant was a first-generation college student.

Duke University, located in Durham, North Carolina, stated in an emailed response that it is reviewing the letter and remains committed to adhering to the law "in a manner that is consistent with our academic mission."

Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the DOJ's Civil Rights Division emphasized the department's stance in a news release, stating, "Duke Law School doesn’t get a free pass to discriminate against white and Asian students simply because it thinks it has good intentions." Dhillon added, "Using ‘diversity’ essay questions to identify preferred races for admission is still illegal discrimination based on race."

The Trump administration previously targeted undergraduate admissions at selective colleges, demanding they collect data to show they are complying with the Supreme Court ruling ( Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images )

Affirmative action in college admissions has been illegal since a 2023 Supreme Court ruling. The same ruling said colleges could continue to assess how applicants’ backgrounds might speak to broader characteristics, but President Donald Trump has repeatedly accused colleges of using other proxies to maintain racial diversity, which conservatives view as illegal discrimination.

The department recently found that the medical schools at Yale University and the University of California, Los Angeles, illegally considered race in admissions. It announced in June that it was launching similar investigations into 15 other medical schools.

The Trump administration previously targeted undergraduate admissions at selective colleges, demanding they collect data to show they are complying with the Supreme Court ruling.

In its findings against Duke Law, the DOJ said Black or Hispanic applicants were much more likely to be admitted than white or Asian applicants with the same academic credentials. Further, it said, in 2024 and 2025, the median Law School Admissions Test scores of rejected white and Asian applicants exceeded the median scores of admitted Black applicants.

The department said it was seeking to reach a settlement with Duke Law.

A chief executive running a Southern California homelessness and domestic violence non-profit reportedly received more than $1.6 million in compensation over two years while residing thousands of miles away in Hawaii.

The earnings for Carol Adelkoff, who has led the 1736 Family Crisis Center since 1984, significantly surpass those of executive directors running similar or much larger organizations in the region, according to tax records reviewed by the Los Angeles Times.

Federal tax filings show Adelkoff earned $742,181 in 2024. The prior year, she received $907,923, which included a $495,000 bonus that exceeded her base salary. Before 2023, her annual base pay had hovered around $405,000.

Responding to inquiries about the compensation, Adelkoff said the elevated numbers were driven by a payout for unused vacation days accumulated during her four-decade tenure at the organization.

“It was simply a matter of reducing accrued vacation liability on the books and paying it out,” Adelkoff said, adding that “the salary didn’t jump like that.”

A chief executive running Southern California non-profit 1736 Family Crisis Center reportedly received more than $1.6 million in compensation over a two-year period while residing thousands of miles away in Hawaii ( Google Earth )

Kerry Garvis Wright, an attorney representing the center, confirmed in a letter that the non-profit’s board worked with financial and legal advisors to reduce the accrued liability before Adelkoff’s retirement, according to the Los Angeles Times. Wright noted that the 2024 tax filings were being amended to clarify that $329,243 of her pay stemmed from vacation distribution.

Wright explained that the expanding geographic scale and operational complexity of the non-profit made taking time off difficult for the chief executive.

“As a result, over the course of the decades she served the organization, her vacation pay accrued substantially,” Wright wrote.

The payouts have raised concerns among non-profit governance and accounting experts.

Outside analysts said that while vacation cash-outs were common when an employee departed an organization, substantial payouts to active executives were highly unusual. Standard practice among California non-profits typically caps accrued vacation time to 1.5 times an employee’s annual allotment.

“It’s an unusual benefit,” Marc Owens, a lawyer who previously directed the IRS division regulating non-profits, told the publication. “The amount is stunningly large.”

Brian Mittendorf, an accounting expert at Ohio State University who reviewed the filings, questioned the precedent.

“The bigger question is, was it appropriate for a person to be able to accrue that much money and suddenly get it paid out?” Mittendorf told the newspaper.

Laurie Styron, CEO of the watchdog group CharityWatch, described the arrangement as “highly unusual” and questioned how the board reached its decision.

The 1736 Family Crisis Center relies almost entirely on public funding, with 94 percent of its revenue originating from government grants. Since 2021, it has secured at least $25 million from the Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority. Overall revenue for the non-profit stood at $13 million in 2023, down from a peak of $18 million in 2021.

Despite operating approximately 16 facilities across Los Angeles and Orange counties, Adelkoff has maintained her primary residence on the Big Island of Hawaii for at least 11 years, according to property records and court testimony. Property records show she acquired the residence in 2002 after selling a home in Los Angeles County.

Adelkoff declined to confirm her state of residency to reporters, citing security precautions related to working with domestic violence survivors.

Wright stated that the board explicitly requested Adelkoff remain as CEO following her relocation in 2002, writing, “The organization has clearly thrived under her caring leadership.”

Governance structures at the organization have also drawn attention. Five of the board’s members have served for more than 14 years, a tenure duration that governance experts caution can compromise board independence.

Additionally, Board President Ron Troupe has collected an annual salary ranging from $30,000 to $97,500 since 2005 despite not being an operational employee, a rarity among non-profit boards, which typically consist of unpaid volunteers.

“The board’s No. 1 rule is to oversee the organization and it’s hard to do that if the decisions you make directly affect your pay,” Styron told the Los Angeles Times.

Troupe declined to share board meeting minutes or compensation studies, stating that internal board documentation was private.

The Independent has contacted the 1736 Family Crisis Center for comment.
