The El Economista newspaper reported on Wednesday, Aug. 5, that the appreciation of the peso, after closing at 17.26 on Aug. 4, was “supported by a greater appetite for risk” as currency traders remained “attentive to news about a possible [peace] agreement in the Middle East,” where the United States and Iran have been at war since late February.

Key numerical takeaways from the changes in the USD:MXN exchange rate this century

Between Dec. 29, 2000 and Aug. 5, 2026 — this century, in other words — the Mexican peso depreciated 44.3%.

Put differently, the US dollar appreciated 79.6% between the end of 2000 and Aug. 5, 2026.

The difference between the highest USD:MXN rate this century (25.12) and the lowest (8.94) is 16.18 pesos.

Between May 21, 2001, the day the USD:MXN rate was 8.94, and March 24, 2020, the day that the USD:MXN rate was 25.12, the peso depreciated 64.4%.

The appreciation of the US dollar between May 21, 2001 and March 24, 2020, was 181%.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: Dozens of UK cyclosporiasis victims had vacationed at Riviera Maya resorts
World.content:
Mexico is tightening health surveillance at more than a dozen hotels in Cancún and the Riviera Maya after the United Kingdom reported dozens of cases of cyclosporiasis in travelers, most of whom had recently stayed at all‑inclusive resorts in the state of Quintana Roo.

At the same time, Mexican officials are saying the country is not facing a domestic outbreak, nor has it been identified as the source of more than 10,000 laboratory-confirmed cyclosporiasis cases reported in the U.S. and 67 infections in British travelers.

Mensaje del secretario de Salud, David Kershenobich: Es importante mencionar que los casos de ciclosporiasis que existen actualmente en México representan el 0.00002% de la población, lo que significa que no tenemos un brote activo. pic.twitter.com/UN0wC6qmcH — SALUD México (@SSalud_mx) August 6, 2026

The Health Ministry has confirmed 33 cases of cyclosporiasis in 13 Mexican states between May 25 and July 31 and opened investigations into possible links with U.S. and U.K. infection reports.

Health Minister David Kershenobich said in a video posted Thursday that detected cases represent just 0.00002% of Mexico’s population. He also stressed that Cyclospora cayetanensis infections “are recurrent worldwide” and that there is no scientific evidence to date that Mexico is the origin of the outbreak.

The ministry, working with the Federal Commission for Protection against Sanitary Risks (Cofepris) and the General Directorate of Epidemiology (DGE), has deployed five inspection teams to 16 hotels in Quintana Roo.

The inspections follows a July 30 UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) alert reporting 67 cyclosporiasis cases between April 30 and July 15, with 48 of 51 patients who provided travel information reporting trips to Mexico — mainly to the Riviera Maya and Cancún.

UKHSA said the affected travelers stayed in “a range of different hotels” and consumed varied food and drink in all‑inclusive packages — emphasizing that investigations have not identified any single hotel or product as the source.

In response, Mexican inspectors conducted field visits this week in Quintana Roo during which they collected samples of food, water, fruits and vegetables, according to a Ministry of Health press release.

Laboratory analyses are still in process and authorities say results will be released when testing is complete.

Meanwhile, Mexican authorities are cooperating with U.S. counterparts on a multistate outbreak that officials say has sickened more than 10,000 people and is linked to shredded iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms de Mexico, grown in the central state of Guanajuato and distributed to Taco Bell and other outlets.

Product testing has not yielded any confirmed positive samples, though inspections are ongoing.

In tourist zones in Quintana Roo and elsewhere, Mexico’s Health Ministry has expanded surveillance, reinforced food safety protocols and reminded travelers and residents to wash and disinfect fruits and vegetables, drink potable water and seek medical attention for persistent diarrhea, especially after travel.

Officials also stress that identifying a country as a preliminary origin of a product under investigation “does not, in itself, constitute evidence that the contamination occurred in that place,” and say epidemiological work will continue until conclusive findings are available.

Cyclosporiasis is an intestinal infection usually acquired by eating or drinking contaminated food or water. Symptoms include watery “explosive diarrhea,” stomach cramps, nausea, loss of appetite, fatigue and low‑grade fever.

The 33 patients diagnosed in Mexico remain under observation; no deaths linked to the infection have been reported in Mexico.

With reports from El País, Infobae La Silla Rota and El Heraldo de México

World.title: An American is caught fleeing to the US border after fatal shootings in Saltillo
World.content:
A Texas man is accused of murdering three people in the northern state of Coahuila and then fleeing with his 3-year-old son toward the United States, before being arrested while trying to cross the border.

The suspect, identified as Chad Eberle, a former police officer, allegedly shot and killed two women and a man while seriously wounding another woman inside a home in the Espinoza Mireles neighborhood of Saltillo, the Coahuila state capital, on Tuesday afternoon.

The Coahuila Attorney General’s Office (FGE) said the suspect was apprehended at the Piedras Negras border crossing in his gray Chevrolet Silverado around five hours after the shooting.

The child was retrieved uninjured and was placed under the protection of the Office of the Attorney for Children and Families.

According to initial reports, Eberle arrived at 1221 José Espinoza Fuente Street around 3 p.m. Inside were his ex-partner Litzy Mora (26 years old), her sister Laura Jaquelín (22) and their parents Ana Laura (44) and Emanuel (44), as well as 3-year-old Benjamin.

Eberle, who had a restraining order against him due to accusations of domestic violence and was legally prohibited from seeing his son, demanded to see the boy.

ACTUALIZACIÓN | MULTIHOMICIDIO EN SALTILLO La Fiscalía General del Estado informa que, dentro de la Causa Penal 547/2026JEVF, la Autoridad Judicial giró Orden de Aprehensión en contra de Chad N, por su probable responsabilidad en los delitos de feminicidio y homicidio… pic.twitter.com/hBLpZu42FY — Federico Fernández (@FedericoFdzMx) August 5, 2026

When Litzy refused to let him inside the house, Eberle took out a gun and shot all four adults before fleeing with Benjamin.

An hour later, relatives of the victims forced their way into the house and immediately called 911.

Paramedics found Litzy still alive with a gunshot wound to the head and rushed her to a hospital where doctors said she remains in critical condition. The other three members of the family were declared dead at the scene.

The authorities were able to identify the alleged perpetrator and his vehicle by reviewing security camera footage from nearby homes and businesses, and quickly mobilized a manhunt that included state police, FGE agents, the National Guard and both the Army and the Marines.

Within half-an-hour, the suspect was located about 170 kilometers north headed toward the U.S. border. As he had already passed the Castaños, Coahuila, checkpoint, U.S. Customs and Border Patrol was advised of the situation.

State police established a security perimeter as Eberle approached Piedras Negras and notified U.S. officials. When the suspect got to the border, CBP officers assisted in apprehending him.

The 35-year-old former policeman was then handed over to the FGE for prosecution.

With reports from Zócalo, Univision, La Jornada and Milenio

World.title: US suspends avocado imports from Mexico over unspecified ‘threat against US interests’
World.content:
The U.S. government has once again suspended avocado certifications in Michoacán, paralyzing exports of the fruit to the U.S. market.

The U.S. Embassy announced on Wednesday that activities conducted by U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) staff in the western state were to be temporarily halted, citing “a threat against U.S. interests.”

El gobernador de Michoacán, Alfredo Ramírez Bedolla, afirmó que la suspensión de las certificaciones para exportar aguacate a EE.UU. responde a una medida preventiva de seguridad y confió en que sea temporal. https://t.co/Z9gKKNCb7F pic.twitter.com/xWSA3dPyhF — Aristegui Noticias (@AristeguiOnline) August 6, 2026

The embassy statement did not specify the nature, location or target of that threat, but its mention was immediately followed by a “reminder” that a Level 4 travel advisory (“do not travel”) for Michoacán is still in effect due to terrorism and crime. The State Department has also restricted the movement of U.S. government employees through that state which lies in a region in which four cartels designated as terrorist organizations operate.

The announcement comes in the context of a renewed U.S. effort to “degrade” the powerful Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) as part of U.S. President Donald Trump’s “mission to eliminate narco-terrorist cartels threatening the American people.”

In a related move, Michoacán Governor Alfredo Ramírez Bedolla ordered an additional 300 security operatives to deploy to the avocado-growing region of the state “as a preventive measure.” Then, on Thursday morning, the Defense Ministry announced it had sent more than 1,500 soldiers to the state to “protect avocado producers and packing plants in the region.”

This marks the third time in just over four years that avocado exports have been suspended for security reasons.

In February 2022, inspections were paused for almost a week after a U.S. official working in Uruapan received a threat on his official phone. In June 2024, Washington suspended avocado and mango inspections in Michoacán after two USDA employees were assaulted and temporarily detained while performing official duties.

The latest suspension directly impacts Michoacán’s US $3.65 billion avocado export industry, which employs more than 200,000 people.

After the U.S. Embassy announcement, Gov. Ramírez Bedolla said the temporary halt to inspections was intended to safeguard workers following recent arrests linked to extortion. In a social media post, he said his administration is working with U.S. officials to restore security conditions and “to address any concerns and ensure the swift restoration of operations, always safeguarding the development and tranquility of Michoacán.”

At the same time, the Association of Avocado Producers and Exporters (APEAM) sent its Board of Directors and its CEO to Mexico City to meet with authorities and seek measures to address the situation so as to reduce the impact on the industry.

According to APEAM, 127,000 tons of avocados were shipped to the United States in January, exceeding the 114,000 tons exported during the same month in 2025.

With reports from EFE, NBC News, CNN and Reuters

World.title: Cincinnati Open 2026 Guide: Dates, Players and What to Know
World.content:
The Cincinnati Open returns to Mason, Ohio, this August with one of the strongest combined men’s and women’s fields of the North American hard-court season. The tournament begins with public events and player practices on August 8 before qualifying starts August 11. Main-draw competition begins August 13, with the men’s and women’s singles champions scheduled to be crowned August 23.

Played at the Lindner Family Tennis Center outside Cincinnati, the tournament brings ATP and WTA competition together at the same venue. Both sides carry 1000-level status, placing Cincinnati among the most important events outside the four Grand Slam tournaments.

It also represents one of the final major tests before the US Open, giving players an opportunity to adjust to North American hard courts, earn significant ranking points and build momentum before traveling to New York.

When Does the Cincinnati Open Begin?

The 2026 Cincinnati Open officially opens with Community Weekend on August 8 and 9. The two-day program includes player practices, autograph opportunities, children’s activities, entertainment and the tournament’s inaugural 5K race. A fast-paced Red Bull BassLine exhibition is also scheduled for Saturday evening.

Fans will have another opportunity to watch open practices on Monday, August 10, before competitive matches begin. Qualifying will take place August 11 and 12. The men’s and women’s qualifying draws will each feature 48 players, with 12 men and 12 women advancing into the main tournament.

Main-draw play begins Thursday, August 13. Day sessions are scheduled to start at 11 a.m., with night sessions beginning at 7 p.m. during the early rounds. The singles finals will both be played Sunday, August 23.

Which Players Are Expected to Compete?

World No. 1 Jannik Sinner leads the men’s field and will attempt to regain the Cincinnati title he won in 2024. The Italian is joined by several of the sport’s biggest names, including Alexander Zverev, Novak Djokovic, Daniil Medvedev, Ben Shelton, Taylor Fritz, Alex de Minaur and Frances Tiafoe.

Defending champion Carlos Alcaraz will not compete. The Spaniard withdrew on August 4 as he continues to recover from a wrist injury. The withdrawal removes one of the tournament’s leading attractions, but the men’s field remains deep. Cincinnati has also awarded main-draw wild cards to Stan Wawrinka, Grigor Dimitrov, Jack Draper and Gael Monfils.

Wawrinka and Monfils are both competing in their final ATP seasons, adding another storyline to the opening rounds. Dimitrov won the Cincinnati title in 2017, while Draper has already established himself as a dangerous opponent on hard courts. The women’s tournament is led by Aryna Sabalenka, Iga Swiatek, Coco Gauff and Jessica Pegula.

Other prominent entries include Madison Keys, Elena Rybakina, Naomi Osaka, Mirra Andreeva, Linda Noskova and Jasmine Paolini.One of the tournament’s biggest attractions will come in doubles, where Serena and Venus Williams have received a wild card to compete together. It will be their first Cincinnati Open appearance as a team.

Venus Williams has also been awarded a singles wild card. Other women’s wild-card recipients include Sloane Stephens, Taylor Townsend, Caroline Dolehide and Lois Boisson. Player entries remain subject to change until the draws are finalized.

Latin American Players to Follow

The men’s field includes a sizable Latin American presence, led by Brazilian João Fonseca and Argentina’s Francisco Cerúndolo. Fonseca has quickly become one of the region’s most closely followed young players. His aggressive baseline game and growing international profile should make his matches among the most anticipated of the early rounds.

Cerúndolo arrives as Argentina’s highest-ranked entrant and one of the region’s strongest candidates to make a deep run. Argentina will also be represented by Sebastián Báez, Juan Manuel Cerúndolo, Tomás Martín Etcheverry, Mariano Navone, Román Andrés Burruchaga, Thiago Tirante and Camilo Ugo Carabelli.

Peruvian Ignacio Buse, Chilean Alejandro Tabilo and Paraguayan Adolfo Daniel Vallejo are also listed in the men’s field. On the women’s side, Colombia’s Camila Osorio will be the leading Latin American player in the main draw. Additional players from the region could join her through qualifying.

The strength of the Latin American contingent gives fans throughout the region several players to follow beyond the tournament’s established global stars.

Why Cincinnati Matters Before the US Open

The Cincinnati Open is more than another stop on the summer tennis calendar. Its position immediately before the US Open makes it an important measure of player form. The conditions in Ohio can be hot and humid, and the hard courts reward players who can control points quickly while remaining physically strong through long matches.

A strong week in Cincinnati can change expectations entering New York. It can also expose injury concerns, fatigue or tactical weaknesses at the most important stage of the season. The expanded men’s and women’s singles draws provide additional opportunities for emerging players, qualifiers and lower-ranked entrants to face the sport’s biggest names.

For established contenders, however, Cincinnati is about more than preparation. An ATP or WTA 1000 title carries considerable ranking value and is one of the most prestigious trophies available outside the Grand Slams.

A Transformed Tournament Venue

The Lindner Family Tennis Center completed a $260 million redevelopment before the 2025 tournament. The project expanded and modernized the grounds, adding new courts, improved stadiums, park-style landscaping, additional shade, upgraded fan areas and a new player clubhouse.

The transformation helped the Cincinnati Open earn both the ATP Masters 1000 and WTA 1000 Tournament of the Year awards following the 2025 event. The venue now has 31 outdoor tennis courts, giving spectators more opportunities to watch matches and practices at close range.

When Will the Draw Be Released?

The qualifying and main draws are expected closer to the beginning of competition. Once the draws are published, fans will know each player’s potential route through the tournament, possible early-round matchups and where the leading Latin American players have been placed.

The daily order of play will then determine match times and court assignments. The Tico Times will provide on-site coverage and photography from the Cincinnati Open beginning August 13, with particular attention to Latin American players, major tournament storylines and the final preparations for the US Open.

World.title: Department of Environment investigating fish kill in Belize River Valley, public urged to avoid untreated river water
World.content:
Department of Environment investigating fish kill in Belize River Valley, public urged to avoid untreated river water

By Zoila Palma: The Department of the Environment (DOE) is investigating a fish kill reported in the Belize River Valley and has issued a public advisory warning residents not to consume fish or other aquatic resources from affected areas while the investigation continues.

The Ministry of Sustainable Development, Climate Change and Solid Waste Management said the DOE received reports on August 4 of numerous dead fish floating along sections of the Belize River, prompting a multi-agency response.

According to the department, a joint assessment was launched involving Belize Water Services Limited (BWS), the Ministry of Health and Wellness, the National Emergency Management Organization (NEMO), the Fisheries Department, the Ministry of Infrastructure Development and Housing (MIDH), and other relevant agencies.

The release stated that “the Department is actively responding to the ongoing fish kill issue reported in the Belize River Valley area.”

DOE said the exercise included “water quality monitoring and sampling, as well as assessments of land-clearing activities, potential wastewater discharge sources, and other factors that may have contributed to impacts on the aquatic environment.”

As investigations continue, the DOE is advising residents to take precautionary measures.

The department warned the public “not to consume fish or other aquatic resources from the affected areas and not to drink untreated river water or use untreated river water for cooking or food preparation.” It also advised against using untreated river water for livestock or pets until further notice.

The department emphasized that the advisory applies only to untreated water taken directly from the river and does not affect the public water supply.

The release noted that “BWS has confirmed that the water currently being supplied from its Water Treatment Plant remains safe for consumption and meets the required potable water quality standards. There has been no disruption to the continuity of the water supply.”

DOE noted that technical assessments are ongoing to determine the cause of the fish kill and pledged to keep the public informed as new information becomes available.

The DOE also reminded the public that the release of untreated wastewater, or treated effluent that fails to meet environmental standards, is prohibited under Belize’s Environmental Protection Regulations and constitutes an offence.

World.title: The case for Allan Pollard, measured the way a city should measure a mayor
World.content:
The case for Allan Pollard, measured the way a city should measure a mayor

By Horace Palacio:

The People’s United Party will soon ask its Belize City delegates a single question. Who should carry its banner for mayor in 2027, Councillor Allan Pollard Jr. or Deputy Mayor Eluide Miller?

Today I am going to answer that question openly, and make the case for Pollard. But I will make it the way this column has always insisted arguments be made, on the record, with respect for both men, and by a standard bigger than either of them.

Because before we compare two candidates, remember what the prize actually is. Belize City is not a title. It is the largest, hardest job in municipal government in this country. Flooding that swallows streets. Drains that fail. Garbage that piles. Traffic that strangles. Crime that shadows whole neighborhoods. Whoever wins this convention inherits all of it. So the question for delegates is not who do you like. It is who is readiest, this March, for that load.

Measure the two men by that standard, and the case builds itself on four pillars.

Pillar one. The record. Allan Pollard has served the people of Belize City as an elected councillor for eight years, across three terms, including service as deputy mayor. Eluide Miller, a capable young man, has served two. That is not an insult to Miller. It is arithmetic. Pollard has sat through four times the budgets, four times the floods, four times the hard seasons of that council. He has already held the deputy’s chair Miller holds now, and then kept serving. The city’s problems are too old and too heavy for the top job to double as a classroom. Experience is not everything, but in a crisis city, it is not nothing either. It is the difference between learning the machine and driving it.

Pillar two. Character, tested in the dark. Here is the part of Pollard’s story that tells you more than any manifesto. In 2023, he wanted this same candidacy. The party asked him to step aside for unity’s sake. He swallowed his ambition and did it. Reports say the Prime Minister personally assured him his patience would be honored this cycle. Now, let me be precise about why this matters, because it is not the reason some think. I have written before that no seat in Belize should be awarded by turn, only by merit, and I stand by every word. Pollard does not deserve the candidacy because he waited. He deserves consideration because of what the waiting revealed. A man who can put the team above his own ambition, keep working for three more years without sulking, and return stronger, has shown you his character under the hardest test politics offers, the test of being told no. Most politicians fail that test loudly. Pollard passed it quietly. That is the temperament you want holding a city’s purse and pressure.

Pillar three. Whose hands hold him. Look carefully at the two campaign launches, because launches are confessions. Miller announced flanked by seven fellow councillors, the establishment closing ranks, with the outgoing mayor reportedly grooming him as successor. Pollard arrived with no councillors at all, just a crowd of ordinary city people, family, friends, supporters he did not have to summon. One candidacy was born in the council chamber. The other was born on the street. And a mayor, understand, does not answer to the chamber. He answers to the street. Give me the candidate the people carry over the candidate the machine crowns, every single time. It is also worth noting what Pollard said about that machine, that he wants the door open to new faces, talented people, older, younger, business people, and that whoever the delegates elect to the slate gets his full backing. That is a builder’s posture, not a boss’s.

Pillar four. The money question. There is a figure floating around this race, two hundred dollars per delegate, the whispered price of convention support. I wrote months ago that free is the most expensive thing in Belize, that every bought vote is a purchase the politician later recoups from the public. So hear what Pollard put on the record when the figure was raised. He does not pay for delegates. His relationships with them were built over years of showing up, and, in his words, that is something money cannot buy. A candidate who refuses to buy his way in owes nothing on his way up. That single stance, publicly planted, is worth more to this city than any promise on any flyer. And let me be crystal clear in fairness, no evidence before me says Miller pays for delegates, and I make no such claim. I simply issue the challenge this column must issue. Mr. Miller, plant the same flag, publicly, and let this be the first convention in memory where both camps swear off the wallet and compete on the work.

Now, the fairness Miller is owed, because this endorsement will not be built on his burial.

Eluide Miller has done something in this race that deserves genuine applause. When party heavyweights reportedly leaned on him to step aside and clear the path, he refused, and insisted the delegates decide. That is democratic spine, and it is exactly what I have preached in these pages, conventions over coronations, always. Both camps, let us be honest, have maneuvered behind the scenes in this contest, which is precisely why the convention itself is the clean answer. Miller is young, described even by neutrals in the party as energetic and creative, and if he loses this race well, his future in city politics is real. The party leader himself says both men have talent, and he is right.

But talent is the entry fee, not the verdict. The verdict comes from the standard we set at the start. Which man, this March, is readiest for the hardest municipal job in Belize?

Eight years against two. A deputy mayor’s chair already held, then exceeded. Ambition tested by sacrifice and passed. A campaign carried by the street rather than crowned by the chamber. And a public refusal to purchase what should only be earned. On the record before the delegates, that is Allan Pollard’s case, and it is a strong one.

So to the delegates who will file into that convention, I close with this. You hold a privilege thousands of city residents wish they held. Do not sell it, to anyone. Do not lend it to pressure, from anyone. Weigh the records, question both men hard, and choose the readiest hands.

Weighed that way, honestly and without malice, my case is made.

The city’s next chapter should be written by the man who spent eight years learning to hold the pen.

The views expressed in this article are those of the author, Horace Palacio, and do not necessarily reflect the views or editorial stance of Breaking Belize News.

World.title: Prime Minister meets with stakeholders in sugar industry to discuss mealbug infestation
World.content:
Prime Minister meets with stakeholders in sugar industry to discuss mealbug infestation

By Zoila Palma: Today, Prime Minister John Briceno met with stakeholders in the sugar industry to discuss the mealbug infestation.

In addition, the PM also received updates on two important initiatives —CRESAP and the Building the Adaptive Capacity of Sugarcane Farmers in Northern Belize (BAC-SuF) Project.

The PM explained that financed by the Green Climate Fund and implemented by the Caribbean Community Climate Change Centre (5Cs), BAC-SuF is helping to strengthen the resilience of our sugarcane farmers and safeguard the future of this vital industry.

World.title: Cabinet Approves Amendments to Cybercrime Bill to safeguard freedom of expression
World.content:
Cabinet Approves Amendments to Cybercrime Bill to safeguard freedom of expression

By Zoila Palma: Cabinet has approved amendments to the Cybercrime Bill aimed at clarifying the scope of offences while ensuring the legislation aligns with constitutional protections for freedom of expression.

According to the Cabinet statement, the changes are intended to preserve the Government’s ability to prosecute serious forms of technology-facilitated abuse, including malicious deepfakes, online impersonation, extortion, threats, and targeted harassment.

At the same time, the amendments seek to safeguard freedom of expression, political debate, journalism, satire, and public accountability.

As part of this safeguard, the cabinet release notes that the DPP’s written consent will be required before the prosecution of an offence can occur.

This latest revision comes after concerns were raised by media organizations, civil society groups, and members of the public that earlier provisions of the Cybercrime Bill could have had unintended consequences for free speech and press freedom.

World.title: Cabinet approves US $8 million loan from Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) for efficiency of wage bill
World.content:
Cabinet approves US $8 million loan from Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) for efficiency of wage bill

By Zoila Palma: During Cabinet’s meeting on July 28th and August 4th, 2026, the Government of Belize approved entering into a loan agreement with the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) for US$8 million.

According to the cabinet release, the loan will be used to “improve the efficiency of the Central Government’s wage bill and to increase the efficacy of strategic public employment”.

The funding is expected to help improve the allocation of public resources, promote more efficient staffing across government ministries and departments, and support efforts to modernize public sector management.

The project carries a total value of US$9 million, or roughly BZ$18 million, made up of the US$8 million in IDB financing and US$1 million in local counterpart funding, and is to be implemented over a five-year disbursement period.

World.title: Cabinet approves 20.9 million dollar investment in electric buses and charging infrastructure
World.content:
Cabinet approves 20.9 million dollar investment in electric buses and charging infrastructure

By Zoila Palma: During Cabinet’s session on July 28th and August 4th, 2026, the Government of Belize approved the change of its planned investment in the National Bus Company (NBC) from “terminals to electric buses and related charging infrastructure with a value of approximately BZ$20.9 million”.

The decision will require a revised Public Transportation Investment Bill to reflect this change.

The revision will include a proposed long-term lease agreement under which the Government would lease the bus terminals to the NBC.

The move forms part of the Government’s efforts to modernize Belize’s public transportation system through the introduction of electric buses and supporting infrastructure.

World.title: Youth Shadow Mayor Begins Leadership Journey at Belize City Hall
World.content:
Youth Shadow Mayor Begins Leadership Journey at Belize City Hall

By Zoila Palma: Youth Shadow Mayor Caitlin Aragon officially began her leadership experience with the Belize City Council after being welcomed by Mayor Bernard Wagner during an introductory visit to City Hall.

As part of the visit, Aragon toured the Office of the Mayor and learned about the daily responsibilities of the Mayor’s Office and the Belize City Council’s role in serving residents and guiding the city’s development.

The initiative provides mentorship and hands-on exposure to local government, giving the Youth Shadow Mayor valuable insight into leadership and public service

World.title: Blue Teddy Bear Campaign launches teacher training to strengthen Child Protection in Belize
World.content:
Blue Teddy Bear Campaign launches teacher training to strengthen Child Protection in Belize

By Zoila Palma: The Blue Teddy Bear Campaign has launched Phase II of its national child protection initiative, expanding its efforts to equip teachers, parents, and students with the knowledge and skills needed to create safer environments for children across Belize. The new phase officially began today with teacher training sessions aimed at strengthening child safeguarding practices in schools.

The latest training brought together 22 educators from Wesley College, Excelsior High School, and Gwen Lizarraga High School. It followed an earlier session involving 60 teachers from Maud Williams High School, Anglican Cathedral College, and Sadie Vernon Technical High School. With the support of the Ministry of Education, Culture, Science and Technology, a total of 82 teachers will receive training during this phase of the campaign.

Teachers are among the most influential adults in a child’s life and often serve as the first line of defense for vulnerable children. As mandatory reporters under Belize’s child protection framework, educators play a vital role in identifying signs of abuse, taking appropriate action, and ensuring children receive the protection and support they need.

The training focuses on child protection principles, safeguarding measures, recognizing indicators of abuse, reporting obligations, and practical approaches to supporting children who may be at risk. Organizers said strengthening educators’ understanding of these areas will help ensure schools remain safe spaces where children can learn, grow, and thrive.

The Blue Teddy Bear Campaign is a partnership between the National Commission for Families and Children (NCFC), UNICEF Belize, the Ministry of Human Development, Family Support and Gender Affairs, and the Office of the Special Envoy for the Development of Families and Children. Since its launch, the campaign has promoted awareness and action to eliminate violence, abuse, and exploitation of children. Phase II builds on those efforts by focusing on adults and institutions that play a central role in children’s daily lives, reinforcing the message that protecting children is a shared national responsibility.

World.title: Market Bag: ‘Auntie Bev’ shares old-time market wisdom as prices fluctuate
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica — As Jamaica celebrates Independence Day, this week’s episode of Market Bag takes a nostalgic trip through Coronation Market, where veteran shopper Beverley Thomas Edwards shares decades of experience and the tricks and trades she uses to get the best value for her money.

From choosing produce with brighter colours and firmer textures to selecting clean, quality items, “Auntie Bev” shares tips on comparing prices and shopping wisely to make the most of every dollar.

Meanwhile, prices at Coronation Market continue to fluctuate, with sweet peppers selling for $400 per pound; ginger at $450 per pound; onions at $200 per pound; tomatoes at $200 per pound; Scotch bonnet peppers at $400 per pound; lettuce at $600 per pound; carrots at $300 per pound; and yam at $500 per pound.

Ripe bananas remain one of the more expensive commodities at the market, selling for $1,000 per hand, while plantains are priced at $900 for three.

In the latest feature, Auntie Bev and host Carlysia Ramdeen explore how market culture has evolved over the years, from informal setups of the past to the more organised stalls shoppers see today.

Catch the latest episode of Market Bag on all Jamaica Observer digital platforms.

World.title: How Dis Mek? Handcart craftsman Uriah ‘Prento’ Lawes keeps Jamaican markets moving
World.content:
Have you ever asked yourself how everyday Jamaican things that we sometimes take for granted are made?

As Jamaica celebrates Independence Day the Jamaica Observer honours the creativeness that has helped shape our culture.

Join us for a brand new series as we explore how some enduring Jamaican items that we see, eat, use and even ride come to be.

Craftsman Uriah Lawes kicks off the series with an intimate view of the making of handcarts, the workhorse at markets across Jamaica.

Also called “Prento”, the 65-year old craftsman is originally from St Catherine but honed his craft in Kingston near the Coronation and other downtown markets.

From food to transportation and even games, join us as we find out “How Dis Mek?”

(Video: Gavin Jones)

World.title: Wayne Wonder, Busy Signal to be named Reggae Icons at Grand Gala
World.content:
Among the features at this year’s Grand Gala will be a 1,000-drone show. (Photo: Rochelle Clayton)

Both Wayne Wonder and Busy Signal are the latest dancehall artistes to be recognised at the annual Independence Day Grand Gala.

This year’s event, in celebration of the nation’s 64th anniversary, will be hosted under the theme ‘United in Celebrating Resilience’.

Dancehall music has never been short of colourful characters, especially in the 1980 and 1990s when Wayne Wonder was making his name. Still, the singer says being outrageous has never been his style.

In an interview with the Jamaica Observer, Wayne Wonder, born Von wayne Charles, said: “This is special because being recognised by your country, the Government, is a blessing. It’s an honour to receive this.”

From East Kingston, he got his start on sound systems in areas like his hometown of McIntyre Villa (popularly known as Dunkirk). Wayne Wonder’s career flourished during the 1990s at Penthouse Records and Mad House Records, where he worked with producers Donovan Germain and Dave Kelly, respectively.

That era was noted for risque and violent songs by acts like Shabba Ranks and Ninja Man. There were also infamous artiste clashes at the annual Sting concert and the Bounty Killer/Beenie Man feud.

Wayne Wonder — whose hit songs include Saddest Day of My Life, Joy Ride, and No Letting Go — says avoiding confrontation has never been a problem.

“Over di years, dat’s jus’ my personality, jus’ conduct myself with principle an’ respect. A jus’ me dat bro, mi jus’ want to be a good yute an’ guh through.”

Artiste Busy Signal hails from St Ann and has been a leading figure in contemporary dancehall since 2003. His first hit single, Step Out was followed buy successful releases such as Nah Go A Jail Again, Smoke Some High Grade, Tic Toc, and Unknown Number.

In 2012, Busy Signal released his first authentic reggae album, Reggae Music Again. He is known for his energetic dancehall style and versatility, blending reggae and dancehall influences.

Busy Signal remains an influential figure in entertainment, particularly his contributions to the global music scene.

Veterans Beres Hammond, Sizzla, and Sanchez have been named Reggae Icons, as well as ska legend Derrick Morgan and reggae band Third World.

Jamaica’s 65th anniversary celebrations next year will mark the final staging of the country’s flagship national celebrations at the National Stadium in Kingston before the facility undergoes major redevelopment.

Minister of Culture, Gender, Entertainment and Sport Olivia Grange made the announcement during a post-Cabinet press briefing held at Jamaica House last week.

“Next year, we have a milestone year, Jamaica 65, and it will be the last year that our celebrations will be held at the National Stadium. After that, we will prepare for our expansion and redevelopment. But I’m just putting everyone on alert, Jamaica 65 will be a special year,” she said.

Turning to this year’s celebrations, Minister Grange said members of the public who are unable to secure tickets for the Grand Gala at the National Stadium, will still be able to enjoy the event through a special watch party at Independence Village.

She explained that the arrangement was made in response to an overwhelming demand for tickets.

“I am making a special appeal that if… we’re unable to provide you with tickets for the stadium, that you will accept the tickets we have available for Independence Village where you can be a part of the watch party,” she said.

The Gala will conclude with its customary fireworks display, alongside an expanded drone show featuring 1,000 drones, as well as a motorcycle display by the Jamaica Constabulary Force.

— Howard Campbell

World.title: ‘No court decision can erase the pain of losing a loved one’
World.content:
The entrance to The University Hospital of the West Indies in St Andrew.

THE University Hospital of the West Indies (UHWI), in acknowledging that last Friday’s judgement by the Supreme Court, which ordered it to pay millions following a medical negligence suit, “may cause concern among patients, families and the wider public”, has reaffirmed its commitment “to transparency, transformation, accountability and continuous improvement, ensuring that every opportunity to strengthen [its] systems contributes to safer, higher quality care”.

In a statement issued to the media following the publication of the judgement in the Jamaica Observer Wednesday, the UHWI said “our thoughts remain with the family, whose loss is deeply tragic”.

“We recognise that no court decision can erase the pain of losing a loved one, and we extend our sincere condolences,” the hospital said.

In the meantime, the entity said it has “in recent years taken significant steps to strengthen its clinical governance, patient safety and quality assurance systems, while investing in modern technology, digital transformation, staff development and enhanced multidisciplinary care and improved governance”.

“These improvements reflect the hospital’s ongoing commitment to continuously strengthening the quality, safety and experience of care for every patient,” the UHWI said in the statement.

At the same time, the UHWI’s legal officer Kimani Brydson said, “As is standard practice following a judgement of this nature, [the entity’s] attorneys are reviewing the court’s comprehensive written judgement”.

“As part of UHWI’s ongoing transformation and commitment to responsive, patient-centred care, we recently launched dedicated customer care channels, providing patients and their families with a direct way to ask questions, share feedback, raise concerns or make complaints. The customer care team can be reached via

WhatsApp at 658-220-2907 or by e-mail at wecare@uhwi.gov.jm,” Brydson said.

“Every day, UHWI’s physicians, nurses, allied health professionals and support teams care for thousands of Jamaicans, performing complex surgical and medical procedures, treating critically ill patients and helping many recover. That responsibility is one we carry with humility and a steadfast commitment to continuously transforming and strengthening the quality and safety of the care we provide,” the UHWI said further.

Supreme Court Justice Anne-Marie Nembhard, in handing down the judgement, said the facility “fell below the standard of care” expected of it and also “breached the duty of care” provided to a 16-year-old girl, who died six days after being admitted to the hospital in March 2018.

The teen’s parents had sued the hospital’s board of management for failing to “use all proper professional skill, care, competence, and diligence during their investigation, diagnosis, management, and treatment” of their only child.

The court on Friday awarded approximately $1.7 million “for pain and suffering” endured by the child prior to her death. For loss of life/loss of expectation of life, the court awarded just over $344,000 with interest at three per cent per annum from April 15, 2021 to July 31 this year. In assessing how much the child, who was described as “a perennial high achiever”, would have lost in terms of earnings from before the trial to the last hearing date, the court awarded $6 million. In satisfying the parents’ claims for special damages, the court awarded just over $975,000 plus interest of three per cent per annum, from the date she died to the date the judgement was handed down. It also awarded US$8,000 in respect of the report prepared by the expert witness relied on in the case.

According to the civil negligence and estate lawsuit filed by the parents, on admission to UHWI, the parents informed the medical team that they suspected that their daughter was suffering from another bout of meningitis, an illness she had been previously diagnosed with. They were told that their daughter was suffering from hemiplegic migraine. After some 18 seizures and two heart attacks, the teen, who had also been placed on life support, was pronounced dead on April 5, 2018.

According to court documents, two medical professionals who gave evidence on behalf of the hospital maintained that the UHWI and its medical teams acted in accordance with standard practices and that there were no actions of negligence in the diagnosis, treatment and/or management of the teen.

However, the court, in choosing to rely on the evidence of an expert witness called by the parents, said there were “aspects of negligence on the part of the UHWI, which were of great concern”.

World.title: DREAM OVER
World.content:
Reggae Boyz Under-20 and Mount Pleasant Academy midfielder Jabarie Howell (foreground) is a key figure in Jamaica’s team to the Concacaf Under-20 Championship in Mexico, a qualifier for the FIFA Under-20 World Cup. The top four teams from the championship will qualify for the World Cup. (Photo: Concacaf)

JAMAICA’S campaign at the Concacaf Under-20 Championship ended in defeat on Wednesday night as a 1-3 extra-time loss to Canada at Estadio Cuauhtémoc ended their chances of qualifying for the FIFA Under-20 World Cup and the Los Angeles Olympic Games.

Rodolph Austin’s team fought back to force extra time after an unbeaten group stage, but two goals in that period sent Jesse Marsch’s Canada through to the semi-finals.

Canada controlled the early stages with a high press that made it difficult for Jamaica to keep the ball in midfield. Richard Chukwu broke through in the second minute to set up Lucas Lima, who shot wide, before Owen Graham-Roache missed a similar chance five minutes later.

Jamaica struggled to build attacks under Canadian pressure. Their best chance of the first half came in the 26th minute when Raequan Campbell-Dennis crossed to Jahmarie Nolan at the back post, but the forward’s header missed the target. Canada held 62 per cent of possession in the first half and kept Jamaica without a shot on target.

The second half was more open. Jahmani Bell nearly caught Canada goalkeeper Nathaniel Abraham off his line in the 54th minute with a shot from 60 yards that went just wide. However, Canada took the lead three minutes later. Liam Mackenzie ran through the Jamaican midfield, beat several defenders, and shot past Joshua Grant.

Canada continued to create chances, but Grant made key saves to keep Jamaica in the match, while Marius Aiyenero had a goal ruled out for offside by VAR in the 73rd minute.

Jamaica found an equaliser late in regulation time.

In the 86th minute, substitute Giovanni Taylor was fouled in the box by Dylan Jonelson. Captain Nolan scored the 87th-minute penalty, marking his fourth goal of the tournament and the fourth-straight game Jamaica scored in the final five minutes of regular time.

However, Canada retook the lead early in extra time. In the 93rd minute, Campbell-Dennis brought down Aiyenero in the box, and Mackenzie scored the penalty for his second goal of the match.

“I think it’s just a mindset thing,” Nolan said after the match regarding the extra-time collapse. “One slip-up in the back and we gave away a penalty. Other than that, I think we fought to the end. We just have to regroup and come again.”

Jamaica pushed for another equaliser, but Orel Miller missed the target from a lobbed pass in the 105th minute. By the end of the match, Canada held a 10-2 advantage in shots on target.

Canada secured the win in the 116th minute. Grant cleared a cross from Marsel Bibishkov into the path of Max Vogele, who volleyed the ball into the net from the edge of the box.

“It’s just unfortunate that we tried our best but lost, so we just have to come again in the next qualifiers,” Nolan said. When asked about Jamaica’s future his focus was on, “Preparation, trying to finish off the games better, and just try again to qualify for the World Cup.”

The result ends Jamaica’s tournament despite an encouraging group phase during which they went unbeaten, scored in three straight games for the first time since 2018, and picked up points against two Central American teams for the first time in competition history. Canada advances to the semi-finals and earns qualification for both the Under-20 World Cup and the Los Angeles Olympics.

World.title: Shan’s Crispy Fried Chicken Tacos
World.content:
(Photo: Alan Smith)

Next take my crispy fried chicken and turn it into a fun, flavour-packed taco! These tacos combine crunchy fried chicken with fresh homemade salsa, creamy guacamole, crisp purple cabbage, Mexican cheese, sour cream, and a simple creamy sauce, all tucked into crunchy taco hard shells.



Ingredients

For the Tacos

• Crispy fried chicken, prepared using my fried chicken recipe

• Hard taco shells

• Purple cabbage, thinly shredded

• Mexican cheese, shredded

• Sour cream

• Fresh lime wedges, for serving

Simple Salsa

• 2 ripe tomatoes, finely diced

• ¼ small red onion, finely diced

• 1 small Scotch bonnet pepper, finely chopped, or to taste

• Fresh cilantro, finely chopped

• Juice of ½ lime

• Salt, to taste

Simple Guacamole

• 2 ripe avocados

• Juice of ½ lime

• 1 little red onion, finely diced

• 1 little Scotch bonnet pepper, finely chopped, optional

• Salt, to taste

Creamy Sauce

• Mayonnaise

• Fresh lime juice

• Hot sauce, to taste

Method

1) Prepare the salsa: In a bowl, combine the tomatoes, red onion, Scotch bonnet pepper and cilantro. Add the lime juice, season with salt and mix well. Set aside.

2) Prepare the guacamole: Scoop the avocado into a bowl and mash until creamy but still slightly chunky. Add the lime juice, red onion and Scotch bonnet pepper, then season with salt to taste.

3) Make the creamy sauce: Mix the mayonnaise with a squeeze of fresh lime juice and hot sauce to taste. Stir until smooth and creamy.

4) Prepare the chicken: Prepare the crispy fried chicken according to my fried chicken recipe. Once cooked, cut or break the chicken into bite-sized pieces.

5) Assemble the tacos: Prepare the hard taco shells according to the package instructions. Fill each shell with crispy fried chicken, then add shredded purple cabbage and Mexican cheese.

6) Add a spoonful of the home-made salsa and guacamole, followed by a dollop of sour cream. Drizzle with the creamy sauce and finish with a squeeze of fresh lime juice.

Serve immediately while the chicken and taco shells are crisp.

Kitchen Note: The crispy chicken, crunchy purple cabbage, creamy guacamole, fresh salsa, Mexican cheese, cool sour cream, and tangy sauce come together for the perfect balance of textures and flavours.

Photos: Alan Smith

World.title: Jamaica plants 100 Kenyan Wambugu apple trees in import substitution drive – Green
World.content:
Designed for resilience, the Wambugu apple tree flourishes in both hot and cold conditions, making it ideally suited for tropical environments.

One hundred Wambugu apple trees were recently imported to Jamaica from Kenya and planted across agro parks at Amity Hall, Ebony Park and Parnassu, as the Caribbean island steps up its programme to support import substitution of apples and to diversify the earning potential of farmers.

Minister of Agriculture, Fisheries and Mining, Floyd Green made the announcement at the 72nd staging of the annual Denbigh Agricultural Industrial and Food Show in Clarendon last weekend.

“These demonstration plots will allow us to evaluate performance while encouraging wider adoption among farmers,” Green said of the development.

“A single acre can accommodate as many as 500 trees,” he continued, adding that “Within approximately five years, each tree can produce up to 500 apples and, with proper care and management, yields can reach between 30 and 40 tonnes per acre annually.”

The Wambugu apple is a crisp, juicy red variety similar to American apples. It was developed by Kenyan farmer Peter Wambugu to grow in warmer, tropical climates, which makes it suitable for Jamaica.

In the project spearheaded by the Agro-Investment Corporation (AIC), Jamaica aims for the crop to become a viable addition to local fruit production, contributing to agricultural diversification and farmer profitability.

Peter Wambugu’s daughter, Catherine conducted training sessions in Jamaica last year and distributed seedlings to agro park farmers as part of the programme.

Emphasising the potential of the initiative, Green noted that last year alone, Jamaica imported more than 1.4 million kilogrammes of apples at a cost of more than J$260 million.

“Just imagine what could happen if even a portion of that market could be supplied by Jamaican farmers,” he said.

“The Wambugu apple gives us an opportunity to do precisely that,” he added, noting that the fruit has demonstrated tremendous potential as a commercial crop.

The agriculture minister stressed that the introduction of a new crop “requires more than simply putting trees into the ground”.

“It requires research, training, monitoring and strong partnerships. That is why the Agro-Invest Corporation will continue to work closely with farmers as we assess the long-term potential of this crop under local conditions,” he said.

Green urged farmers who are interested in participating to contact the Agro-Invest Corporation to learn more about the programme and the opportunities that it presents.

World.title: UHWI at fault
World.content:
A view of the University Hospital of the West Indies

The University Hospital of the West Indies (UHWI) has been ordered to pay millions in damages after the Supreme Court found that the facility “fell below the standard of care” expected of it and also “breached the duty of care” provided to a 16-year-old girl, who died six days after being admitted to the hospital in March 2018.

The girl’s parents later sued the hospital’s board of management for failing to “use all proper professional skill, care, competence, and diligence during their investigation, diagnosis, management, and treatment of their only child”.

The court on Friday awarded $1,687,380.19 “for pain and suffering” endured by the child prior to her death. For loss of life/loss of expectation of life, the court awarded $344,127.70 with interest at three per cent per annum from April 15, 2021 to July 31 this year. In assessing how much the child, who was described as “a perennial high achiever” and a “polyglot” (a person who knows, speaks, or writes several different languages) would have lost in terms of earnings from before the trial to the last hearing date the court awarded $6 million. In satisfying the parent’s claims for special damages, the court awarded $975,573.41 plus interest of three per cent per annum, from the date she died to the date the judgement was handed down. It also awarded US$8,000 in respect of the report prepared by the expert witness relied on in the case.

The teenager who was described as “an accomplished and promising fifth-form student at Campion College, St Andrew” was preparing to sit the May/June sitting of the Caribbean Secondary Examination Council (CSEC) examinations at the time of her passing. She was said to have “entrepreneurial dreams and aspirations to become a scientist or a medical researcher”.

According to the civil negligence and estate lawsuit filed by her parents in the civil division of the Supreme Court in 2021, the young girl, on or around March 30, 2018 was admitted by the UHWI for treatment at its medical facility. Her mother said the ordeal began on March 27, 2018 when her daughter complained of what had become a persistent headache. She said after being examined by the family doctor, her daughter — who had also been warm to the touch — was prescribed medication. When that headache persisted three days later, along with weakness the parents — who said they began to “suspect that their daughter was suffering from another bout of meningitis, an illness with which she had been diagnosed at the age of eight years” — decided to take her to the UHWI.

Once there, they said they informed medical staff of her symptoms and history of meningitis as well as their suspicions. The parents said on March 31 after blood samples, a CT scan and an unsuccessful lumbar puncture procedure (which was to be done over), they were informed that their daughter was suffering from hemiplegic migraine. After some 18 seizures and two heart attacks, the teen who had also been placed on life support was pronounced dead on April 5, 2018.

Unmoored and set adrift by the loss of their child, the parents asserted that they suffered emotional and psychiatric distress. The father alleged that he became unable to focus, depressed and angry, making it difficult for him to hold onto a job. His wife maintained that, as a sales manager, the mental distress caused by, and the toll of, her daughter’s death affected her so drastically that she could not do her job as well as she did before.

According to court documents two medical professionals who gave evidence on behalf of the hospital maintained that the UHWI and its medical teams acted in accordance with standard practices and that there were no actions of negligence in the diagnosis, treatment and/or management of the teen.

However the court, in choosing to rely on the evidence of an expert witness called by the parents, said there were “aspects of negligence on the part of the UHWI, which are of great concern”.

“The documentary evidence discloses that, during the course of [her] admission to the UHWI, it was noted on three separate occasions that a diagnosis of meningitis was to be ruled out… in fact, it is readily apparent from the medical docket that no further attempt was made to rule out or to exclude the differential diagnosis of meningitis. This court is of the view that there is an absolute need for a physician to ensure that sufficient tests and detailed investigations are conducted before ruling out one disease over another. Negligence must be ascribed to the UHWI, by its servants and/or agents, for its failure to properly employ all usual diagnostic aids in ruling out the possibility of meningitis, including a lumbar puncture test,” the court said.

“The court finds that the UHWI was negligent in the failure on the part of its servants and/or agents to recognise that [name withheld] was brain-dead on 1 April 2018 at 11:00 pm. The evidence of the rapid deterioration in [the child’s] condition in the five days following her admission to the UHWI is concerning,” said the ruling handed down by Supreme Court Justice Anne-Marie Nembhard.

“The court finds that there was no clear plan of treatment, on the part of the servants and/or agents of the UHWI, to treat [her] in the face of her rapid deterioration, whilst being admitted as a patient to the UHWI. Nor does there seem to have been a corresponding, commensurate escalation in the UHWI’s plan of treatment or course of treatment in the face of her rapid deterioration,” the justice added.

In additional findings, the court said based on the evidence of the expert witness, an accurate diagnosis could have been arrived at, had a lumbar puncture been performed.

World.title: UK Labour membership plummeted under Keir Starmer
World.content:
Starmer faced a tricky 2025 after winning a landslide victory the previous year, which brought the center-left party back into power after 14 years.

He was forced into a series of policy U-turns by his party, and sacked Peter Mandelson as U.K. ambassador to the U.S. after fresh details on the closeness of his friendship with convicted sex-trafficker Jeffrey Epstein emerged.

Membership swelled under Starmer’s predecessor Jeremy Corbyn, with the party recording more than half a million Labour members at the peak of his popularity.

But under Starmer and his Chancellor Rachel Reeves, the party moved rightwards economically and on issues such as immigration and benefit payments, and expelled left-leaning party stalwarts such as Corbyn and Diane Abbott.

Such changes put the leadership at odds with its members, sections of whom are notably more left wing than the British public at large. The removal of the whip from several Labour MPs for voting against government welfare policies in 2024, and again in 2025, were watershed moments.

In 2023, Starmer told members: “If you don’t like the changes that we’ve made, I say the door is open, and you can leave.”

World.title: EU can’t depend on neighbors for border control, migration chief says
World.content:
“We must cooperate with our neighbors, of course. But as long as control depends on the goodwill of one neighboring state, we remain … vulnerable,” he added.

Brunner described last week’s events in Ceuta, when around 72,000 migrants forced their way into the Spanish exclave, as “solid proof that we need a strong and effective tool — and different tools — to combat smuggling.”

Ceuta Mayor-President Juan Jesús Vivas, who also attended the meeting, said that around 100 people died during the mass border crossing, and that between 3,000 and 5,000 remained in the exclave.

Brunner said the EU should use all available leverage to secure the cooperation of countries bordering the bloc.

“It’s about further strengthening the work with partners … [We need to] step up our migration diplomacy by reinforcing comprehensive partnerships to stem this illegal migration, secure effective returns and create the right opportunities for people at home,” he said.

Brunner said cooperation with non-EU countries was essential “because the goal there is to make sure such events never happen again.”

The conservative Austrian commissioner’s party colleague Integration Minister Claudia Bauer warned on Thursday in a written statement that “another attempted mass crossing” in Ceuta could happen on Aug. 15, quoting Spanish media.

“In light of reports of another attempted mass crossing, Spain must immediately and significantly reinforce border protection in its African enclaves and ensure that this time it will hold,” she said.

World.title: US stresses Ceuta is Spanish territory but slams Sánchez for not defending it
World.content:
Many in Madrid expressed fears Washington could decline to rein in Rabat, and pointed to a recent U.S. Congress report that described Ceuta and Melilla as being in “Moroccan territory” and was supportive of negotiations on the “future status” of the cities. But U.S. State Department Spokesperson Tommy Pigott insisted that there has been no change in U.S. policy on the exclaves.

“The United States unequivocally supports Spain’s sovereignty over Ceuta and Melilla,” he told POLITICO.

The State Department noted that the congressional report did not represent U.S. law.

Pigott said that allegations suggesting Washington was questioning Spain’s continued control of the cities had been “pushed by nefarious actors who wish to distract from the Spanish government’s shameful refusal to defend its people from the migrant invasion of its territory in Ceuta.”

He also argued the Spanish government was solely to blame for the crisis in the exclave, into which 72,000 unauthorized migrants surged last week.

“The invasion of tens of thousands of migrants into Ceuta is a direct consequence of the Spanish government’s refusal to defend their sovereignty, secure their borders, and protect their people,” he said.

World.title: Spain’s far left and far right unite to oppose Morocco co-hosting 2030 World Cup
World.content:
Less than 24 hours later, Vox filed a nearly identical motion questioning the wisdom of hosting the World Cup alongside a country that “is not a loyal partner, neither for organizing a sporting event of this magnitude nor for any neighborly matter.”

“The very serious events that took place in Ceuta on July 30 and 31 have completely shattered the foundations of trust and cooperation on which a shared candidacy necessarily rests,” asserted Vox’s proposal, stating that co-hosting with Morocco would constitute “a deliberate humiliation that Spain must vehemently oppose.”

Both proposals are non-binding and do not oblige Madrid to take action. However, the legislative initiatives show that lawmakers from across the political spectrum are uniting in their resentment of Rabat’s perceived role in the crisis, which many in Madrid view as an example of Morocco using migrants to exert political pressure on its neighbor.

Spain’s Socialist-led government has avoided blaming Morocco, looking to find a speedy resolution to the crisis.

In addition to Sumar and Vox, Spain’s far-left Podemos party and Portugal’s environmentalist Livre party have also called for the Iberian neighbors to host the next World Cup without Morocco.

In 2023, world football’s governing body FIFA awarded the 2030 tournament to Spain, Portugal and Morocco, with games to be held in stadiums such as Madrid’s Santiago Bernabéu Stadium, Lisbon’s Estádio da Luz, and a new custom-built facility in Casablanca that Moroccan authorities say will be the largest football stadium in the world.

The future host cities also made headlines on Wednesday, as controversial FIFA President Gianni Infantino allegedly offered Moroccan officials the right to host the tournament’s final match in exchange for a declaration of support from the country’s football federation, according to The Times newspaper. FIFA denied the report, insisting the football chief had made no such commitment.

This article has been updated.

World.title: Leipzig drone incident fuels fears of Russian election meddling
World.content:
“We do of course see that Russia attempts every day, in one way or another — through hybrid means and various measures — to exert influence here in Germany in a manner that seeks to undermine our democracy and erode trust in politics and politicians,” said Martin Giese, a foreign ministry spokesperson.

Russian disinformation campaigns have portrayed German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and his government as warmongers. They aim to undermine the already unpopular chancellor and boost Russia-friendly forces such as the AfD and the far-left Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) — both of which are strong in eastern Germany.

“The state elections in Saxony-Anhalt and in eastern Germany are, of course, a major target of Russian influence, because these are pivotal elections in the heart of Europe,” said Stefan Meister, a Russia expert at the German Council on Foreign Relations.

He said that it is too early to attribute the explosive-laden drone to Russia as investigations are still ongoing. But he added that Moscow is clearly waging a broad hybrid campaign targeting the region ahead of next month’s votes.

“This could be the first time right-wing populists come to power,” Meister said. “And with that, the chancellor might even fall — or at the very least, the coalition would be severely weakened — and a pro-Russian party would come to power in one of the federal states.”

“There is a major campaign underway on the Russian side to influence these elections in favor of the AfD and the BSW,” he added.

World.title: Hormuz deal with Oman in final stage, says Iran
World.content:
Ships sail near the Strait of Hormuz on July 13, 2026. | AFP via Getty Images

The countries are finalizing an agreed route for shipping in case the strait reopens.

Negotiations between Iran and Oman on delineating a shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz have reached the final stage, the Iranian Foreign Ministry confirmed on Wednesday.

The shipping lane would primarily lie within Iranian territorial waters, with parts extending into Omani waters.

Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei told journalists that “the geographical coordinates of the proposed maritime route have been agreed upon by both sides,” adding that the bilateral process was “professional” and “forward-moving.”

World.title: German interior minister suggests state actor behind drone attack
World.content:
"Of course, we all want to know which foreign powers are involved. But it would be reckless to give credence to any kind of speculation at this point," he added.

Leipzig Airport serves as a strategic hub for NATO, including for military transports to Ukraine. The airport is also international courier service DHL’s largest European air hub and serves as a temporary home for some Ukrainian Antonov aircraft, protecting them from Russian attacks. The armed drone was found just meters away from such a plane, said officials Wednesday.

Armin Schuster, minister of the interior for Saxony — where Leipzig is located — told ZDF that the incident represented a new threat level.

"Without wanting to preempt the investigation, I would describe this as a suspected attack scenario because this is the first time we’ve had a drone that was also loaded with explosives," he said. "That’s new."

An airport worker found the drone Tuesday night. Officers disarmed the device by removing its detonator, which had failed to go off. In a separate incident at the same airport, another flying object struck a DHL cargo aircraft as it was being diverted away from the airport after the explosive-laden drone was found.

World.title: Former PM joins list of French presidential candidates reportedly targeted by Russian interference
World.content:
Gabriel Attal gestures as he visits his old family home on Île-aux-Moines, France on July 25, 2026. | Sebastien Salom-Gomis/AFP via Getty Images

Three presidential hopefuls have reported Kremlin disinformation efforts against them over the past two weeks.

PARIS — Former Prime Minister Gabriel Attal is the latest in a string of French presidential candidates allegedly targeted by a Russian disinformation campaign.

Attal, the candidate of President Emmanuel Macron's Renaissance party, said on Thursday he had been "a victim" of an electoral "interference" attempt originating from Russia, and that he expected such "destabilization efforts" to increase ahead of France's April 2027 election.

Viginum, the country's agency for fighting online disinformation, confirmed it had detected the operation against Attal and attributed it "with a high level of confidence" to "pro-Russian" disinformation tactics.
