World.title: Trump administration to pay €1.06 billion to cancel RWE offshore wind leases
World.content:
Washington will fork out $1.22 billion (€1.06 billion) to German energy firm RWE to cancel the company's offshore wind leases.

 

RWE said on Thursday that it had reached a settlement with the US Department of the Interior (DOI) to relinquish leases off the coasts of New York, California, and Louisiana.

"After careful consideration, it was determined there is no path forward to permit these projects in the U.S. for the foreseeable future," the company said in a statement.

Trump vs wind energy

US President Donald Trump, long a critic of wind energy, has embarked on a campaign to halt a number of such projects across the US.

Trump has repeatedly dismissed wind turbines as unsightly and has labelled them an "economic and environmental disaster." He previously said that he did not want "even one" built during his time in office.

In March, French energy giant TotalEnergies announced that it had also reached an agreement with the US Interior Department to cut its leases at Carolina Long Bay and New York Bight. The DOI said it would pay TotalEnergies around $1 billion as part of the agreement, which would see the French firm instead invest in natural gas projects.

RWE said it would also be investing in gas projects across the US "to meet rapidly growing energy demand." That includes a $900 million investment to acquire a 16% stake in a Louisiana liquified natural gas project.

"RWE Americas has announced plans to invest approximately €17 billion in the U.S. over the next six years to grow its generation capacity from approximately 13 GW across 27 states today to 22 GW by 2031," the company added.

Doug Burgum, the US Interior Secretary, has praised the deal, writing on X: "We welcome RWE’s agreement and voluntary investment in projects that strengthen our nation's energy security, provide dependable baseload power and help keep electricity affordable for hardworking Americans today while supporting our country's long-term energy future."

World.title: Reports: Spanish authorities concerned over possible Ceuta migrant crossing on 15 August
World.content:
Spain's Civil Guard has produced a six-page report examining the possibility of another mass migrant crossing into the Spanish territory of Ceuta on 15 August.

 

The document, obtained by Spanish media outlet Mañaneros, is based on a campaign circulating on social media that, according to the report, has reached groups with hundreds of thousands of followers.

The analysis relies entirely on open-source information - social media posts and media reports - and was intended to determine whether the online call to make the crossing was genuine, how widely it had spread, and the degree of coordination behind it.

The report stops short of drawing firm conclusions, however. As cited by RTVE, it said there was no basis for estimating how many people might take part or for assuming that the events seen in late July would be repeated on 15 August.

Its conclusion is that an active online campaign exists with the potential to mobilise people, but whether it will actually result in a mass crossing, how many people would be involved, and who is behind it all remain unknown. The report added that much will depend on Morocco's preventive measures on roads, at transport hubs, in the town of Fnideq, and along the coast, as well as on Spain's security operation.

What prompted the investigation?

According to the Civil Guard, the messages first began circulating in late July and early August, when young Moroccans started sharing calls for another collective attempt to reach the North African territory of Ceuta around 15 August.

The report compares coverage from both Spanish and Moroccan media, noting that the issue is no longer confined to Spanish social media. Investigators also examined Facebook, WhatsApp, and Instagram groups with memberships ranging from around 400,000 to just over 422,000 people, although the report itself cautioned against reading too much into those figures.

Investigators say the most significant factor is not the size of those groups but the recurring patterns they identified: repeated references to 15 August, the same geographical locations, discussions about how to organise the crossing, and the persistence of these messages over several days. Monitoring continued until 4 August.

The report also found a significant amount of misinformation circulating online, including claims that the border would be opened, that migrants would receive asylum or financial assistance, or that anyone reaching Ceuta could not legally be returned.

Who is behind the drive?

The report describes the online campaign as decentralised. Rather than identifying a single organiser, investigators found that the proposed date appeared to spread organically from one online group to another.

Migrants who crossed into Spain from Morocco gather on a beach in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, Monday, Aug. 3, 2026. AP Photo

Based on the open-source material reviewed, the Civil Guard said it had been unable to identify those responsible for promoting the campaign. It also said it had found no evidence linking it to the Moroccan government, Moroccan security services, or any specific migrant-smuggling network.

But the report dismissed the idea that the campaign was spontaneous. It concluded that there appears to be "some degree of digital facilitation"- in other words, some level of coordination behind the online activity - even though its source and extent remain unclear.

Brussels keeps watch

The European Commission said it was closely monitoring social media ahead of 15 August.

"We remain fully vigilant before, during, and after 15 August," Commission spokesperson Guillaume Mercier said.

However, Brussels urged caution, stressing that many of the reports circulating online "have not been verified" and that the overall picture remains "unclear." The Commission said it was staying in close contact with both the Spanish and Moroccan authorities.

It also said it had detected Russian-linked channels that began rapidly amplifying the migration issue from 30 July onwards.

The Commission noted that the European Union can use legislation such as the Digital Services Act (DSA) to tackle online disinformation. The law requires major digital platforms and search engines to assess and mitigate systemic risks to public security. Spain has not, however, activated the DSA's crisis mechanism, which would allow for enhanced coordination with the platforms.

World.title: Belarus designates Euronews’ website as 'extremist' media
World.content:
The Ministry of Information of Belarus has designated Euronews’ website as “extremist” media, adding it to its “Republican List of Extremist Materials” following a national court order, according to Belarus-based media outlets.

 

The Euronews website will now be restricted in Belarus, and readers could face administrative penalties for "storing or distributing" its content, after many years in which Euronews has been the main European source of information in the country, according to Euronews’ audience data in Belarus.

The state decision was taken by the Horki District Court in the Mogilev Region on 4 August and is "subject to immediate execution in accordance with Article 302 of the Code of Civil Procedure of the Republic of Belarus." Minsk now joins Moscow in banning both Euronews’ television and digital news medias, depriving Belarus audiences of a vital source of factual and independent journalism which also covers Belarus, Russia and the war in Ukraine.

Euronews’ Editorial Director Claus Strunz condemned the decision declaring that a state that brands Euronews as “extremist” and blocks access to independent, impartial journalism reveals its own fear of free reporting.”

“We have not been informed of this decision and await the authorities’ justification. Our commitment remains unchanged: we stand with our audiences in Belarus and will continue to provide factual, independent journalism guided by our core editorial values,“ Strunz said.

Belarus authorities have yet to announce the decision and their arguments that led to this extreme ruling by which Euronews and several other digital medias are now labelled “extremist media” in Belarus.

Euronews’ television channel broadcast was banned by Belarus authorities in 2021 on a legal procedural basis, before the Kremlin decided to cut Euronews’ television and digital output across the Russian Federation right after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The independent Belarusian Association of Journalists suggested that the suspension of Euronews broadcasts was linked to attempts to restrict access to sources of information.

World.title: UEFA may still boycott FIFA events as it says Infantino apology 'changes nothing'
World.content:
European football governing body UEFA has threatened to go ahead with a boycott of FIFA events despite FIFA offering an apology over its handling of a proposed private investment plan.

 

In a statement on Thursday, UEFA said: "UEFA’s associations were very clear about the conditions attached to the non-participation in FIFA competitions."

"First, the proposals to sell off the major competitions had to be withdrawn and secondly, assurances have to be made that such attempts to disfigure the game in this way will never be made again," it continued, adding: "These conditions have not been met."

On Wednesday, FIFA President Gianni Infantino and other senior FIFA figures gathered in Morocco for a crisis meeting to discuss the failed $20 billion FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal and how the world governing body would move forward.

The plan, which would have invited third parties to take minority, non-controlling stakes in the FFE, a new subsidiary that would have run FIFA’s commercial and event operations, faced major pushback from across the football world, with UEFA announcing at the time that its 55 member associations would boycott FIFA competitions "for so long as these proposals remain alive."

However, following the talks in Rabat, FIFA issued a statement saying that Infantino had the "full support" of its Secretary General Mattias Grafström and members of the FIFA management board.

FIFA also acknowledged that "mistakes" were made with regards to the FFE and said it had apologised to member associations.

Addressing the announcement on Thursday, UEFA said: "Yesterday’s announcement that some people employed by the FIFA President (and whose careers depend on his favour) agree with him changes nothing.”

FIFPRO, a global representative body for professional football players, also delivered a ferocious statement on the FFE and FIFA's Morocco meeting on Thursday, saying the fiasco was "not merely a governance failure" but a "profound abuse of presidential power."

"We have noted FIFA's internal update from its meeting in Rabat, Morocco with deep concern," it said. "Rather than confronting what happened, it reaffirms support for the organisation’s leadership while reducing a fundamental governance and constitutional failure to a matter of 'processes and communications' to be 'improved'".

World.title: France to ban unsolicited telemarketing calls from next week
World.content:
Cold calling is about to come to an end. Or at least in its current form. On Tuesday 11 August, a law backed by Emmanuel Macron's government will come into force, tightening the rules and banning these unsolicited nuisance calls. The aim is to protect consumers from intrusive commercial solicitations and to protect vulnerable people from fraudulent practices.

 

From now on it will be illegal to contact consumers without their prior consent. Consent that "can be withdrawn at any time", says Alice Vilcot, chief of staff at the Directorate-General for Competition, Consumer Affairs and Fraud Control.

However, the practice will still be allowed in two situations: when a company has already obtained your agreement, for example during a purchase, a visit to a shop or via a form, and when the call concerns a contract you have already signed.

The government says the law responds to years of consumer complaints. Authorities estimate that around three quarters of people in France receive at least one unsolicited sales call every week, and many receive more.

Content creator Micode highlights the same problem on his YouTube channel. In a lengthy investigation carried out over several months (source in French), he sheds light on how these call campaigns work, from aggressive techniques to schemes that discourage victims from taking legal action.

Back in 2024, eleven consumer organisations issued a joint call for a ban, denouncing the "relentless harassment of consumers through countless unwanted marketing calls to landlines and mobile phones, an intrusion that has become a regular part of their daily lives".

And the penalties for violating the law will be severe. Individuals may be fined up to 75,000 euros per call. Companies could face fines of up to 375,000 euros per call.

So far, ineffective measures

Over the past fifteen years, numerous measures have already been introduced: a ban on canvassing from mobile numbers starting with 06 or 07, as well as at certain times of the day or at weekends. But this ban applied only to a few sectors, such as the Personal Training Account, home adaptations for disability or old age, or energy-efficiency renovation. From now on, it will cover almost all sectors.

Another measure that had been introduced was signing up to a platform in order not to be contacted. "We are thus moving from an opt-out system to one based on prior consent", the finance ministry, Bercy, says with satisfaction.

But for the consumer association Que Choisir (source in French), the battle will not end there. Deprived of telephone calls, "many fraudsters will try to change the playing field and operate via door-to-door canvassing", warns its president, Marie-Amandine Stévenin. She is already calling for this practice to be regulated.

Concern in Morocco

The new French law has sparked concern in Morocco, where Employment Minister Younes Sekkouri told MPs that up to 50,000 jobs were at risk in the country's call centres. He said the industry had attracted around 100 million dollars in investment and generates more than one billion dollars in annual revenue in the country.

Low labour costs, a large French-speaking workforce and relatively weak trade unions have made Morocco an attractive destination for international companies, particularly French firms seeking to reduce their costs.

Youssef Chraïbi, president of the Moroccan Outsourcing Services Federation, told local daily Le Matin that the French market has historically accounted for more than 80% of the sector's revenue. "Pure telemarketing now accounts for only 15% to 20% of total activity", he added, noting that the sector has diversified beyond traditional call centre services.

Measures in other countries

Germany has had a similar system in place since 2009. The Netherlands strengthened its rules on canvassing last month. The country had already banned unsolicited sales calls, but companies can now no longer phone their own customers with promotional offers without prior permission.

Many other countries have adopted measures based on opt-out systems. In the United States, people can sign up to the National Do Not Call Registry, which reduces unwanted sales calls.

Canada has its own "Do Not Call List", while the United Kingdom has the Telephone Preference Service. Companies that call people who have opted out can be fined up to 500,000 pounds (583,000 euros) per call.

World.title: Ceuta mayor tells MEPs migrant 'invasion' left city traumatised, demands immediate deportations
World.content:
Ceuta Mayor Juan Jesús Vivas has described the breach of the Spanish enclave's border with Morocco as an "invasion" and demanded the immediate return of migrants still there after last week's border incident.

 

Vivas made the remarks in his testimony before the European Parliament's Committee on Civil Liberties, Justice and Home Affairs on Thursday. The hearing was convened after roughly 80,000 migrants entered Ceuta by sea in what has been described as one of the largest migration crises in the EU's history.

The Spanish government declined its invitation to attend the session; the European Commission was represented by Magnus Brunner, the commissioner responsible for migration.

"According to the Royal Spanish Academy's dictionary, the second definition of 'invasion' refers to the anomalous or irregular occupation of a specific place. This is precisely what happened on 30 and 31 July, when some 80,000 people – equivalent to the entire population of Ceuta – stormed into our city," Vivas told MEPs.

The mayor said the episode had called into question the integrity of Ceuta, Spain and the European Union as a whole. Although most of the migrants have since returned to Morocco, he said the crisis had left the city traumatised.

"We faced a humanitarian emergency of enormous proportions, compounded by disturbances to public order and a serious risk to public safety," he said.

Vivas added that between 3,000 and 5,000 migrants remain in local reception centres, which are overwhelmed.

"This in no way allows us to say that our city has returned to normal for its citizens," he said, adding that the exact number of migrants still in Ceuta had not been disclosed owing to a lack of resources.

He renewed his calls for stronger border controls and the immediate return of migrants who entered the city irregularly.

"We demand the immediate expulsion of the Moroccans who have entered our city irregularly and who remain here," Vivas said, while noting that unaccompanied minors could be returned to their country of origin only with their consent.

Responding to a question from an MEP, Vivas said he had no information on whether any jihadists previously expelled from Europe had entered Ceuta during the crisis.

"We don't know from local authorities whether there are any jihadists among those who entered," he added.

Vivas said Ceuta had warned Spanish authorities before last Thursday's surge about rising numbers of irregular arrivals from Morocco.

"We told the ministries about the situation we were experiencing, and we pointed out that there had been an alarming increase in arrival flows," he said.

He also said the city had been unable to establish contact with Moroccan authorities, who had refused to engage.

"What has become apparent," he said, "is that our border is porous and vulnerable."

World.title: Trump signs new orders restricting birthright citizenship
World.content:
The US president's move comes just two months after the Supreme Court ruled that his first executive order on citizenship was unconstitutional.

US President Donald Trump dismissed a previous Supreme Court decision on citizenship as "very unfortunate" while signing two new executive orders restricting birthright citizenship on Thursday.

"It was close, but a very, very unfortunate decision," Trump said of the 6-3 vote top court ruling two months ago.

The ruling rebuked Trump's previous attempt to challenge the constitutional provision that allows individuals born on US soil automatic citizenship.

Birthright citizenship is enshrined in the 14th ​Amendment of the US Constitution. The rule guarantees citizenship for babies born in the US with only narrow exceptions, such as the children of foreign diplomats or members of an enemy occupying force.

"This was done for a different reason. This ​was done right after the Civil War. This ‌was for the babies of slaves, and what's happening now?" Trump said on Thursday.

What are the new executive orders?

Trump's close advisor and the architect of his immigration policy, Stephen Miller, said one of the orders signed Thursday seeks to deny birthright citizenship to children of members of "foreign terrorist organizations" as well as "large categories of people who lobby and act on behalf of foreign governments."

Miller added that the order "ensures that large numbers of people who wrongly (would) be getting birthright citizenship will no longer be eligible for those benefits."

ICE targets South Asians for removal from United States To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The second executive order targets what Trump called "birth tourism." The expression refers to visitors securing visas and traveling to the US so they would give birth while in the country, so their children are entitled to US citizenship.

"That practice of birth tourism is, as of ​the signing of this order, hereby banned. What that means is that no one in the world is anymore allowed to obtain a ​visa for this ‌fraudulent purpose," Miller added.

Currently, there are no official figures depicting the number of foreigners who come to the US for the explicit purpose of giving birth to obtain citizenship. But the Trump-aligned Center for Immigration Studies claims that between 20,000-25,000 mothers did so 2016-2017.

Trump: 'Our country suffers'

The White House has argued that the new executive orders do not fall within the limits of the Supreme Court ruling.

Still, the orders are expected to be challenged in court.

"I thought we were going to win it at the Supreme Court," Trump said on Thursday. "Unfortunately, we had a bad decision, very unfair decision. Our country suffers because of it and we’re ending it a different way," Trump said.

Currently, no US law bans so-called birth tourism, but a federal regulation implemented in 2020 during Trump’s first term prohibits using temporary tourist and business visas for the primary purpose of obtaining US citizenship for a newborn.

World.title: Ebola: Africa CDC plans to use vaccine for different strain as outbreak spreads
World.content:
The head of the Africa Centres for Disease Control pledged to deploy a vaccine for a previous Ebola strain in the current DRC outbreak, with test cases indicating a potentially live-saving level of protection.

African health authorities say they would start using a vaccine for the prior Zaire ebolavirus strain to treat the current outbreak involving a different, fast spreading strain known as Bundibugyo. The ongoing outbreak is centered in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).

The director general of the African Centres for Disease Control, or Africa CDC, Jean Kaseya, told reporters in a videoconference on Thursday that there was evidence of the vaccine eliminating deaths, if not symptoms, in the test cases conducted so far.

The Africa CDC and the World Health Organization also plan to launch research checking for a possible mutation or some other abnormality in the current outbreak, as the virus spreads at a rate six to eight times faster than any past outbreak on record.

The warnings come amid continued strikes and protests in the hardest-hit regions by some medical staff complaining either of non-payment or of inadequate pay and conditions.

Medics trying to contain the virus are noting an unusually high rate of infection Image: Dirole Lotsima Dieudonne/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

What did Kaseya say about the speed of the spread?

Kaseya was speaking from Brazzaville in the neighboring Republic of Congo,after meeting with World Health Organization Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus in Kinshasa the previous day.

The Africa CDC chief said authorities estimated 4,000 cases have been confirmed by now, given that 3,973 had been confirmed as of Tuesday in the latest available data. That data also pointed to 1,801 confirmed Ebola deaths. The current oubreak was only declared in mid-May and is already the second-largest on record.

Compared to the West Africa outbreak, which took place from 2014 to 2016 and is considered the largest ever, the current strain was causing deaths 6 times faster.

"As Dr. Tedros shared with me yesterday, it's time for the WHO and Africa CDC to conduct studies to check that there is no issue, additional issue, or maybe if the virus is not mutating, because the level of severity of this Bundibugyo outbreak is unprecedented," Kaseya said.

"This outbreak is just expanding."

Everyone in Ituri at risk

Kaseya said cases had now been logged in 51 health zones, compared to nine in May.

He also drew attention to the numbers of cases identified as a share of the contact tracing program's size. During the most virulent and deadly outbreak on record, the Zaire strain outbreak in DRC between 2018 and 2020, one patient was identified from every 57 contacts identified as being at risk.

Across the border in Uganda, which says it has eradicated the small number of cases it experienced this year, it had an average of one confirmed case from every 41 contacts in the list.

In DRC this year, meanwhile, there was one confirmed case for every 10 people in the contact list. Kaseya said that in his estimation, a point had been reached where anybody in the hardest-hit city of Bunia or the worst-affected region of Ituri should be considered potential contacts.

DR Congo launches Ebola trial for high-risk contacts To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What did Kaseya say about the Zaire strain vaccine?

Doctors have had only limited chances to treat or test against the Bundibugyo Ebola strain as it had been considered rare. There are also no recognized vaccines or treatments. However, medical experts have already started working on a new jab.

During the Thursday conference, Kaseya said that the Africa CDC planned to start dispensing an existing Ebola vaccine for the Zaire strain in the current outbreak. During limited testing, while people vaccinated against the Zaire strain did experience some symptoms, "we saw zero deaths among people who are vaccinated."

He said that this "means there is a level of protection" provided by the vaccine.

Kaseya said authorities also planned to expand the use of the antiviral drug remdesivir in affected areas.

Neighboring Uganda had reported successes treating its limited number of cases with redemsivir. It recorded 20 cases and said that only two of the patients died.

It wasn't immediately clear how many supplies of the vaccines or treatment were ready and available to dispense in a fairly remote region of the DRC that's close to active insurgencies and other forms of conflict. Africa CDC's Professor Placide Mbala said any initial rollout would be a relatively small trial.

What's the latest on the stranded barge in Maluku near Kinshasa?

Meanwhile, authorities near the DRC capital of Kinshasa continued screening more than 300 people traveling on a river boat after the death of a passenger reported to have Ebola-like symptoms.

Health teams deployed a mobile laboratory to the vessel to conduct precautionary tests in Maluku where it was intercepted, northeast of the capital.

The ship was intercepted and halted in Maluku on Thursday, and authorities have started screening the passengers as a precaution Image: Wendy Bashi/DW

The city has so far avoided being exposed to the Ebola outbreak.

Kaseya on Thursday told reporters that the boat had come from Mongala province, where no Ebola cases have been reported. Prior reports had said the vessel hailed from Kisangani, the capital of Tshopo province, which is an affected area. Kaseya said that initially even the government had received this erroneous information.

He said health authorities and the government nevertheless decided to screen all passengers to try to minimize risk, with results still pending.

World.title: How drought threatens electricity supplies in Europe
World.content:
Droughts, heat and falling water levels in the Danube are hitting central and southeastern Europe hard. Hungary and Romania are experiencing an energy crisis — whereas countries like Bulgaria are better prepared.

Riverbeds reduced to tiny streams, asphalt melting like butter, dried-up fields — these are currently the images of drought in Central and Southeastern Europe. The record-breaking lack of rainfall in recent months and this summer's heatwaves have caused severe damage to the region's economy and infrastructure.

In the agriculture sector, it has been clear for some time that harvests in Southeastern Europe, especially maize and sunflower crops, will be significantly below average. The heatwaves are also repeatedly disrupting road, rail and, above all, shipping transport. But, most importantly, the drought has triggered an unprecedented crisis in electricity generation in several Central and Southeastern European countries, forcing companies to halt production due to the historically low water level of the Danube.

Hungary and Romania are currently most affected by the energy crisis. Other countries bordering the Danube — Austria, Slovakia, Serbia and Bulgaria — are also suffering from low water levels, although not as severely as Hungary and Romania.

DW outlines the situation in each country and explains why, despite facing similar weather conditions, some are more severely affected than others.

Hungary: Most severe energy crisis in decades

No country in the region is currently as severely affected by drought and heat as Hungary. For months, there has been little or no rainfall in large parts of the country. On Wednesday, temperatures reached 43 degrees Celsius (109.4 degrees Fahrenheit) in the capital Budapest, and exceeded 40 degrees in many places across the country.

Due to the record-low water levels of the Danube, the Paks nuclear power plant south of Budapest had to largely shut down operations, as there is no longer sufficent cooling water available and the temperature of the Danube water is too high. The plant is currently operating at around 12% of its capacity. If Danube water levels continue to drop, the plant will have to be shut down completely.

Due to the energy crisis, the Hungarian government has been urging large energy consumers to conserve electricity. As a result, several car manufacturers, including Audi Gyor, oil and gas company MOL and other large companies have scaled back production. Hungary's energy crisis — the worst in decades — is so severe because of the country's unfavorable energy mix. Paks generates around 50% of the electricity produced in Hungary and about one-third of the electricity consumed. Although Hungary has significant solar energy capacity, it lacks storage facilities, has too few modern gas-fired power plants and very little wind or hydropower capacity.

In Prahovo (eastern Serbia), the Danube's low water level has revealed the remains of a German WW II warship Image: Darko Vojinovic/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Even if the Danube water levels rise significantly again, the Paks nuclear power plant cannot simply be brought back online quickly — the process takes a considerable amount of time. Therefore, Hungary's energy crisis will continue for at least several more weeks, during which the country will have to import electricity at high prices. In response to the crisis, the new government under Peter Magyar has announced a comprehensive review of Hungary's energy development strategy.

Romania: Blasting rocks to redirect water

Romania is experiencing a similar, though somewhat less severe, energy crisis. The Cernavoda nuclear power plant, also located on the Danube in the southeast of the country, produces roughly one-fifth of Romania's electricity. Due to the river's exceptionally low water level, one of the plant's two 700-megawatt reactors was taken offline last week.

Southwest of the Cernavoda plant, Romanian authorities blasted a rock formation this week to divert more water into the Danube's eastern branch, where the nuclear plant is located. In addition, dozens of tons of rock were dumped into the river to channel more water into that branch.

Romania's navy carried out a controlled blast of submerged rocks to allow more water to flow into the eastern branch of the Danube Image: Vadim Ghirda/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Romania has a relatively balanced energy mix consisting of hydropower, nuclear energy, natural gas, coal and wind power. However, because hydropower accounts for around one-fifth of the country's electricity generation — primarily through the Iron Gate hydroelectric plant on the Danube — Romania is particularly vulnerable to droughts such as the current one.

Due to the energy crisis, several major companies, including Dacia and Ford Romania, have scaled back production. The government has announced that it would, if necessary, issue a decree ordering large factories to suspend production.

Romania is also among the Southeastern European countries most affected by aridification — the long-term climatic process through which regions become increasingly dry — and desertification, as soils gradually become barren and take on desert-like characteristics.

Serbia: An unfavorable energy mix

Serbia, too, is suffering badly from drought and the Danube's low water level. Its energy mix is similarly ill-suited to prolonged dry periods. Around 65% of its electricity is generated by coal-fired power plants, while about 25% comes from hydropower.

The two Iron Gate hydropower plants are currently generating only a fraction of their average electricity output. The coal-fired power plants Kostolac A and B east of Belgrade, which rely on Danube water for cooling, have also had to cut back production.

In Hungary, dropping water levels of the Danube threaten the complete shutdown of the Paks nuclear power plant Image: David Balogh/Xinhua/IMAGO

Serbia relies heavily on the Danube as a transport route for coal and petrochemical products. However, due to the low water level, cargo vessels can currently only carry a fraction of their normal loads. Nonetheless, the energy crisis has so far not been so severe that large industrial plants have had to scale back production.

Slovakia, Austria less affected

In Slovakia, some 60% of electricity is generated by nuclear power plants, with another 20% by hydropower. Unlike Hungary and Romania, Slovakia's two nuclear power plants, Bohunice and Mochovce, are located on smaller rivers and use cooling towers rather than once-through cooling systems. Once-through cooling requires large quantities of river water that are drawn from the river and then channeled back to it at a higher temperature. In contrast, cooling towers recirculate water in a closed system, releasing heat mainly through evaporation. As a result, Slovakia's nuclear plants require much less river water and are therefore less affected by the current drought.

In comparison, Slovakia's Gabcikovo hydropower on the Danube has been significantly affected by the low water level. At present, only one of its eight turbines is in operation. Electricity generation in Gabcikovo, however, is only about 12% lower compared to the same time last year. So far, Slovakia has not experienced any major industrial production stoppages.

Austria, which generates around 60% of its electricity from hydropower, has also been less severely affected than Hungary. One reason is that part of Austria's hydropower capacity comes from storage and pumped-storage plants rather than run-of-river facilities.

Run-of-river plants depend directly on the volume of water flowing through rivers, whereas storage and pumped-storage plants can generate electricity using water stored in reservoirs when needed, making them less vulnerable during prolonged heatwaves and droughts.

In addition, Austria generates some 30% of its electricity from other renewable energy sources.

Cargo ships anchor near Petrovaradin, Serbia, on the Danube amid extremely low levels of water following an extended period of drought Image: Darko Vojinovic/AP Photo/picture alliance

Bulgaria: Large battery storage capacity

Unlike in neighboring Romania, drought and heat are not yet causing an energy crisis in Bulgaria.

The country generates up to 40% of its energy through the Kozloduy nuclear power plant, which is also located on the Danube. Its cooling system, however, is better designed to operate under low-water conditions than those of Hungary's Paks plant and Cernavoda in Romania. As a result, it is currently operating at almost full capacity.

At the same time, Bulgaria depends only marginally on hydropower and has, in recent years, considerably expanded its solar and wind energy capacity.

The biggest difference to all the other countries lies in Bulgaria's large-scale battery storage facilities. The country currently has storage systems with a capacity of 3.4 gigawatts and a storage capacity of 8.6 gigawatt-hours. This storage capacity corresponds to 16% of the country's total installed power generation capacity — a figure unmatched by any other country in the world.

These storage facilities enable Bulgaria to balance supply shortages and peak demand, without relying on expensive imports. At the same time, the country is developing into a regional market leader in new energy concepts and as a hub for power grid stabilization and greater price stability in the electricity market.

World.title: Ceuta leader says 100 migrants died in border rush
World.content:
With over 3,000 migrants still in Ceuta after rushing the border last week, Ceuta leader Juan Jesus Vivas warns the situation in the Spanish exclave is "unsustainable." Hundreds of those migrants are minors.

Ceuta's leader Juan Jesus Vivas told EU lawmakers at the European Parliament on Thursday that some 100 people had died during last week's border surge.

He also said the city was still reeling from the event and now dealing with unaccompanied migrant minors who remain in Ceuta.

Vivas called the situation "unsustainable," and pleaded for government help.

His visit to Brussels comes a week after some 72,000 migrants rushed through the border between Morocco and Spain's North African territory of Ceuta.

The incident caused a spat between several EU countries and Madrid, with Italy suspending the Schengen free-travel pact with Spain.

On Wednesday, Spanish NGO Caminando Fronteras said some 141 people had died on July 30, with 63 bodies found in Morocco and 78 in Ceuta.

Vivas said the large number of unaccompanied migrant children poses 'a high risk for order and public security' as reception centers were overwhelmed Image: Javier Fernández/Europa Press/IMAGO

Ceuta asks for more security resources

The Spanish government said that nearly all of the migrants had returned to Morocco, but Vivas noted that between 3,000 and ‌5,000 migrants were ⁠still in Ceuta.

Vivas also said Ceuta lacked the security resources necessary to deal with the situation.

"Security forces have not been deployed with the intensity required by the situation ⁠we are still facing," he told a European Parliament committee.

"Immigration services have not ⁠been sufficiently reinforced to ⁠handle the border rejections," he added.

Right groups warn some children living on the streets had been beaten and assaulted Image: Violeta Santos Moura/REUTERS

Large number of migrant children in Ceuta

Morocco said it is ready "to work towards identifying unaccompanied ‌minors with a view to their return ‌to ​their homeland," state ​news agency MAP reported on Thursday evening, citing a diplomatic source.

It is estimated that hundreds of unaccompanied minors are currently facing limited access to food, water, shelter and sanitation in Ceuta.

Some children have been beaten and assaulted, says Jose Miguel Morales, head of Federacion Sur Acoge, a migrant rights and assistance group from southern Spain.

"Every day that passes without a solution and without safe accommodation means leaving these children — especially these girls — exposed to all kinds of abuse," he told Spanish public television.

"We are talking about real children — 10 years old or younger in some cases. Many are under 14."

Another charity, Save the Children, urged for all minors to be registered. It also warned that girls face "heightened risks of violence, trafficking and exploitation."

Minors likely to be distributed to ther parts of Spain

In 2025, after a surge of migration overwhelmed reception centers in the Canary Islands, Spain passed an immigration law reform. The new law mandated the redistribution of unaccompanied minors from overstretched territories within 15 days of their case file being completed.

However, the redistribution of the children to the rest of Spain is expected to meet resistance from regions governed by the center-right Popular Party (PP) and the anti-immigration, far-right Vox party.

But Spain's socialist government already has warned against the pushback, with Deputy Prime Minister Carlos Cuerpo saying that PP and its regional governments "must comply with the law just like everyone else."

Skip next section RWE settles with Trump administration to cancel offshore wind projects in US

08/06/2026 August 6, 2026 RWE settles with Trump administration to cancel offshore wind projects in US

One of RWE's offshore wind farms is the Kaskasi site north of Helgoland in Germany, which opened in 2023 Image: Christian Charisius/Pool/REUTERS

German energy giant RWE announced it is abandoning its offshore wind power projects in the US, citing regulatory hurdles, and turning towards investments elsewhere.

The company said in a statement that it had reached a $1.22 billion (roughly €1.05 billion) settlement with the US government to relinquish its offshore wind leases in the New York Bight and off the coasts of Louisiana and California.

"After careful consideration, it was determined that there is no path forward to permit these projects in the US for the foreseeable future," RWE said.

The company said it now planned to reinvest the money in natural gas projects in the US "to meet rapidly growing energy demand" instead of focusing on wind turbines and renewable energy.

US President Donald Trump, who has become a vocal supporter of the fossil fuel industry, seems to reserve a particular distaste for what he typically calls "windmills."

Last week he returned to the issue in comments related to the UK, saying "any time you see windmills, you see a failing country," and claiming — falsely on both counts: "They're all made in China. They're not used by China, but they're made in China."

RWE said it was still investing in its US operations and aiming to almost double its power generation capacity by 2031. It also noted its continued heavy presence in offshore wind projects beyond Germany's borders.

World.title: The Mata Hari affair: Courtesan, spy, legend
World.content:
Regarded the most famous female spy of all time, dancer Mata Hari had men falling at her feet — but was executed for treason. Did she really betray state secrets?

Mata Hari was already a legend in her own lifetime. When she stepped into the Parisian limelight in 1905, she swept high society off its feet.

"She danced with veils and jewel-encrusted bustiers and almost nothing else," the Parisian press reported. "Never had anyone dared to appear unveiled before the gods with such trembling ecstasy. And what wonderful movements she made — both daring and demure at the same time."

Mata Hari had convinced audiences and the press that she was an exotic temple dancer — but the dark-haired performer was actually Dutch.

One of the hallmarks of the Belle Époque era was a heightened fascination with cultures the Parisians deemed to be exotic. Driven by financial desperation, she exploited this demand by pretending to be Indian. To make her act more credible, she fabricated a backstory claiming to be the daughter of a highly esteemed Brahmin.

Mata Hari's sensual dance was her own creation Image: Scherl/SZ Photo/picture alliance

"My mother, first bayadere [dancer] of the Ranganathaswamy Temple, died at the age of fourteen, on the day I was born. After the temple priests cremated her body, they adopted me and named me Mata Hari, which means 'Eye of the Day [a Malay word, Hari means sun]."

She claimed to have learned the sacred temple dances from a young age. During her performances, one veil after another would fall away. Later, she said, "I never danced well. The only reason people came to see me was that I was the first to dare to present myself naked to the public."

From Dutch hatmaker's daughter to Mata Hari

High society couldn't get enough of Mata Hari, unaware that her real name was Margaretha Geertruida Zelle and that she came from the small Dutch town of Leeuwarden.

Born on August 7, 1876, Mata Hari was the daughter of a hatmaker who had become wealthy through stock market speculation. He often spoiled his daughter with lavish gifts. For her sixth birthday, he gave her a carriage drawn by goats.

At the age of 13, Mata Hari's life of luxury ended abruptly. Her father went bankrupt and abandoned the family. Two years later, when her mother passed away, she moved in with relatives. Eventually, she met her husband through a newspaper ad: "An officer from the Dutch East Indies [now Indonesia], currently on home leave, seeks the company of a nice young woman with potential for future marriage. Financial circumstances irrelevant."

The MacLeods around 1900 Image: akg-images/picture alliance

Mata Hari and John Rudolf MacLeod, a Dutch nobleman of Scottish descent who was 20 years her senior, quickly became a couple. In 1897, she accompanied her husband to the Dutch East Indies. But her dream of a happy life never materialized. Frequent arguments strained their relationship. Then, their two-year-old son was tragically poisoned to death. When the MacLeods returned to Europe in 1902, their marriage fell apart. MacLeod left Mata Hari, taking their daughter with him and refusing to pay any alimony, leaving her to fend for herself.

She began her career in Paris as a model for painters and tried her luck at the circus. But it was her creation of the exotic stage persona Mata Hari that ultimately made her famous. She performed at prestigious venues across Europe, including Vienna and Monte Carlo, staying in luxurious hotels. She danced at soirées hosted by the Rothschild banking family and entertained Crown Prince Wilhelm, the son of the German Emperor Wilhelm II. Her success gave her access to the highest social circles, where she formed relationships with diplomats and high-ranking military officers who paid generously for her company.

Mata Hari around 1906: All of Paris wanted to see her Image: akg-images/picture alliance

World War I agent driven by financial hardship

Eventually, Mata Hari's popularity began to wane. Younger dancers began imitating her, and thrill-seeking audiences in Paris moved on to the next sensation. When World War I broke out in 1914, Mata Hari could no longer sustain her luxurious lifestyle.

She accepted an offer from the German consul in the Netherlands to help pay off her debts. She was promised even more money for gathering intelligence from influential figures on the opposing side of the war. Her initial fee was 20,000 francs, a substantial sum at the time. And just like that, she became Agent H 21.

Then, when the French intelligence service approached her and offered her even more money, Mata Hari became a double agent. But she miscalculated the situation. The French had enlisted her so they could catch her spying for the Germans. At the same time, due to increasing suspicion of her activities, the British intelligence service also monitored Mata Hari as she traveled through Europe. On February 13, 1917, she was arrested.

Official photograph of the defendant Margaretha Geertruida MacLeod from 1917 Image: akg-images/picture alliance

On October 15, at the age of 41, Mata Hari was executed for high treason in the moat of the Château de Vincennes, near Paris. Eyewitnesses reported that she faced the 12-man firing squad with her head held high and even blew them a kiss. She refused to wear a blindfold and instead addressed her final words to the commander who gave the order to fire: "Thank you, monsieur!"

Mata Hari's status as a so-called master spy remains questionable. According to documents from the British intelligence service — which remained classified for several decades — any information she may have shared likely did not impact the course of World War I.

It seems that Mata Hari was used as a convenient scapegoat at a time when public enthusiasm for the war had significantly waned. And the French military court needed someone to blame. She herself denied having spied until the very end. Regardless of whether or not she was a master spy, she was undoubtedly a master of self-promotion until her last breath.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Can UN chief's initiative kickstart resolution for Cyprus?
World.content:
UN chief Antonio Guterres considers a resolution to the Cyprus issue to be vital for regional stability and has initiated a new diplomatic effort. What are the prospects for its success?

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres last week became the first UN chief to visit Cyprus in 16 years.

While there, he met the leaders of the island's two communities: Nikos Christodoulides, president of the Republic of Cyprus, and Tufan Erhurman, Turkish Cypriot leader and president of the self-declared Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, which is only recognized by Turkey.

His aim in doing so was to determine whether the conditions exist for restarting negotiations on the Cyprus issue.

Guterres (center) travelled to Cyprus to meet the leaders of the two Cypriot communities, Nikos Christodoulides (center right) and Tufan Erhurman (center left) Image: TRNC Presidency/Handout/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO

Progress on talks has remained stalled since the collapse of negotiations in Crans-Montana, Switzerland, in 2017, when the United Nations made its most comprehensive effort to broker a reunification agreement for the island.

Why now?

So, why has Antonio Guterres decided to launch a new initiative now?

According to diplomatic sources, the answer lies less in developments surrounding the Cyprus issue itself and more in the rapidly changing geopolitical landscape of the wider region.

War in the Middle East, deteriorating relations between Israel and Turkey, and growing strategic competition in the Eastern Mediterranean have heightened UN concerns that the unresolved Cyprus conflict could undermine the stability of the entire region.

Guterres said as much after the joint meeting on July 29. "I do believe that a solution in Cyprus is absolutely crucial, not only to preserve the interests and the peace of the Cyprus people, but also as a factor of stability in what is becoming a dangerously unstable region," he said.

Speaking to DW, Andreas Mavroyiannis, former permanent representative of the Republic of Cyprus to the United Nations and former chief negotiator of the Greek Cypriot side, shared the same concern.

"The strengthening of relations between the Republic of Cyprus and Israel, combined with the deterioration of Israel–Turkey relations, increases the risk of the Cyprus issue being instrumentalized," he told DW.

According to Mavroyiannis, the UN secretary-general fears that Cyprus could, instead of serving as a pillar of stability in the Middle East, become increasingly entangled in regional rivalries and emerge as one of the area's most vulnerable flashpoints.

The European dimension

The UN is not alone in viewing the Cyprus issue through the prism of regional security. The EU has also shown increasing interest in playing a more active political role in efforts to revive the peace process.

A significant step came on July 7, when the European Commission appointed Executive Vice-President Raffaele Fitto as the EU's Special Representative for the Cyprus issue.

His mandate is to support the UN-led process and strengthen the bloc's involvement in efforts to restart negotiations.

A more active role for the EU has long been one of President Nikos Christodoulides' key policy objectives.

During Cyprus' recent presidency of the Council of the European Union, he reminded fellow European leaders that he was "the president of the only EU member state that remains under illegal military occupation."

President Nikos Christodoulides has long been keen for the EU to play a more active role in the search for a resolution to the Cyprus issue Image: Laia Ros/REUTERS

The Cypriot government believes that the EU agenda could provide Ankara with incentives to contribute constructively to progress on the Cyprus issue.

Among the issues viewed as potential leverage are the modernization of the EU–Turkey Customs Union, visa liberalization for Turkish citizens, Turkey's participation in the EU's SAFE defense financing instrument and the prospect of gradually reviving its long-frozen EU accession process.

The next step

While Guterres' decision to announce a new informal expanded 5+1 meeting involving the two Cypriot communities, the three guarantor powers (Greece, Turkey and the UK) plus the UN was widely seen as a positive signal, he deliberately stopped short of setting a date.

Instead, he made it clear that the meeting would only be convened once sufficient progress had been made on confidence-building measures, methodology and the substance of the process.

So, it was no coincidence that he stressed upon arriving in Cyprus that "it depends obviously on the Cypriots themselves," underlining that responsibility for moving the process forward rests primarily with the two communities.

His remarks are directly linked to the lack of tangible progress on confidence-building measures.

The UN Secretary-General says that a 5+1 meeting will only take place once sufficient progress had been made on confidence-building measures, methodology and the substance of the process Image: Petros Karadjias/REUTERS

Despite months of discussions, the two sides failed to reach agreement even on the opening of new crossing points — a step which, according to the UN Secretary-General, could have "a tangible impact on the daily lives of Cypriots," while helping to restore a minimum level of trust ahead of the next phase of negotiations.

Ankara's position remains crucial

The key question, however, extends beyond the two communities themselves and concerns Turkey's willingness to engage.

The real test for the UN is whether Ankara is prepared to return to negotiations conducted within the framework of the UN Security Council resolutions and the agreed basis of a bicommunal, bizonal federation, moving away from the two-state solution it has advocated since the collapse of the Crans-Montana talks in 2017.

So far, Turkey has made no public statement indicating such a shift. The only possible indication comes indirectly from Antonio Guterres' remark that he has "the consent of both sides and the guarantor powers to move towards another 5+1 meeting, provided there is adequate preparation."

The wording suggests that, at least procedurally, Ankara is willing to participate in another informal conference under UN auspices. Whether this also signals a substantive change in Turkey's long-standing position remains, for now, an open question.

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

World.title: Why Iran is sending mixed signals on talks
World.content:
Trump says talks with Iran are underway. Tehran says it is discussing the Strait of Hormuz with Oman, not Washington. Analysts say the gap reflects competing political pressures.

US President Donald Trump on Monday said that negotiations with Iran were ongoing over the Strait of Hormuz, adding that the Islamic Republic was facing a "last chance before decapitation."

Trump told reporters at the White House that he agreed to continue to pursue talks with Iran at the request of Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar and other countries.

His remarks appeared to contradict public statements from Tehran, which has so far denied that negotiations with Washington were taking place.

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei nevertheless confirmed that Tehran was holding talks with Oman over the strategic waterway.

The two sides may therefore be describing the same diplomatic channel in different terms, each using language aimed at its own domestic audience.

Washington describes the Omani mediation as negotiations with Iran. Tehran portrays it as a technical discussion with Oman about shipping through the strait.

Hormuz remains the main obstacle

The Strait of Hormuz has become the main sticking point.

Commercial traffic through key waterway remains severely restricted, while ships continue to face attacks near the strait.

According to data from maritime analytics company Kpler cited by Reuters news agency, only six commercial vessels crossed the route on Monday, down from seven the previous day.

The uncertainty surrounding the key waterway has also affected global markets.

Hopes of diplomatic progress recently pushed oil prices lower and helped stock markets rise. But those movements reflected how sensitive markets remain to any news about the strait, rather than evidence that the crisis had been resolved.

Iran wants some measure of control over vessels entering the Persian Gulf to be recognized. The United States wants the strait fully reopened to unrestricted international shipping.

Babak Dorbeiki, a London-based political analyst and former official at Iran's Strategic Research Center, told DW that the disagreement is no longer simply about whether the two sides are talking.

"The question is what to call those talks and what each side hopes to gain from them," he said.

Trump describes the indirect channel as negotiations because he needs to show that military and economic pressure has brought Tehran back to the table, Dorbeiki said.

He suggested that Iran avoids the same terminology because acknowledging negotiations with Washington could be seen by its domestic opponents as surrender.

The two sides remain far apart.

"Iran wants control over vessels entering the strait, while the United States wants completely free passage," Dorbeiki said. "These positions cannot easily be reconciled."

Divisions inside Iran

The contradictory messages also reflect divisions between rival political factions inside Iran.

Dorbeiki identifies two broad camps.

"The first, which could be described as the 'development and reconstruction through agreement' camp, believes that without sanctions relief and the reopening of Hormuz, Iran's economy cannot recover or even sustain itself," he told DW.

According to Dorbeiki, Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf and some Revolutionary Guard figures with economic interests may be closer to that view.

The opposing camp, which includes the Paydari Front, a small, ultra-conservative party, "sees an agreement with the United States as an ideological defeat" and favors continued resistance.

Leadership vacuum adds to uncertainty

The lack of a clear leader in Iran has added to the uncertainty.

Strait of Hormuz: Iran's most powerful weapon? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Since the country's then supreme leader Ali Khamenei was killed in an airstrike on February 28 the first hours of the US-Israeli war against Iran, authority has become more fragmented.

His son Mojtaba Khamenei was named new supreme leader, but his role remains unclear and he has not been seen in public since the war began amid speculation he was severely injured in the strike.

Dorbeiki says this has allowed rival groups to claim they speak for the leadership.

"Indirect talks through Oman are likely to continue," he told DW. "Pezeshkian will remain under pressure, but he is unlikely to be removed for now because the domestic and international political costs would be high."

Dorbeiki noted that keeping Pezeshkian in office leaves open the option of blaming him if the negotiations fail.

Three competing camps inside Iran

Hassan Asadi Zeidabadi, an Iranian political analyst based in Tehran, believes the main decision-makers in Tehran have already accepted the need for negotiations.

However, he says there are three main camps within the Iranian establishment.

The first consists of government officials dealing with the economic effects of the war and blockade, making them more inclined toward negotiations.

"The second group is made up mainly of military figures who want to improve their position in the conflict before negotiating and remain skeptical of US intentions," Zeidabadi told DW.

"The third group is made up of ideological hardliners who believe that reaching an agreement with Washington after the war and the killing of Iran's supreme leader would mark the end of the Islamic Republic's traditional identity, which is rooted in opposition to the West."

"They fear the day after an agreement," Asadi Zeidabadi added. "For them, a deal with the United States would mean the end of the ideological era they represent and, ultimately, their own removal."

Why the US wants to bring Iran back to the negotiating table To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Zeidabadi said these hardliners retain influence in parliament, the security establishment and the state's propaganda apparatus, and fear the changes a deal could bring.

The future of the talks may depend less on Muscat or Washington than on which factions gain the upper hand in Tehran.

If supporters of an agreement convince the leadership that continued isolation threatens reconstruction, the economy and ultimately the system's survival, diplomacy could move forward.

If hardliners succeed in presenting any compromise as surrender, even the indirect talks could collapse.

Based on the positions outlined by both analysts, further reports of progress are likely to be accompanied by contradictory public statements.

Edited by: Keith Walker

World.title: Sira Rego, ministra de Infancia: “Es lamentable que PP y Vox hagan un uso propagandístico y electoral de Ceuta”
World.content:
El audio de esta noticia utiliza una voz sintética generada por Inteligencia Artificial y podría tener algunas inconsistencias.

La ministra de Juventud e Infancia acaba de llegar a la ciudad autónoma y anuncia en una entrevista con EL PAÍS que el traslado de los menores a las comunidades será inminente

La ministra de Juventud e Infancia, Sira Rego (52 años, Valencia) ha llegado a Ceuta este jueves para gestionar una de las mayores crisis migratorias de España. Rego ha atendido a EL PAÍS por teléfono y anuncia que el traslado de los menores migrantes a las comunidades autónomas se hará en “unas semanas”. Reconoce que todavía no tiene cifras de cuántos niños y adolescentes han llegado a la ciudad autónoma y critica la gestión política del PP y Vox en las últimas horas.

Pregunta. ¿Cuál es la cifra exacta de menores no acompañados que han llegado a Ceuta en los últimos días?

Respuesta. Ahora mismo no estamos en condiciones de dar una cifra definitiva. Están apareciendo niños que estaban escondidos o de los que no teníamos conocimiento de que estuvieran en Ceuta. Ahora trabajamos en todo el proceso que tiene que ver con la identificación y sobre todo con el análisis de las distintas casuísticas y la atención humanitaria de los niños.

P. ¿Manejan alguna horquilla? Las crónicas periodísticas locales hablan de entre 5.000 y 6.000 menores.

R. Honestamente, no creo que lleguemos a ese número, pero no quiero ser irresponsable y dar un dato que ahora no tengo la capacidad de dar.

P. ¿Qué perfiles tienen?

R. Nos estamos encontrando con un número significativo de niños de 12 años y también de niñas. Es una realidad muy diversa en términos de edad y de género. Y esto supone un desafío porque los servicios de atención a la infancia, con las distintas realidades que hay, se tienen que adaptar a esto.

P. ¿Se les ha hecho ya la prueba de edad o se les va a hacer en la península?

R. Sí, quiero destacar que Ceuta va a hacer un enorme esfuerzo para que las pruebas de determinación de la edad se hagan aquí y esto es una buena noticia. Por otro lado, hay muchos niños que son muy pequeños y no hace falta que se les haga prueba de la edad. En estos casos, daríamos el trámite de inmediato.

P. ¿Cuál es la primera solución?

R. La reagrupación familiar. Para esto necesitamos una buena entrevista individualizada a cada niño para conocer su situación concreta. Esto no puede hacerse con brocha gorda. Algunos manifiestan que quieren volver con sus familias y aquí toca hacer un trabajo delicado y muy concienzudo. Se trata de conectar con la familia y, lógicamente, coordinarse con Marruecos para poder proceder a la reagrupación familiar. Y luego, aquellos cuyo retorno no sea posible, se integrarán en el sistema de acogida de nuestro país con todas las garantías.

P. ¿Hay algún país que predomine?

R. No, hay niños que vienen de zonas de conflicto, como Sudán y otros países en conflicto, que son solicitantes de asilo por estar en guerra. Luego también hay niños de otros lugares, como Marruecos, fundamentalmente.

P. En el caso de Marruecos, ¿se sabe ya cuántos han sido reclamados por sus padres?

R. No. No lo tenemos. La situación de desborde ha sido tan grande que ahora estamos todavía en el proceso de registro de menores y está siendo muy complicado.

P. ¿Cómo funciona entonces el sistema ahora?

R. Está siendo gradual. Muchos menores van a la policía y se registran. Y si hay alguna familia que les ha dado cobijo y los ha atendido, tienen que facilitar que estos chiquillos puedan llegar a puntos de atención para que se les haga el registro adecuado. A partir de ahí entran en el servicio de acogida con carácter de emergencia. Y luego nosotros ya podemos empezar a trabajar con la situación concreta de cada menor y ver las circunstancias que tiene. Necesitamos unos días para ver todas las cifras. El 16 de agosto se va a trasladar un equipo del ministerio para trabajar en los protocolos y en las opciones de acogida. Hemos aportado una partida presupuestaria de 25 millones de euros que se llevará al último consejo de ministros de este mes.

P. Hemos visto imágenes de menores con soldados siendo trasladados a la frontera. ¿Qué le parecen estos vídeos y fotos?

R. Preocupan. Vamos a pedir que se aclare cualquier circunstancia. Tenemos en marcha todos los dispositivos para evitar que no haya ningún tipo de vulneración de derechos fundamentales. La situación de desborde ha sido muy grande y, más allá de estas imágenes que, insisto, son dolorosas, nosotros llamamos a que se eviten.

P. ¿Irán a la fiscalía si las imágenes están perfectamente documentadas?

R. Vamos a ver primero la situación que hay. A partir de ahí, todas las garantías para cumplir la ley.

P. En cuanto al traslado de estos menores a otras comunidades, ¿se sabe ya cuándo puede empezar?

R. No tengo una fecha concreta, pero hablamos de unas pocas semanas. No puedo dar un día concreto. Estamos explorando varios mecanismos dada la situación de excepcionalidad. Uno es el artículo 35 de la Ley de Extranjería, que nos permite todavía generar más traslados a península para la acogida vinculante y solidaria del conjunto de comunidades autónomas.

P. Sin embargo, a los menores que solicitan asilo les corresponde al Gobierno su gestión.

R. Sí, y por tanto tienen un trato diferenciado, pero para estos menores el traslado también se hará en las mismas fechas.

P. El PP dice que acatará la ley, pero Vox se niega a acoger a estos menores. ¿Qué puede pasar si se niegan?

R. No pueden negarse. Hay una ley y la ley se cumple, salvo que quieran prevaricar. No se me ocurre que vayamos a llegar a esta situación, francamente. PP y Vox están haciendo un uso propagandístico de lo que ha ocurrido aquí, algo absolutamente lamentable. Estamos hablando de más de 140 personas fallecidas. De un momento de muchísima tensión, de un componente de tragedia humana extraordinario y, por tanto, lo que toca en este momento es tener un poco más de lectura y, sobre todo, no utilizar a la infancia como un elemento para hacer caja electoral o caja partidista.

P. Algunas otras comunidades también se quejan de las capacidades para acoger a estos menores. ¿Tienen previsto revisarlo?

R. La mayor parte de las comunidades tienen plazas libres. No tenemos todavía el feedback con ellas, pero hemos convocado una comisión sectorial para la semana que viene. La idea es que todos los procedimientos se aceleren para esta acogida.

P. ¿Qué le diría a aquellos ciudadanos que ven en la acogida un problema?

R. Que acudan a información veraz y a los datos. A lo largo de este último año hemos gestionado 2.000 expedientes de niños migrantes, fundamentalmente de Canarias, Ceuta y Melilla. No hemos tenido ningún incidente. Invita a pensar. ¿Qué ocurriría si fueran nuestros hijos e hijas?, ¿y si viviéramos en un país que no diera oportunidades o estuviera en guerra? Hay personas palestinas entre algunas de las personas que han llegado a Ceuta. No hace falta explicar más. Nadie, nadie se lanza al mar y se pone en riesgo, salvo que lo que deja en tierra es todavía peor que lo que puede encontrarse en el mar. Siempre hay que intentar acercarse a las historias de vida de la gente.

P. Ha pasado una semana ya y muchos ciudadanos se preguntan cómo ha podido pasar esto. ¿Cómo en una ciudad de 80.000 personas entran más de 70.000 en unas horas? El Gobierno habla de mafias y de una sentencia del Tribunal Supremo y otros expertos apuntan a Marruecos…

R. No creo que haya una sola causa y creo que es importante que se investigue y se aclare lo que ha sucedido. La situación en la frontera sur y en la frontera del Mediterráneo central en Europa no son situaciones migratorias recientes. Sabemos lo que está sucediendo en muchas fronteras exteriores de la Unión Europea y sabemos que una buena parte de lo que está ocurriendo tiene directamente muchísimo que ver con la política migratoria de la Unión Europea. Esto es el resultado de un fracaso de un modelo migratorio, el de la Unión Europea, que se ha empeñado en externalizar fronteras y poner la gestión de fronteras en terceros países que en muchos casos tienen intereses que no son intereses compartidos con los de los territorios europeos con los que hacen frontera. Estamos ante la urgencia de pensar en un modelo migratorio diferente.

P. ¿La cooperación con Marruecos en materia de infancia y protección de menores funciona?

R. Por nuestra parte no tenemos una relación directa. Hay otros mecanismos que se establecen más a través de fiscalía y del ministerio de justicia y de otros ministerios.

P. ¿Cree que Marruecos es un socio fiable?

R. Marruecos tiene unos intereses que no son necesariamente compartidos con nuestro país y yo creo que poner la política migratoria en terceros países no es una buena idea.

P. Sumar y Vox coinciden en excluir a Marruecos de la organización del Mundial 2030 junto a España y Portugal...

R. No he tenido oportunidad de hablar con la ministra de Deportes del asunto, pero comparto la posición de mi grupo (Sumar). Ahora tenemos la oportunidad de abrir un debate más amplio, que tiene que ver con la participación de países que deben cumplir un mínimo de derechos humanos a la hora de participar en eventos deportivos de carácter internacional.

P. Hace unas horas hemos conocido que no estará en ninguna lista electoral del año que viene. ¿Se retira?

R. De la política institucional, sí, y creo que es muy saludable. Ahora toca hacer una reflexión profunda acerca del momento de la izquierda. La izquierda tiene que repensarse en términos de proyecto político y de proyecto estratégico.

World.title: Vivas ante la Eurocámara: “La seguridad de Ceuta está en manos de un tercero, Marruecos, que no reconoce nuestra soberanía”
World.content:
El presidente de la ciudad autónoma de Ceuta, Juan Jesús Vivas, ha dejado claro este jueves en el Parlamento Europeo que, para él, lo sucedido los días 30 y 31 de julio “no es una crisis migratoria al uso”. “Es un episodio a través del que se ha puesto en jaque nuestra integridad: La de Ceuta, la de España, la de Europa. [...] Nuestra seguridad está en manos de un país tercero, Marruecos, que no reconoce nuestra soberanía”, ha señalado el veterano dirigente en una sesión extraordinaria de la Comisión de Asuntos de Interior de la Eurocámara, que se ha reunido por videoconferencia. En ese foro, el ceutí ha destacado, además, que la ciudad todavía no ha vuelto a la normalidad y que necesita refuerzos para resolver, entre otras cosas, “el colapso de los centros de acogida de migrantes”.

La sesión celebrada este jueves por la tarde ha sido extraordinaria, convocada por el presidente de la Comisión, el popular español Javier Zarzalejos. Él, como otros eurodiputados conservadores, ha lamentado que no hayan comparecido los ministros de Interior, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, y de Seguridad Social y Migraciones, Elma Saiz. Ambos estaban invitados a la sesión, aunque su presencia no es obligatoria. Sí que ha estado presente el comisario de Interior, Magnus Brunner, quien ha recordado que “la situación en Ceuta es, ante todo, competencia de las autoridades españolas, que son las encargadas de gestionar el sistema de acogida”.

El presidente ceutí, Juan Jesús Vivas, tras su reunión con el rey Felipe VI este jueves en Mallorca. Ballesteros (EFE)

Vivas ha comenzado su intervención ante los eurodiputados subrayando que es “uno de los momentos más difíciles en la historia reciente de la ciudad”. Él ha calificado de “invasión” lo sucedido. “Esta calificación coincide con la que dio el presidente del Gobierno de España, quien el mismo viernes manifestó que estábamos ante un ataque, una violación de la integridad territorial”, ha continuado tras ilustrar que las 80.000 personas que entraron en Ceuta entre el pasado jueves y viernes eran una cantidad “equivalente a toda la población de Ceuta”. “Es como si en España entraran 50 millones de personas”, ha comparado en otro momento.

El presidente de Ceuta también ha reclamado la “expulsión inmediata” de los migrantes irregulares que cruzaron la frontera y todavía están en la ciudad autónoma. Según los números que ha facilitado en el Parlamento, serían entre 3.000 y 6.000 personas. “El hecho de que todavía no conozcamos las cifras en estos momentos de las personas que permanecen en la ciudad pone de manifiesto la precariedad de medios con la que todavía se está actuando”, ha explicado ante los eurodiputados.

A esto, Brunner, el comisario austriaco, ha añadido: “Esperamos que las autoridades españolas, en colaboración con las autoridades marroquíes, cumplan su compromiso de garantizar que las medidas que adopten en respuesta a la situación no tengan repercusiones en el espacio Schengen. Esto refleja las opiniones expresadas por los Estados miembros en la reunión informal de Justicia y Asuntos de Interior celebrada el martes. La Comisión está en estrecho contacto con las autoridades españolas para evaluar rápidamente sus necesidades y prestar apoyo cuando sea necesario”.

Futuro viaje de Felipe VI a Ceuta

También este jueves, Felipe VI ha recibido al presidente ceutí, ante el que se ha comprometido a visitar la ciudad autónoma, según ha asegurado Vivas a la salida de la audiencia, celebrada en el palacio de Marivent en Palma. La reunión de Felipe VI con Vivas, que no se había anunciado hasta media tarde de este miércoles, es el último acto de la agenda del Monarca antes de viajar a Colombia para asistir a la investidura del nuevo jefe de Estado del país sudamericano, Abelardo de la Espriella, este viernes en Cali.

El Rey VI junto a Juan Jesús Vivas a las puertas de Marivent, este jueves. Raúl Terrel (Europa Press)

Tras el encuentro, Vivas ha asegurado que el Rey visitará Ceuta, aunque no hay fecha aún para ese viaje. “El Rey está comprometido con la visita a Ceuta y estoy convencido de que la realizará, porque siempre cumple sus compromisos, lo que no puedo decir es cuándo tendrá lugar esa visita”, ha asegurado el ceutí. “A mí no me cabe la menor duda de que el Rey nos va visitar”, ha insistido a preguntas de los periodistas. Preguntado por los rumores de una posible nueva intentona de aluvión para el 15 de agosto, Vivas ha apelado a un refuerzo de la seguridad. “A la vista de la experiencia vivida los días 30 y 31 de julio, confiamos plenamente en nuestras Fuerzas y Cuerpos de Seguridad del Estado y en las Fuerzas Armadas para evitar que vuelva a producirse una entrada masiva de esas características”.

El Rey, que ha estado en contacto con Vivas a lo largo de la semana, lo ha recibido en torno a las 17.50 de esta tarde al pie de las escaleras de entrada del palacio, y la reunión ha concluido minutos después de las 19.00. Durante el encuentro, el Monarca ha transmitido “un mensaje de cariño, apoyo y ánimo” para los ceutíes, según ha referido luego Vivas, que ha asegurado salir de la reunión “reconfortado” por las palabras de Felipe VI.

Vivas, el presidente autonómico con un mandato más longevo (lleva 25 años ininterrumpidos en el cargo), ha cargado en la última semana contra su país vecino. “Marruecos ha demostrado que no es fiable, hay que exigirle respeto”, señaló en una entrevista a EL PAÍS en la que apuntaba que lo ocurrido difícilmente se podía “calificar eso de crisis migratoria” y añadió que “la gente tenía la percepción de que esto, si no orquestado, era favorecido o permitido por parte de Marruecos”. Los servicios de inteligencia españoles han concluido que Rabat permitió y utilizó la oleada humana sobre Ceuta, pero no la planeó. “Todos queremos que haya unas buenas relaciones, pero si Marruecos no quiere tenerlas, pues habrá que pedirle que por lo menos respete”, apuntó también Vivas.

Tras el aluvión, Felipe VI aseguró haber seguido “con gran preocupación e indignación los graves acontecimientos en Ceuta y en menor medida en Melilla”, según comunicó la Casa Real tras la llegada de migrantes. En la misma nota se indicaba que el Rey cree necesario adoptar “todas aquellas medidas que transmitan de forma unida, clara y determinante a las poblaciones de Ceuta y Melilla el apoyo y cariño del resto de España” y aseguró que “el Estado debe velar por su seguridad y por evitar que estos hechos –que, además, se han traducido en una triste y trágica pérdida de decenas de vidas– vuelvan a repetirse”.

Previo al encuentro con el Rey, el presidente autonómico se ha visto también este jueves con su homóloga en Baleares y compañera de filas en el PP, Marga Prohens, con la que ha compartido que su ciudad sigue aún en una situación de “incertidumbre” y “lejos de la normalidad”. Vivas ha venido insistiendo, ya desde antes del 30 de julio, el día del aluvión de migrantes, que su ciudad no cuenta con los recursos suficientes para hacer frente a un fenómeno así. “Consterna escuchar al presidente de Ceuta confirmar que advirtió semanas antes al Gobierno de España del incremento de personas que estaban cruzando ilegalmente la frontera”, ha asegurado Prohens en redes sociales tras su encuentro con Vivas, que se ha prolongado durante más de una hora.

World.title: La CIA refuerza su presencia en Cuba para presionar por un cambio de régimen
World.content:
Estados Unidos considera a la isla una prioridad de sus agencias de inteligencia y los equipos en el terreno buscan obtener más información en un momento en que no está descartada una operación militar

Estados Unidos aprieta el puño sobre Cuba en busca de un cambio de régimen. Está aplicando una estrategia de asfixia progresiva para forzar la caída del castrismo.
