World.title: From “rapid response” to possible law: who are Georgia’s national values being protected from?
World.content:
The Georgian government has not ruled out introducing legislation against what it describes as the erosion of national identity. Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze says the proposed rules could cover insults directed at saints, monarchs and prominent public figures. No draft law has been introduced yet. However, experts argue that the groundwork is already being laid. Members of the ruling team have already begun discussing penalties and possible regulation of the media.

As the ruling Georgian Dream party debates possible punishment for insulting national values, it is worth examining what such measures could cover and what Russia’s experience suggests.

From assaults to a campaign to “protect national values”

The debate over possible legislation followed an attack on comedian Onise Okriashvili over a joke he made on YouTube. Late on 22 July, a man assaulted him near his home in Tbilisi. The attacker, Niko Khurtsilava, said he acted because Okriashvili had insulted Georgian national culture.

Even before the assault, pro-government television channels had launched a media campaign against Okriashvili. They broadcast a clipped excerpt from his YouTube show in which he referred to renowned Georgian writer Nodar Dumbadze using obscene language.

The writer’s grandson, Nodar Macharashvili, publicly backed the attacker. A few days after the incident, MMA fighter Giorgi Kartvelishvili, who also described himself as Khurtsilava’s friend, announced the creation of a new movement that would provide “rapid response” to insults directed at sacred values, ancestors, religion and history.

“If protecting our culture and national identity requires it, we will not shy away from any threat. We are ready to take responsibility for every action we take and, if necessary, even go to prison,” Kartvelishvili said.

He did not specify what he meant by “rapid response”. He also declined to answer journalists’ questions about the use of physical violence and vigilantism.

On 28 July, the group applied to the Public Registry to register its newly established organisation under the name National Generation.

A week after the attack on Okriashvili, on 30 July, another initiative group emerged to “protect national values”. It brought together actor Giorgi Shanidze, director Giorgi Sikharulidze and Kote Mzhavia, director of the Batumi Theatre.

Unlike the first movement, this group called for legal mechanisms rather than “rapid response”. Its members said the law should protect the church, sacred sites, historical heroes and national values.

“Freedom of expression is a fundamental value. However, that right cannot become a tool for insulting the sacred symbols and core values that form the country’s historical, cultural and spiritual foundation,” Giorgi Shanidze said.

The statement refers to “externally funded destructive groups” whose activities, it says, are creating confrontation between the Georgian nation and small minority groups.

“To prevent the situation from escalating further and reaching the point where even the wise Georgian people could lose patience, responsible steps must be taken and the existing problems must be resolved through legal and peaceful means,” the statement says.

The group plans to hold consultations with lawyers, historians, artists and athletes before drafting a legislative proposal.

However, neither the bill nor its concept has been published, so it remains unclear which actions could become punishable. The proposed form of liability and possible penalties also remain unknown.

What could a law on national values include?

On 3 August, Irakli Kobakhidze told journalists that he did not rule out adopting such legislation. However, he said the authorities had not yet discussed any specific proposals.

“There is indeed a need to respond to the coordinated attack against our identity,” Kobakhidze said.

He also identified possible subjects of future regulation, including saints, kings and prominent public figures.

According to Kobakhidze, insults directed at Georgian saints and kings are part of “a chain of coordinated, commissioned actions.”

“These are not simply untalented people. These are people carrying out a specific assignment. The purpose of that assignment is simple: they are trying to weaken our national identity. That is why they are doing all this,” he said.

Kobakhidze did not specify who had allegedly commissioned the campaign. He also provided no evidence to support the claim.

“We must take every possible measure to counter such processes. If that requires adopting a law, we can discuss that as well.”

Kobakhidze’s remarks do not necessarily mean such a law will be adopted. However, they indicate that the initiative has already received political backing from the prime minister.

Meanwhile, MPs aligned with the ruling party have outlined possible restrictions in greater detail.

Georgian Dream MP Irakli Kadagishvili linked the issue to public swearing, abusive language and hooliganism.

“When people use obscene language against a specific individual or institution at a rally, is that freedom of expression or simply abusive language and hooliganism? We cannot just leave it like this.”

Kadagishvili said he did not know what the legislation might ultimately contain. At the same time, he suggested that the media could also fall within its scope.

The MP claimed that certain television channels — referring to opposition broadcasters — had aired 3,500 “anti-church” reports over the past year and a half. He did not explain how he arrived at that figure or what criteria he used to classify the reports as “anti-church”.

Kadagishvili also suggested that “offensive” media content could become subject to legal regulation.

Guram Macharashvili, a member of the People’s Power party, openly called for penalties for public insults. He said the law should protect faith, the church, the patriarch and national traditions.

“When you publicly insult values such as faith, the church, the patriarch or our traditions, that should, of course, be punishable.”

Macharashvili argued that Georgia had offered excessive protection to dissenting views.

“Dissent has always enjoyed a certain degree of protection in Georgia. But recently, I would say it has been protected in an ultra-liberal, excessive way, and that needs to change.”

What counts as an “insult” — and who decides?

Article 17 of Georgia’s Constitution guarantees freedom of thought and expression. It also prohibits persecution for expressing an opinion.

The constitution also guarantees media freedom and prohibits censorship.

The state may restrict freedom of expression only by law and only when necessary in a democratic society. Such restrictions may serve aims including public safety and the protection of other people’s rights. The constitution does not list “insulting national values” as a separate ground for limiting freedom of expression.

At the same time, freedom of expression is not absolute. The law may restrict incitement to violence, threats, harassment or defamation. However, such restrictions must be clearly defined and predictable.

By contrast, “insulting national values” is a far more ambiguous concept. It remains unclear whether the proposed law would protect the reputation of specific individuals or instead safeguard abstract values or historical figures.

It is also unclear who would decide which saints, kings and public figures deserve legal protection. Would the law apply only to historical figures? Where would the line be drawn between legitimate historical criticism and an “insult”?

For example, pro-government television channels also launched a campaign against literary scholar Levan Berdzenishvili after he criticised the policies of Georgian King Erekle II. Berdzenishvili neither joked about the king nor used obscene language. Nevertheless, Georgian Dream MPs and pro-government media sharply attacked him.

It also remains unclear whether the proposed restrictions would apply to satire, works of art or academic research. Another unanswered question is whether critical media coverage of members of the clergy could be treated as an “insult to sacred values”.

Protecting patriotism or deepening political divisions?

Opposition politicians see the initiative as an attempt to mobilise political support.

Giorgi Sharashidze of the For Georgia party argues that the government is trying to claim a monopoly on patriotism.

“They have a very calculated strategy — to gain exclusive ownership of patriotic issues. Everything serves that goal. They want everyone else to appear as opponents of Georgia’s identity, traditions and church, while presenting themselves as the sole defenders of those values.”

Giorgi Shalamberidze of the First Georgia party believes the proposed law could serve another political purpose.

“It could be a political manoeuvre. It may help mobilise a particular segment of voters, or it could mark the beginning of a much broader tightening of legislation in the long term.”

Shalamberidze acknowledged that freedom of expression can be restricted in certain circumstances. However, he pointed to Georgia’s current political environment.

“If this becomes law and is used as a tool, the question is how it will affect political actors, political parties and their freedom of expression, and to what extent it will become a mechanism for restricting their rights.”

Historians’ concerns

It remains unclear where the proposed law would draw the line between insulting a historical figure and offering a critical assessment. That uncertainty raises concerns for historians, researchers and authors.

Assessing historical figures often requires revisiting disputed facts, competing interpretations and long-established narratives.

If the state decides which interpretations are acceptable, the law could become a tool for restricting academic research and scholarly debate.

It also remains unclear whether the proposed rules would apply to academic publications, public lectures, textbooks or documentary films.

Another unanswered question is who would decide where legitimate historical criticism ends and an “insult” begins.

Historian Irakli Khvadagiani argues that placing faith and artistic expression into legal categories contradicts their very nature.

“Faith and creativity do not recognise prohibitions, nor do they accept categories imposed unilaterally. The idea of banning them through legislation is absurd. Humanity went through this centuries ago. It is simply the obsession of a dictator trying to bend society to his will.”

Risk of creating artificial divisions?

Conflict analyst Paata Zakareishvili believes the proposed legislation could fuel ethnic and religious tensions. In his view, the vague concept of “protecting national identity” risks creating new fault lines within society.

“There are not enough supporters of this ideology in Georgia for Georgian Dream to sustain permanent tensions between Christians and Muslims, between Georgians and non-Georgians, or between Georgian speakers and those who do not speak the language.”

Zakareishvili sees elements of far-right ideology in the government’s approach. He argues that it runs counter to the principles of equality and justice.

“This is a classic example of pure far-right ideology. Humanity has gone through this countless times, and it has repeatedly led to catastrophe and world wars, bringing nothing but destruction.”

The conflict analyst also links the initiative to the electoral cycle. Georgia’s next parliamentary elections are not due until October 2028. However, Zakareishvili believes the ruling party has already begun preparing its campaign.

“Georgian Dream is getting ready for the elections. Before the vote, it needs to create exactly these kinds of flashpoints.”

Cases of violence carried out in the name of “protecting traditions” Invoking the need to protect national and religious values is not a new phenomenon in Georgian politics. In 2023, a man attacked Zurab Japaridze, leader of the Girchi – More Freedom party, in the city of Gori. The attacker said he acted because Japaridze had insulted the church and was “corrupting children”.

Later that year, protesters disrupted a lecture by Levan Berdzenishvili in Kvareli. They accused him of insulting King Erekle II and Christian values. In Tbilisi, demonstrators also threw eggs at Berdzenishvili.

On 5 July 2021, opponents of Tbilisi Pride attacked journalists and activists. They justified the violence by saying they were defending the family, the church and traditional values. More than 50 journalists were injured.

In November 2019, far-right and anti-LGBT groups tried to disrupt the premiere of the film And Then We Danced. The Georgian Orthodox Church described the film as “an insult to Georgia’s traditional values”. Protesters attempted to storm cinemas. One of them threw a stone at civil activist Anna Subeliani, causing a serious head injury. Police arrested 12 people that evening.

In January 2024, activist Nata Peradze splashed paint on an icon in Tbilisi’s Holy Trinity Cathedral depicting Saint Matrona of Moscow alongside Joseph Stalin. Far-right groups later gathered outside Peradze’s home, demanding that she be punished.

On 17 May 2013, thousands of people, including members of the clergy, attacked participants in an anti-homophobia rally. At least 17 people were injured. In 2021, the European Court of Human Rights ruled that the violence had taken place in circumstances of the state’s effective acquiescence.

Lessons from Russia: when the state decides what people can joke about

Russia’s experience is particularly relevant in this context because the substance and rationale behind many legislative initiatives promoted by Georgian Dream resemble measures introduced in Russia years earlier.

The clearest example is the Law on Transparency of Foreign Influence. Russian authorities initially justified their version as a tool to ensure transparency over foreign funding. They later expanded it into a mechanism used against independent media outlets and civil society organisations.

Lessons from Russia: when the state decides what people can joke about

Russia’s experience is relevant here because both the substance and the rationale behind many legislative initiatives promoted by Georgian Dream resemble measures introduced in Russia in recent years.

The clearest example is the Law on Transparency of Foreign Influence. Russian authorities initially presented their version as a transparency measure for foreign funding. They later expanded it into a tool used against independent media and civil society organisations.

It is therefore worth looking at how Russia gradually developed legislation under the banner of protecting “traditional values”, religious feelings and historical memory.

Russia did not build its legal framework for protecting religion, historical memory and “traditional values” overnight. The system evolved step by step.

Offending religious feelings

In 2012, members of the punk group Pussy Riot staged an anti-Vladimir Putin performance inside Moscow’s Cathedral of Christ the Saviour. A court convicted them of hooliganism motivated by religious hatred.

A year later, Russia toughened Article 148 of its Criminal Code by criminalising public acts that show clear disrespect for society and are committed with the intention of offending the religious feelings of believers.

One of the best-known cases under the law involved blogger Ruslan Sokolovsky, who filmed himself playing Pokémon Go inside a church and posted the video online. In other videos, he also criticised religion and the Russian Orthodox Church.

In 2017, a court gave Sokolovsky a three-and-a-half-year suspended prison sentence. The case involved several criminal charges, including offending believers’ religious feelings and inciting hatred.

In 2024, the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Sokolovsky’s conviction had violated his right to freedom of expression. The court found that offensive or vulgar speech does not automatically amount to hate speech.

“Traditional values” as state policy

In November 2022, Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree on protecting “traditional Russian spiritual and moral values”.

The document lists patriotism, dignity, life and the traditional family among those values. It also includes service to the fatherland, historical memory and continuity between generations.

According to the decree, external forces threaten these values by acting inside Russia through extremist and terrorist organisations.

The decree also identifies the United States and other “unfriendly states” as sources of those threats.

Russian authorities have explicitly linked cultural and values policy to national security.

A similar narrative has emerged in Georgian Dream’s campaign. Both initiative groups have spoken of a coordinated attack on Georgia’s “national identity”. Prime Minister Kobakhidze has used the same wording.

Legal protection of history

Article 354.1 of Russia’s Criminal Code is titled “Rehabilitation of Nazism”. Lawmakers originally introduced it to prohibit the denial of crimes established by the Nuremberg Tribunal.

However, the law goes much further. It also bans the dissemination of what authorities consider to be “knowingly false information” about the Soviet Union’s actions during the Second World War. The article also protects the honour and dignity of war veterans.

In 2021, lawmakers added a new offence covering the “insulting of the memory of the defenders of the Fatherland”. The law also criminalises offensive use of military glory symbols.

As a result, the legislation does more than prohibit denial of historical facts. It also protects the state’s official interpretation of the Soviet Union’s role in history.

According to a 2025 study by the human rights project OVD-Info, Russian courts handed down 25 convictions under Article 354.1 between 2015 and 2019. Many of the cases concerned interpretations of the Soviet Union’s actions and historical comparisons.

Between 2022 and May 2025, OVD-Info recorded 212 prosecutions under the same article.

A court gave Kazan resident Zulfiya Sitdikova a two-year suspended sentence over posters reading “No to war” and “9 Way”. She replaced the “M” in “May” with a “W”, and investigators interpreted this as desecration of Victory Day symbols.

Authorities also opened a criminal case against historian Mikhail Belousov. Investigators accused him of denying facts established by the Nuremberg Tribunal and spreading false information about the Soviet Union.

Prosecutors also opened two cases against historian Tamara Eidelman. They argued that her video lectures showed disrespect for Russia’s military remembrance days.

Russia has therefore created a system in which historians and society no longer have the final say in historical debates. Instead, investigators, expert witnesses and the courts have become the ultimate arbiters.

Where will Georgia draw the line?

Georgia has not yet introduced such a bill, so it is impossible to say whether it will follow the Russian path.

However, statements by members of the ruling party already suggest a broad range of protected subjects, including the church, the patriarch, saints, kings, public figures, traditions and even media content.

Russia’s experience also suggests that broadly defined protected values can gradually expand over time.

Protecting national values in Georgia

World.title: First images show Moon's fresh crater after stray rocket impact
World.content:
A South Korean satellite has captured the first images of the Moon's new impact site caused by a stray SpaceX rocket stage.

The Korea Aerospace Research Institute's Danuri spacecraft passed over the impact site soon after the Falcon 9 upper stage inadvertently ploughed into the Moon on Wednesday, about 4:35pm AEST.

Danuri made multiple passes, snapping photos from lunar orbit that the space agency later released.

The terrain is noticeably darker where the rocket hit and carved out a crater, ejecting dust and rock across the surface.

KASA says its lunar orbiter captured the new images. (Reuters: Korea AeroSpace Administration)

Korean space officials said Danuri gathered before-and-after shots.

NASA expects its Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter to flyover the crash site next week to view the aftermath.

SpaceX launched Danuri from Cape Canaveral in 2022.

The company also sent a pair of private lunar landers to the Moon last year.

The upper stage from that launch is what crashed into the Moon this week at 8,700 kilometres an hour, after being placed on an accidental collision course by solar activity and gravity, according to SpaceX.

Before the satellite images were released, a telescope in Chile had spotted what astronomers identified as the debris plume resulting from the impact.

The team detected a stream of sodium and lithium stretching for tens of kilometres into space for at least five to 10 minutes following the impact.

AP

World.title: Athletes go missing after Commonwealth Games
World.content:
Several athletes, including four members of the Ugandan boxing team, have reportedly failed to return home after competing in the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

Ugandan sports website NBS Sport said four members of the nation's boxing squad had gone missing in Scotland and had not rejoined the rest of the delegation before the team's scheduled return to Uganda.

The Pakistan Today newspaper also reported boxer Qudrat Ullah did not return home with the Pakistani team.

Scottish police are investigating the reports after the games finished last Sunday, local time.

"Police Scotland has received reports of several athletes who are unaccounted for," a spokesperson said.

"Enquiries are ongoing to assess the circumstances, and early engagement is taking place with the Home Office."

'No idea what type of asylum'

Uganda's chef de mission, Godwin Kayangwe, said he hoped the missing athletes would return before their visas expire in October.

"I don't know anything about why they decided not to fly home, but I know they communicated with their team manager and said they would be coming back," Mr Kayangwe said in an interview with BBC Scotland.

"But after that their phones went off, so they have definitely broken the camp rules because no athlete is supposed to leave without permission.

"I have totally no idea, absolutely no idea what type of asylum they would be seeking. It's nothing political, it's nothing to do with gender or something [like that]. I have absolutely no idea why they would be doing that."

NBS Sport identified the missing Ugandan athletes as two men and two women: Angel Katushabe, Nuhu Batte, Ibrahim Khemis and Emily Nakalema.

Team Uganda during the athletes parade at the Commonwealth Games opening ceremony. (Reuters: Hannah Mckay)

There have been numerous cases of athletes seeking asylum following previous Commonwealth Games, including 2018 on the Gold Coast and 2014, also in Glasgow.

Former Iranian footballers granted citizenship Fatemeh Pasandideh and Atefeh Ramezanisadeh sought asylum after the Asian Cup in March this year, due to fears of reprisal from the Iranian government.

In March, five Iranian football players were granted asylum in Australia after competing in the 2026 AFC Women's Asian Cup, after they escaped from their handlers.

Three of the players returned to Iran, while two remained and were eventually granted Australian citizenship.

Glasgow 2026 chief executive Phil Batty said the games were working with the police.

"We want to deliver a safe and secure games, so we work really closely with Police Scotland, the Border Force, and UK visas and immigration to make sure everyone arrives and departs in line with regulation," Mr Batty said.

Some 3,000 athletes from 74 nations attended the 11 days of the Glasgow Games.

World.title: Elizabeth Young wants the system that 'killed' her daughter fixed
World.content:
Peak mental health groups and the mother of a Bondi Junction stabbing attack victim have warned the state government's response to the incident will not prevent similar tragedies.

The state announced this week it would accept the recommendations of the coronial report into the incident, but the groups say its full response tells another story.

The recommendations were the result of a five-week coronial inquest into the deaths of six people at Bondi Westfield in 2024, killed by Joel Cauchi during a psychotic episode.

The six people killed, clockwise from top left: Yixuan Cheng, Faraz Tahir, Jade Young, Pikria Darchia, Dawn Singleton and Ashlee Good. (Supplied)

The state this week said it supported 11 recommendations in full. Two others — for modelling of short-term accommodation in Greater Sydney for those experiencing mental health issues and homelessness and a review of NSW Ambulance's major incident response plan — were supported in principle.

The six groups, which represent mental health consumers, carers, and psychiatrists, said the government has declined to commit to concrete action and was withholding a key report into gaps in mental health funding.

The groups include BEING Mental Health, Mental Health Carers NSW, the Mental Health Coordinating Council and the Australian Society of Psychiatrists.

Elizabeth Young, whose daughter Jade Young was killed in the attack, said she was "cynical" about the government's response.

"I lined up 50 years of political activity or inactivity with the near 50 years of my daughter's life, and she was killed because our system failed," Ms Young said.

"Although I'm pleased that [the government] has addressed 11 of the 13 recommendations, I'm fairly sceptical about what will actually be done in the practical sense."

'Goodwill is just a promise on paper'

Australian Society of Psychiatrists chief executive Pramudie Gunaratne said the government's "in principle" commitments to key recommendations "kicks the can down the road".

"We've already seen how the years of inaction have resulted in a tragedy, and even after that tragedy, if nothing concrete happens … then it's a ticking time bomb waiting for another tragedy to occur," Dr Gunaratne said.

Pramudie Gunaratne said "concrete" action was needed. (ABC News)

She called on the government to act on recommendations to commit to fully funding supported housing for people experiencing mental health issues.

Giancarlo de Vera, the chief executive of BEING Mental Health, which represents people living with mental health issues in New South Wales, called on the government to do more.

"We want to translate the goodwill into actual commitment," de Vera said.

"Goodwill is just a promise on paper; we really need commitments to address the structural issues that the coronial inquest found."

Government under pressure to do more

Opposition leader Kellie Sloane has called on the government to release the report into mental health funding gaps and address the "enormous strain" on the system.

"We are in a world of pain if this isn't addressed properly," Ms Sloane said.

"The state Labor government has a habit of commissioning reports and then not revealing the details.

"This is too important to hide away."

NSW government accepts recommendations from Bondi Junction inquest The NSW government has announced it will accept all recommendations directed towards it from the Westfield Bondi Junction coronial inquest, six months after the findings were handed down.

Minister for Mental Health Rose Jackson on Wednesday acknowledged the government needs to do more.

"We accept the principle that there does need to be more support for people who are living with complex mental illness to stay stable in their accommodation, but we're rolling out different programs in order to provide that," Ms Jackson said.

She said the government is planning to release the gap analysis into mental health funding and was working with the Mental Health Alliance to finalise it.

World.title: Dogs coach says he would have signed concussion waiver to keep playing
World.content:
As the AFL and Geelong continue to face questions about their handling of a concussion issue, Western Bulldogs coach Luke Beveridge believes players are looked after better than ever.

The Cats avoided any sanction from the AFL for making a deal with a player who had a history of concussions that required him to assume all legal responsibility for future brain trauma.

Geelong had a secret arrangement in 2024, which was revealed on Thursday, with an undisclosed player who signed the agreement in a bid to exonerate the club and its medical staff from future court action.

Calling it a "complex and unique case", the AFL insisted it was "satisfied that the letter was not used by Geelong to allow a medically unfit player to return to play".

The Cats also issued a statement, saying they would remove the waiver from the contract.

Geelong avoided punishment and said it would remove the waiver in the unnamed player's contract. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: Michael Willson)

"The club was not attempting to vary the terms of the AFL standard playing contract, or attempting to avoid its responsibilities under health and safety laws," the Geelong statement read.

When asked about the bombshell revelation out of Geelong, Beveridge spoke generally about concussion rather than commenting directly on the Cats' case.

"I think every player wants to keep playing until your boots fall off," Beveridge said after the Bulldogs' shock loss to North Melbourne.

"All I know that when I was playing, we all had concussions, and if I had to sign a waiver to keep playing, I would have.

"We're so careful with our players now.

"The way we train, as far as the duty of care goes, we really look after them."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Kangaroos coach Alastair Clarkson, who earlier this year sprayed insurance company Zurich for rejecting concussion insurance claims, insisted he knew nothing about Geelong's case.

New AFL Commission chair Craig Drummond was the president of the Geelong board at the time the deal was struck.

Drummond was not mentioned in the statement from the AFL.

Deciding not to front the media to explain the situation, Drummond issued a three-line statement on Thursday night calling concussion a "challenging medical and legal issue for all contact sports globally".

Multiple AFL players, including former Melbourne star Angus Brayshaw, champion West Coast defender Jeremy McGovern, premiership Magpie Nathan Murphy and former number one pick Paddy McCartin, were forced into retirement due to repeated concussions.

Several deceased players, including Danny Frawley, Shane Tuck and Graham "Polly" Farmer, were posthumously diagnosed with degenerative brain disease chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE).

There is also a multi-million-dollar concussion class action case against the AFL, led by former Geelong defender Max Rooke, in the Supreme Court of Victoria that is set to go to trial next year.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

World.title: Victoria moves to tighten rules for councillors eyeing parliament
World.content:
Victorian councillors who nominate for state or federal parliament have no legal obligation to stand down during an election race.

Under the Local Government Act 2020 a councillor is not in breach of the law so long as they keep their election campaign and council work distinct.

The lack of explicit direction leaves the decision of whether to take leave up to the individual, but that would change under proposed amendments being considered in parliament.

What are the rules?

At the moment there is only one guide for councillors seeking state or federal election and its recommendations are not mandatory.

Among its 10 guidelines, the Municipal Association of Victoria (MAV) advises that nominees take a leave of absence from their council no later than the date of their nomination as a political candidate.

The MAV suggests this could help councillors avoid potential conflicts of interest and the perception of misuse of their position and council resources.

This approach is taken in other, jurisdictions including New South Wales, Western Australia, South Australia and Tasmania, where leave is not mandated and arrangements are largely managed through council policies or guidance.

But under the proposed changes to the Local Government Act councillors would have to take a leave of absence once they officially nominated, which in effect would be an enforcement of the MAV guidelines.

Mayors and deputy mayors would also be required to stand down far earlier than the day of nomination and all councillors would be required to notify the chief executive of which election they were contesting and when they declared their candidacy.

If the councillor is a member of a political party this would have to be done as soon as possible after pre-selection.

If they are not a member of a party, this must be done as soon as possible after publicly announcing an intention to be a candidate.

Failure to do so in either case would attract a fine of $25,092.

When a mayor or deputy mayor completes this process, the chief executive must deem them incapable of performing their duties, including acting as mayor.

They can remain a councillor until they officially nominate with either the Victorian or Australian Electoral Commissions.

The rules would only apply to elections held on or after January 1, 2027.

Kate Kendall stood down as mayor of Macedon Ranges Shire Council to run for the Liberals in the state election. (Supplied: Macedon Ranges Shire Council)

Some Victorian councillors have already resigned or indicated they will take a leave of absence to begin campaigning for the state election.

They include Kate Kendall from Macedon Ranges Shire and Rochelle Halstead from Bass Coast Shire who both resigned their mayoral positions to begin their campaigns.

Jo Armstrong from Ararat Rural City Council has indicated she will take a leave of absence.

Managing conflicting duties

Labor MP Paul Hamer, who introduced the amendments into state parliament in June, said they would provide clear rules for councillors to manage potential conflicts of interest during election periods.

"It is essential that councils continue to operate effectively during a state election and that the community knows who is representing the interests of the council and who is campaigning as a parliamentary candidate," Mr Hamer said.

Mildura MP Jade Benham, who is in her first term in Victoria's Parliament, was mayor of Swan Hill Rural City Council prior to being pre-selected by the Nationals as a candidate in 2022.

She was pre-selected in late May 2022 and stood down as Mayor in early July, ahead of the election in November.

She said there were not any clear parameters at the time.

Jade Benham says the changes are long-awaited. (ABC News: Wade Stephens)

"It was kind of vague, it was a bit of a grey area. There wasn't any real advice," Ms Benham said.

"It's so hard to distinguish between what is campaigning and what isn't, particularly when you're in a public role, going to any community event could be seen as campaigning.

"But again, that's also the role of the mayor, the deputy mayor and any number of councillors. So where is the line?"

Ms Benham questioned what the definition of public declaration was for mayors and deputy mayors who were not members of a political party.



"Is [a public declaration] a comment in the local press or on the radio, or is it a Facebook comment, is it a press release?" she said.

What problem does it solve?

Mildura Mayor Ali Cupper served in the previous Victorian parliament as the Member for Mildura before losing the seat to Ms Benham.

She has declared her intention to contest the upcoming Victorian election and said she wished to remain mayor until she started campaigning.

Ms Cupper described the proposed mandate to stand down mayors and deputy mayors as overreach.

"I'm trying to find out what this rule is designed to do, or what is the problem it's seeking to solve, because I don't really see it as a problem," she said.

Ali Cupper says she doesn't know what problem the proposed rules are trying to solve. (ABC News: Wade Stephens)

She said mayors and deputy mayors should have the right to choose when to begin political campaigning.

Ms Cupper said the new rules read as inflexible and could limit participation in mayoral or deputy mayoral roles.

"Community leaders are going to want to do community leadership," she said.

"If they're good at what they do, if they're acting in good faith, why would you put arbitrary barriers in their way and restrict their leadership?"

Problematic timelines

Election analyst Kevin Bonham said candidates having the option to campaign while being mayor or deputy mayor was problematic.

"Partly that they have divided loyalties — they're acting as councillor while also campaigning for election and also they may not be in a position to do their full normal amount of work," he said.

Kevin Bonham says the amendments could eliminate some problems. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Dr Bonham said mandating mayors and deputy mayors to stand down could either delay the launch of a political campaign or see a campaign launch prematurely.



"It's possible you get cases where people are entertaining the idea of running for some time without completely committing to it," he said.

"There might be cases where it resulted in candidates holding off on formally declaring so they can hold off on going on leave."

Local Government Minister Tim Richardson was contacted for comment.

World.title: Prominent queer figure facing backlash for Geelong Liberal candidacy
World.content:
One of Geelong's most prominent LGBTQIA+ figures is facing backlash from the queer community, after being announced as a Liberal candidate for the upcoming state election.

Andy Pobjoy, an openly-gay small business owner, was last month named as the Liberal candidate for the seat of Geelong.

Mr Pobjoy is one of the most recognisable faces in Geelong's queer community.

His Piano Bar business bills itself as "Geelong's home of inclusivity", has long held drag queen performances, and has sponsored queer advocacy group Geelong Rainbow.

But, local views of the Liberal Party's record on LGBTQIA+ issues resulted in a wave of criticism for Mr Pobjoy — a reaction he labelled both "perplexing" and "disappointing".

Andy Pobjoy, known locally as 'the Piano Man', is the owner of popular Geelong business the Piano Bar. (Supplied: Andy Pobjoy)

Queer community figures speaking out

Geelong Rainbow, which hosts the annual Geelong Rainbow Festival, this week issued a statement noting they were "disappointed" by Mr Pobjoy's Liberal preselection.

"Many of our members viewed Piano Bar Geelong as a safe place to go out to where many late-night venues in our town are not so accepting," the statement noted.

"To see Andy standing alongside Geelong-based Liberal Party members such as Bev McArthur who actively oppose the kinds of art forms and people he has platformed and profited from not only feels like an odd move, it feels like a betrayal to many LGBTQIA+ people in Geelong.

" We hope that if Andy is elected, he will show up for and defend the LGBTQIA+ community as he has claimed he will do, no matter what the Liberal Party's policies are. "

Andy Pobjoy at Geelong Rainbow's 2020 Geelong Pride March. (Supplied: Geelong Rainbow Inc)

Bev McArthur is the Liberal Party's member for Western Victoria Region and is seen by the wider rainbow community as an arch-conservative.

Ms McArthur has already featured prominently in Mr Pobjoy's campaigning.

In 2024, Ms McArthur railed against the state government's introduction of the Rainbow Toolkit in Victorian libraries, launched partly due to backlash against drag storytime events, arguing it would subject children to "radical gender ideologies".

Bev McArthur has already been involved in Andy Pobjoy's campaign. (ABC News: Rudy De Santis)

At the time, Ms McArthur publicly rejected any notion her push against the toolkit was about intolerance, indifference or hate.

She also broke party ranks to vote against banning gay conversion therapy in 2021, and has repeatedly questioned "the movement to let men parade as women and demand female recognition".

Drag performer Goldie Cox, who has worked with Mr Pobjoy, said many in the local queer community felt a sense of betrayal by his decision to join the Liberal Party.

"For anyone to align themselves with any group that does not have the best history when it comes to LGBTQIA+ issues, especially someone who has run a business for over 10 years that has built itself on being a safe space for members of the LGBTQIA+ community, including employing trans and gender diverse people, is nothing but a slap in the face," Ms Cox said.

Drag queen Goldie Cox has worked across Geelong, including with Andy Pobjoy. (Supplied: Goldie Cox)

"Finding safe LGBTQIA+ places, especially in regional towns, is not easy, and when things like this happen you can't help but second-guess the intentions of a venue that you enter that claims to be a safe place for the community.

"At the heart, it's not about being aligned to one political party over another — it's about the feeling of betrayal from someone who you thought was in your corner."

The backlash has been particularly prominent in Mr Pobjoy's social media comment sections.

Pobjoy's plan to affect change

Mr Pobjoy said the greatest disappointment in the backlash came from being judged simply for a "political label".

"It's disappointing," he said.

"For a group that has said they're chronically under-represented, for someone like me — who's been a leader in our community, and stuck my neck out more than once and financially taken risks to support [the community] — then as soon as one of us puts our hand up, everyone loses their mind."

The Piano Bar has long platformed drag queens in Geelong and other regional centres — including popular drag bingo events. (Supplied)

The long-time businessman said his Liberal values were not mutually exclusive from queer values.

"The emphasis Menzian Liberal values puts on the importance of the individual and individual freedoms could not be more akin to what queer people have been fighting for all this time," he said.

"I'm not compromising my values by joining the Liberal Party … and I think people are completely misguided if they think that it's just one type of person that is a member of the Liberal Party."

For Mr Pobjoy, the ability to become a part of the Liberals meant an opportunity to add his voice and views to those already present in the party — particularly when it came to LGBTQIA+ issues.

"How can you affect change from outside? You have to be inside the tent," he said.

"The real change comes from when you're sitting in the room and they're going around the table and looking for voices and perspectives.

"That's the beauty of it. If you don't have the diversity of experience in the room, you end up, unfortunately, sometimes, with very close-minded views."

World.title: Council decides to sell off farm donated 'in good faith' to community
World.content:
A country council is facing intense scrutiny after deciding to wind up, lease the land and sell off assets from a beloved community farm once valued at $1.3 million.

The 596-hectare mixed farm known as Rylington Park was donated to the Shire of Boyup Brook by local farmer and community stalwart Eric Farleigh.

His only wish was that the property be retained "for the benefit of persons within the shire and for research purposes".

The property was run by volunteers for more than three decades and became a mainstay for community field days, shearing schools and agricultural research.

Rylington Park is about 30 kilometres south of the Boyup Brook townsite. (ABC South West WA: Andrew Williams)

The Shire of Boyup Brook took direct control of the farming enterprise in 2020, but earlier this year decided to wind down the operation by selling off assets and leasing out the property.

Retired farmer Richard Turner said the decision dishonoured the legacy and wishes of Mr Farleigh and the efforts of countless volunteers.

"He gave his farm in good faith … to see it going the way it is going is very disappointing," he said.

The shire said the "new management model" would ensure community cropping, research trials and scholarship funding continued in a manner consistent with Mr Farleigh's wishes.

Shire faces scrutiny

Mr Turner is a former chairman of the Rylington Park committee, which voluntarily managed the farm until 2020.

He said local farmers built Rylington Park into a profitable business that had combined assets worth about $1.3 million.

Richard Turner was involved with the Rylington Park committee for about 10 years. (ABC South West WA: Andrew Williams)

"Sheep were donated, the machinery was pretty run down … and over the years they got it up to running pretty well," he said.

By 2020, when the shire opted not to renew the group's lease, it had been running two community field days and eight shearing schools a year.

"We were putting through a hundred students a year — that's shearers and shed hands," Mr Turner said.

The council's decision to cease operations was attributed to the financial risk of a shire with a population of less than 2,000 running a large operation.

Most of the land will be leased, and all farm equipment and livestock will be sold by early 2027. The proceeds are to be reserved for a future attempt to restart the farm.

All livestock is to be sold by the end of January 2027, with all proceeds to be put in a quarantined account. (ABC South West WA: Andrew Williams)

But the explanation has received a mixed response from the community. The town's July 30 council meeting had to be paused due to repeated interjections from the public gallery over the issue.

Focus on farm's sustainable future

A spokesperson said the council was focused on securing the property for future generations while limiting the financial burden faced by ratepayers.

It said changing conditions across the agriculture sector had also had a significant impact.

Research agreements and trails at Rylington Park remain in place, but there are no plans to continue shearing schools. (ABC South West WA: Andrew Williams)

The spokesperson also acknowledged members of the community who were disappointed by the decision.

"The shire understands that community members have questions, and has sought to provide information through public council meetings, regular updates and community matter information sessions," they said.

"Our focus is on ensuring the community has access to accurate information and understands the reasons for council's decision."

Impact on legacy questioned

Mr Turner and eight other farmers the ABC has spoken with said the decision went against the charter of the farm and Mr Farleigh's wishes.

"They're not doing what Mr Farleigh wanted," Mr Turner said.

Eric Farleigh was posthumously inducted into the Royal Agricultural Society of WA's Hall of Fame for his pioneering research into improving soil quality. (Supplied: Royal Agricultural Society of WA/Felicia Lowe)

In response to public concern, the shire released a statement of support from Mr Farleigh's grandson David, a former resident of the area.

"I am satisfied the new management model as explained to me and adopted by the Boyup Brook Shire Council will retain the original intent of the gift given by Eric Farleigh," David Farleigh said.

"I am reassured Eric Farleigh's legacy and gifting of Rylington Park to the Boyup Brook Shire Council will continue his vision and benefit the local community into the foreseeable future."

World.title: Some of rugby league's truest believers await the NRL in Perth
World.content:
Most of the time when we talk about an expansion team it's all about firsts.

It starts with the first signing, then it's the first look at the jersey, then on to the first match, first win and first loss as they settle into their new place in an older world.

The Perth Bears are midway through that process right now. With 27 players on their books, their roster has well and truly come together and on Friday afternoon they'll reveal their playing strip to the world ahead of their NRL debut next year.

But amid all the firsts there will also be a last. The jersey unveiling will be held in conjunction with Melbourne's game against Manly this weekend, which is the final NRL game that will be played in Perth before the city has a team of its own.

The next NRL game Perth Oval hosts will be the local side's home debut. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre )

As the old world dies, plenty expect the new one to struggle in birth.

Much has been written and said about the new franchise's lack of star power and whether they can be competitive as they fight against the tyranny of distance and the money monster of their fellow expansion team in Papua New Guinea.

But their entry goes both ways as the beginning looms. It's not just about what awaits Perth in the NRL, but what awaits the NRL in Perth.

With the elite level of the sport about to finally put real roots down, how fertile is the soil? The spark of the game has been flickering for decades, but can it catch fire? Ahead of the last game before the start of forever for the Bears, what is rugby league in Perth really like?

A player's life at the outpost

Samisoni Langi is used to life on rugby league's frontiers. It's where he spent his finest playing days and where he helped make history.

The 33-year old got his start with the Sydney Roosters back in 2013, playing a handful of NRL matches before a long career in Europe, highlighted by five years with Catalans Dragons in France.

Langi played five-eighth for the Super League club when they won the Challenge Cup in 2018 to become the only non-English side in the competition's 125-year history to win the trophy.

He also represented Tonga while he was in the NRL and played for France at the last World Cup after qualifying through residency.

After finishing at the top level at the end of the 2023 season, Langi resettled in Perth to be closer to his wife's family and before long rugby league came calling.

Langi spent five years playing with Catalans Dragons in France. (Getty Images: Tim Clayton )

"It wasn't anything to do with footy, just for family. But a few clubs reached out when they found out I was here," Langi says.

"The players and the clubs here, they live and breathe rugby league. The people in the background are so passionate, they love their club and they love the sport.

"When I first came over there was only five teams in the first grade competition, that's up to nine now. It's a tough competition with lots of pride that's growing each year.

"There's so many volunteers who are at the fields setting up from 6am on Saturday for seniors and they all back up for the juniors on Sunday.

"They love it so much, and they're looking forward so much to the Bears."

Langi linked up with South Perth Lions, a local powerhouse with 20 premierships to their name since their formation in 1948, and got into the world of West Australian rugby league.

Langi played the 2025 season with South Perth Lions and was named the competition's player of the year. (NRLWA)

As Langi got about in that first season, which ended with him being named the competition's player of the year and the Lions making the grand final, the Bears slowly came to life.

In the 18 months since, they've put together their roster and now their first pre-season is well and truly on the horizon.

The discerning football fan might notice a lack of big names, but according to Langi that won't matter to most in Perth.

Australian Rules remains the biggest game in town by an indomitably huge margin and rugby union is firmly in second with the Western Force celebrating its 21st season this year.

For league to carve out a niche the key isn't in brand name players, as much as they'd help the on-field prospects, but in the name of the team itself.

There's a core of league fans that can provide a base for the club — crowds for NRL matches in the west have held steadily over 30,000 for the double headers at Perth Stadium and over 10,000 for one-off matches at the Bears' future home, Perth Oval.

Attendances and interest at NRL matches in Perth have held steady. (Getty Images: Paul Kane )

But for the Bears to become part of the fabric of the city they need to tap into the general sports population and the way to do that is strengthen the links to the community as much as possible.

In terms of sustainability, local pride beats imported star power every time and parochialism is a way of life in rugby league which should serve the city well, given Perth fans would show up to a letter-opening, so long as it's a letter about Perth.

"Everyone's excited to have a team of their own. A lot of footy people still have their teams from back east, the Roosters have come over and the Sharks and Raiders were here a few months ago, but having the Perth Bears will be different," Langi says.

"Nobody's too fussed about the players, they're just excited a team will be here.

"The biggest thing is being visible and accessible. Spend time in schools, visit junior clubs, support local competitions, build genuine relationships in the communities across Perth. Young players need to see the club as something they can be a part of.

"Whenever there's an NRL game coming here it's always big. The entire comp either has the week off or we push our game to Friday night or Sunday afternoon so everyone can get along to the NRL.

Why Luai's move to PNG has changed everything Jarome Luai's decision to sign with Papua New Guinea is a showcase of the economic power behind the Chiefs and marks the start of the greatest rugby league gold rush since Super League.

"You can feel the buzz around the city. It also inspires young players and they can see what's possible and dream to be out there playing professionally. Even the captain's run is big — I teach at a high school and nobody comes the day before the game, all the kids go to the open training session."

Langi doesn't just teach at Baldivis College to the city's south, he also runs the school's girls rugby league program, the first of its kind anywhere in Western Australia.

Finding a game for his charges isn't always easy but their enthusiasm is inspiring to Langi and while it could take the better part of a generation for work like his to bear fruit, the fact that the Bears are coming into a world where that work is already being done bodes well for their future.

"At the start I didn't know what I was getting myself into — the first thing they want to do every session is tackle, they're always asking when we're going to start tackling and I have to say 'we have to go through technique first, we have to catch and pass' and all these other things. But they love it," Langi says.

"The girls so look forward to games and sometimes they get cancelled and that can be disheartening.

"But we're trying to grow the game and with the Bears coming it should get a really good push, I'm looking forward to that."

Langi will be on the frontlines to see it as well. This year he transferred from the Lions to the newly promoted Kalamanda Bulldogs and he is keen to run around again in 2027.

"I'm just trying to help some of the young guys find their way. The club has come into first grade from reserve grade this year, so it's been a big step up," Langi says.

"We're pushing for the finals right now but next year and past that they'll be able to give it a real crack.

"I'll play for another year or two, then it'll be into coaching. I don't think I'll ever give up footy."

The age of the Bear begins

Perth's rugby league future might be more upscale than its past but it'll be nowhere near as colourful.

South Perth Lions, Langi's old club, have enough yarns alone to fill many a front bar session.

There was the time in the 1950s when a local dairy owner auctioned off one of his milk cart horses to raise money for the club but neglected to mention the horse in question had passed on after being hit by a car the day before.

This was around the same time the Lions home ground was next door to Perth Zoo and due to a lack of facilities players would wash in the zoo's artesian hot pools after matches.

A few decades later the team had managed to build its own clubhouse but were having trouble getting a liquor license because it required permission from the nearest publican.

After much resistance from the proprietor of said boozer, two enterprising club officials managed to win him over by approaching him on a Sunday morning in a moment of weakness as he battled a hangover that could kill a brown dog and a nasty bout of gout.

Perth hasn't had a team in the NRL since the Western Reds folded at the end of 1997. (Getty Images)

The club's end of season parties were always a highlight, particularly the year when, in an effort to keep the players out of the local watering hole, each pub donated an 18-gallon keg. It took them four days to get through all 15 of them.

Then there was the time the club had a partnership with a local company to unload produce trucks, which was put in jeopardy when the players unloaded watermelons by forming a makeshift backline and spiral passing them along.

Or the day a plane crashed on Como Reserve during an off-season game of cricket and the boys sprang into action to save the passengers, who fortunately survived the crash, with one man freeing them while still wearing his wicket-keeping gloves.

Some of these stories might be truer than others, but what's certainly true is they're all stories.

What's more iron-clad is South Perth's brilliant record on the field. Amid producing NRL talent like former Newcastle forward Cory Paterson, brothers Bronx and Bryson Goodwin and former Manly prop Kurt de Luis, they have 20 premierships to their name since 1948, the most of any team in the competition.

Other sides, like Joondalup Giants, Fremantle Roosters and North Beach Sea Eagles, had their glory days over the years but those same days never seemed to come around for the Willagee Bears, competition stalwarts since 1966.

When current coach Nelson Davis, who has lived in Perth for more than two decades, first took more than ten years ago the club had played for half a century without ever winning a first grade premiership.

Davis has lived in Perth for over 20 years and been involved with Willagee Bears for a decade. (NRLWA)

Davis, who had been coaching since he was 16 back home in Auckland, was initially daunted when his best mate and current assistant coach, Conrad Ramea, asked him to lend a hand.

"I said 'I'm only a juniors coach, I wouldn't know what to do with seniors.' But I've been at the Bears ever since," Davis says.

"We started from rock bottom. We had a really good base of players and at the time we were one of the strongest junior clubs, we had nearly one team in every grade.

"A lot of our players would come through the 16s and 17s but going to other clubs because we didn't have a first grade team.

"We did go up for two years in 2018 and 2019 and we lost every game. We learnt a lesson then."

After a few years away from the sidelines as the club's coaching co-ordinater, Davis took the reigns of the first grade side again in 2023 and was determined to learn from the pain of the past.

Willagee's trip to the grand final last year was years in the making. (NRLWA)

"I was ambitious. I gave the club a list of things we'd need to go up to first grade because I knew we had to learn those hard times," Davis says.

"I talked about paying players, upskilling staff, getting more support in terms of strength and conditioning and assistant coaches and my president, the man he was, came back to me a few months later and made it happen."

The Bears got to work, signing enough players to give their kids a team they could aspire to and setting new standards.

The results were remarkable. Just a few years after they could barely win a game, Willagee won the club's inaugural first grade premiership by downing Langi's Lions in the 2025 grand final.

It was a triumph of vision, development and self-belief, amid a transformation that would have made any club proud.

Nine of the players in the grand final side had played in the club's reserve grade team the year before and the club's entire spine and front row were local boys.

Willagee scored their breakthrough premiership in 2025 after a lifetime of waiting. (NRLWA)

"Just talking about it now makes me a bit teary. It was one of the greatest days and nights of our lives, to do it with my family and my best mate, it's what rugby league is about — those memories, the people, the bonds and the friendships you make," Davis says.

"That's what matters more than anything, more than any trophy.

"I look back at us getting belted 80-0 five or six years earlier and I never thought I'd be there for a Willagee first grade premiership.

"I thought I might have an influence on it if it happened a long way in the future but for it to happen so quickly was surreal.

"There were so many people who put in so much hard to work to get us there."

When Davis said it was a win for the many he's not kidding — Willagee has 411 people registered at the club and nearly a quarter are volunteers.

Loading Instagram content

Davis doesn't take a salary and several of his players now say they'll play for the club for free.

"That's the passion the guys have for the club and that's what drives a lot of clubs over here — the passion, the loyalty, the community feel and the family environment," Davis says.

"We aren't the biggest club, but we pack a punch and we have high aspirations for where we want to be."

Said aspirations are quickly being realised. Willagee have backed up their breakthrough premiership with a season for the ages and are undefeated at the time of writing just a few weeks out from the finals.

Their reserve grade side is set for the minor premiership as well and a clean sweep could be in the offing given their under-17s team is top of the table.

The family feel is already coming through with their links to their NRL big brother. Davis pinpoints Kaino Gudgeon, man of the match in last year's grand final win, as the club's key signing for their turnaround and his brother Ammaron, a local product, will take up a train and trial deal with Perth over the summer after a standout season with North Sydney in NSW Cup.

Plus none other than Mal Meninga himself, living Immortal and the NRL's sides foundation coach has been along to several Willagee matches and for Davis, those efforts to forge a link with the local league scene will be crucial.

Meninga's role in strengthening the Bears ties with the community will be vital. (Getty Images: Paul Kane )

"Mal's been to a few of our games already and that means a lot to the players and the coaches," Davis says.

"There's a lot of kids I coach who have dreams to play in the NRL and you have to be straight up with them about how hard it is and what the pathways are like — I just hope the Perth Bears can create that for them.

"I do believe there's some real talent here and some kids who could be knocking on the door.

"I know the Bears have big plans with the Tracks Academy and there's some very, very good 16 and 17-year olds, even in our club.

"I've got one player and I'd have had him in first grade the day he turned 17 but his mum won't let him."

Few would dispute that Perth Bears have a huge task ahead of them, but Willagee Bears are proof of what's possible.

People like Davis and the army of volunteers across the clubs that have kept the flame of rugby league alive so far from the game's strongholds have not just given the NRL side an example to aspire to, they've given them a community to serve, a rock on which the elite level of the game can build its church.

For decades, love of the sport was all that kept the lights on and now those lights are about to be so bright as to be dazzling.

Their game has come to them at last and it is a reward they never expected for a passion that never waned.

"People walk around with the Bears shirts on around the streets. When I'm wearing Willagee Bears gear everyone thinks it's for Perth," Davis says.

"There's a strong core community here, it's not the biggest, but it'll only grow with them coming. Even if we have teams already - I'm still a Warrior because I have been since day dot - we're all foundation members, I can guarantee you that.

"I just hope they can be semi-competitive those first few years and give the locals something to turn up for.

"It's been a positive impact already and we're so excited. Every club has seen an increase in numbers already. The banners are up, the billboards are up. I can't wait."

World.title: ASX retreats after Wall Street slides; Atlassian surges; Rio, BHP summoned to Trump meeting
World.content:

The Australian sharemarket has slid lower at the open after stocks retreated in the US as oil prices rose while Atlassian surged as it posted results after Wall Street’s closing bell. The S&P/ASX 200 was down 47.6 points, or 0.5 per cent, to 9224 in early trade, retreating from its record close on Thursday. The Australian dollar is steady at US70.32¢. Wall Street retreated on Thursday. Bloomberg Mining stocks are mixed, with BHP losing 0.9 per cent, Fortescue down 1.1 per cent and Rio Tinto 1 per cent in early trade as iron ore prices slide lower. BHP and Rio Tinto executives have reportedly been invited by the White House to a meeting with Donald Trump on the weekend to demonstrate the administration’s commitment to wean the US off supply chains dominated by China. Northern Star added 1.1 per cent while Evolution Mining dipped by 0.3 per cent with the price of gold steady above $US4200 an ounce. Financial stocks lost ground, with all the big four banks retreating. Commonwealth Bank lost 1.3 per cent, National Australia Bank fell 1.2 per cent while Westpac and ANZ Bank each gave up 1.1 per cent.



Energy stocks climbed after oil prices rose again on reports that Iran attacked “hostile targets” in the Strait of Hormuz, with Tehran seeking to bar US ships from the critical waterway in a deal with Oman. West Texas Intermediate rose above $US78 a barrel, after surging almost 3 per cent in the previous session, while Brent settled around $US82. Woodside Energy added 1.4 per cent and Santos advanced 1.3 per cent in early trade, while among the refiners, Ampol was up 0.3 per cent and Viva Energy lifted 1.3 per cent. Related Article Opinion

Trump's White House Money, money, money: Trump rakes in the cash from his social media posts Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Technology stocks are mixed with Xero jumping 2 per cent and Technology One advancing 0.4 per cent but WiseTech slid 0.2 per cent and NEXTDC lost 0.5 per cent in early trade. Overnight, the S&P 500 fell 0.2 per cent, and was just below the record it reached on Tuesday (US time). The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.9 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite fell 0.1 per cent. Atlassian, a leading provider of AI-powered collaboration and team productivity software, surged 32.7 per cent in after-hours trade after releasing robust results for its fourth quarter and fiscal year.



Total revenue grew 28 per cent year-over-year to $US1.77 billion ($2.5 billion) and cloud revenue growth rose 31 per cent year-on-year. “Q4 closes out a year that proves our long-term strategy is paying off,” said Mike Cannon‑Brookes, Atlassian’s CEO and co‑founder. Wall Street has calmed over the last two days. Companies from a mix of sectors reported their latest financial results, adding to an already busy round of corporate earnings reports. “August is off to an extremely strong start, but there is still plenty of August left to go, and August is typically a volatile month for stocks,” said Clark Bellin, president and chief investment officer at Bellwether Wealth, in a research note. Warner Bros. Discovery rose 1.7 per cent after reporting earnings that came in ahead of what investors were expecting. Molson Coors rose 1.3 per cent after also reporting encouraging financial results.

That is more than double the shares that were initially offered to the public for sale during the initial public offering for Elon Musk’s company. SpaceX jumped as high as $US225 a share following its market debut in June, but has since slumped below its initial $US135 offering price. The stock closed at $US114.92. The rate of inflation is stuck above 3 per cent and higher costs have been squeezing businesses and households, while threatening to crimp broader economic growth. The US economy expanded at a sluggish 1.5 per cent pace during the second quarter. Households are still spending and the jobs market remains resilient, but worries linger for both areas of the economy. Higher gas prices and added costs for shipping goods could prompt households to shift more spending toward necessities. That could hurt businesses focusing on nonessential items and services for many people, such as travel and entertainment.



Related Article Aviation Qantas long-haul pilots seek more ‘golden days’ in new pay deal Employment remains strong, but growth has been easing. Employers pulled back on hiring in June, adding only 57,000 jobs. The latest monthly jobs report, for July, will be released on Friday. Worries about inflation and the jobs market have prompted the Federal Reserve to hold its benchmark interest rate steady. Stubborn inflation, though, is nudging the central bank toward raising interest rates before the end of the year in order to help tame inflation. Raising rates, though, could also slow economic growth while weighing down prices for stocks and other investments. Treasury yields rose in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 4.67 per cent from 4.63 per cent late on Wednesday. European markets were mostly higher.

World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Judge lifts suppression order as complainant denies financial motive in alleged indecent assault, sexual touching trial
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of the fifth day of Alan Jones’ lengthy criminal trial on charges of indecent assault and sexual touching. Our reporters Clare Sibthorpe and Harriet Alexander will be bringing you the latest from the courtroom today.

This week, the NSW Local Court in Sydney’s historic Downing Centre court complex has heard allegations that Jones indecently assaulted a young athlete, starting with unwanted kissing when the man was a teenager in year 12 in the early 2000s. Jones denies the claims.

Alan Jones arrives at the Downing Centre Local Court on Friday. Louise Kennerley

Our live coverage was paused on Wednesday after Local Court Judge Glenn Walsh temporarily imposed a non-publication order on the cross-examination of “J” by Jones’ barrister, Gabrielle Bashir, SC. That order was lifted on Thursday afternoon.

“J”, now in his early 40s, denied under questioning by Bashir that he had a financial motive for making the allegations against Jones, and denied that they were a fabrication.

“I don’t want to sue him,” he told the court. “I don’t want his money.”

He has given evidence that Jones groped him as he drove the then-radio host to his Fitzroy Falls farm. On Tuesday, “J” told the court that Jones had indecently assaulted him at the property after telling him to wear “a robe and nothing else”.

The complainant said he came forward to police after seeing reports about Jones’ arrest in November 2024 because he wanted justice.

Jones had supported the promising athlete financially, including paying him hundreds of dollars a week to focus on training and giving him a car and a mobile phone, the court heard.

Today, the man known as complainant “J” returns to the witness box for a fifth day. He will face further cross-examination that is expected to conclude this afternoon.

Bashir has asked “J” a series of questions about whether he read media reports containing similar allegations about Jones in 2023 before he spoke to police the following year. He said he did not.

The Crown alleges that Jones indecently assaulted or sexually touched six men between 2003 and 2020, and is seeking to prove 22 charges against him, including nine indecent assault charges against “J”.

The former broadcaster has emphatically denied wrongdoing, and Bashir said on Monday that the credibility and reliability of the complainants’ evidence would be tested.

“Rivalry, treachery, double-dealing, money, hatred, desperation, opportunism and more are all at the heart of this case,” Bashir said in her opening remarks to the court.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.
