World.content:
One Nation leader Pauline Hanson has responded to the news story in this masthead about the use of One Nation funds to pay for her trip to the United Kingdom.

Insisting that “mainstream media publish lies”, Hanson concedes that One Nation paid the travel costs, claiming that Channel Seven was originally going to cover expenses while they travelled with Hanson for the Spotlight program.

“They pulled out forcing One Nation to cover all travel costs.”

Channel Seven has been contacted for comment.

Hanson said she provided Expedia invoices to News.com.au journalist Samantha Maiden to prove she cancelled her London accommodation while she was in Sicily with billionaire patron Gina Rinehart for a Dolce and Gabbana fashion show.

A screenshot of a partial invoice published by news.com.au shows five days accommodation at the five-star Conrad Saint James Hilton from July 15. Hanson’s declaration of interests shows Rinehart paid for flights from London to Sicily via Rome on July 11 and return on July 16.

One Nation did not answer questions about accommodation in London put to them over three days, only stating, as reported, that the Fire the Liar money was kept separate in a trust.

World.title: WA news LIVE: WA parents could be banned from school grounds for aggressive behaviour under these new rules; Man arrested at Perth Airport
World.content:
Parents who send their children to catholic schools and act aggressively will have to answer to a new code of conduct, which makes clear they will face consequences, including being banned from the school grounds.

Catholic Education WA released its code this week, which makes clear that certain behaviours are unacceptable, but its executive director Annette Morey said it reflects what most families already do instinctively.

Catholic school parents have been put on notice, although most are doing the right thing. Phil Carrick

“Most parents will read this and recognise themselves in it, and that is rather the point,” she said.

“This is about supporting the strong relationships that already exist in our schools. When conversations are respectful and collaborative, children see the adults in their lives working together, and that creates an environment where they feel secure and able to flourish.”

World.title: Making the hospo industry safer: Good Food calls for Cultural Change Champion nominees
World.content:
Awarded by The Age and Sydney Morning Herald Good Food Guides, the accolade shines a light on initiatives and programs that foster positive and empowering work cultures.

For the third year, Good Food is shining a light on the people and organisations making the Australian hospitality industry a better place to work by calling nominations for its Cultural Change Champion award.

The Good Food Guide award was introduced in 2024 following investigations by this masthead that revealed the workplace culture of a number of high-profile Australian hospitality businesses were putting women at risk, with allegations of sexual assault, harassment, drug use and misogyny. Further investigations last year revealed more claims, including the underpayment and exploitation of vulnerable workers.

The Cultural Change Champion award – presented by The Age and Sydney Morning Herald Good Food Guides in October 2026 – is about highlighting the exceptional Victorian, NSW and ACT business operators, organisations, not-for-profits, voluntary groups and networks transforming the industry, and trying to make it a more safe and respectful industry.

Jamie Bucirde won The Age’s first Cultural Change Champion award. Carmen Zammit

Former hospitality worker Jamie Bucirde, who was behind the Instagram account Not So Hospitable, was the inaugural Victorian winner. It sparked a nationwide reckoning and brought the systemic, largely sidelined issue to the surface. She consolidated her findings into an academic report with the University of Melbourne to galvanise the movement into meaningful change.

World.title: Police injured as protesters descend on homes for asylum seekers in England
World.content:
WorldEuropeImmigration Police injured as protesters descend on homes for asylum seekers in England David Crowe Updated August 7, 2026 — 9:22am ,first published 4:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Thetford: Angry residents have turned on police in a clash over asylum seekers in an English town where homes have been used to house migrants, with some protesters trying to break into a property to force the new arrivals to leave. A crowd of about 100 residents gathered in the Norfolk town of Thetford over two nights to try to stop local homes from being used to offer emergency accommodation for asylum seekers, including many who cross the English Channel by boat. View post on X Authorities had to evacuate at least five of the migrants when the protest turned violent on Wednesday night, the second night of the protests, as residents threw eggs and rocks at the house as well as the police. The town was calmer on Thursday night (early on Friday, AEST) after police applied public safety powers to require people to remove balaclavas and other face coverings or risk being arrested.



While dozens of people gathered on the third night of protests, police issued 10 dispersal notices to prevent any violence. The unrest is the latest example of violence over migration after years of growing anger at the arrival of thousands of asylum seekers, many of whom are housed in hotels or homes in residential areas. Around 36,000 people arrived by small boat over the year to the end of May, straining the government’s capacity to house them despite plans to turn former military bases into asylum seeker camps. An image of the disturbance on Wednesday night posted by Reform UK councillor Scott Hussey. X Tempers in Thetford, halfway between Cambridge and Norwich, were already raw over government plans to house about 1000 migrants at an air base south of the town. Opponents are planning a public rally against the plan later this month.



The angry scenes over the past few nights included men in black balaclavas confronting police in the apparent belief that the authorities were protecting the asylum seekers rather than the community. While the gatherings were largely peaceful on Tuesday night, they turned violent on Wednesday night when police stopped the protesters trying to break into the ground floor of a home with asylum seekers living upstairs. “As police intervened, members of the group became physically aggressive towards officers,” the Norfolk Police said. “Two were taken to hospital after a male officer was struck with a rock and a female officer was seriously bitten, breaking the skin. A third officer was also spat at.”



Related Article Immigration ‘Impenetrable border’: Farage claims Australian plan can stop the boats to Britain Police said one man, 68, a resident of Thetford, was charged with possession of an offensive weapon – a wooden bat – on Wednesday night. He was released on bail and is due to appear in court on August 25. Another man, aged in his 30s, was arrested after the first night of unrest on suspicion of a public order offence, but was released and issued with a conditional caution. Two men, both in their 40s, were arrested on the third night of the protests. One was detained on suspicion of inciting racial hatred the previous evening. The second was arrested on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly. Assistant Chief Constable Julie Dean said the police supported the right to peaceful protest but would act against violence, intimidation or criminal behaviour.



“Our role is to keep people safe. We have a duty to protect everyone in our communities, maintain public order and prevent harm,” she said on Thursday afternoon, local time (about 10.30pm AEST). “We will not stand by and allow violence to take place, whether that is directed towards members of the public, local residents or police officers carrying out their duties.” Related Article Northern Ireland Reading the riots: Belfast reveals a nation at boiling point One protester drew a direct link with recent violence in Belfast when local residents burned homes being used to house asylum seekers, according to the Eastern Daily Press. “They got them out, kicked them out, and the ones that didn’t go, they burned the house down,” the woman told the local newspaper.



“I’m not saying that we would do it, I’m not an arsonist. “At the end of the day, we got them removed.” View post on X A video shared on TikTok showed dozens of police escorting the small group of asylum seekers while protesters jeered, with some yelling: “Get them out.” Related Article Analysis

Immigration How the storming of Ceuta shifts Europe to the right



Reform UK councillor Scott Hussey, a cabinet member at Norfolk County Council, highlighted the scale of the police response in a post on X that said “half of Norfolk police” were guarding the house with migrants. A key issue in public debate is how a residential property can be converted into a “house of multiple occupancy” (HMO) where each room can be rented under a separate tenancy. Companies including Serco have used HMO properties to provide housing services to the Home Office to help with the arrival of asylum seekers, but this is controversial in residential areas where local people oppose the new arrivals in their neighbourhoods. The Labour MP for South West Norfolk, Terry Jermy, condemned the violence and said some local residents told him they feared for their safety. Jermy, a former mayor Thetford, said he opposed the plan to turn the air force base at nearby Barnham into a camp for asylum seekers.



About 193,000 people crossed in small boats to reach the UK over the seven years to 2025, according to the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford. An anti-immigration “Unite the Kingdom” rally in central London in September. Getty Citizens of six countries – Iran, Afghanistan, Iraq, Albania, Syria and Eritrea – made up 65 per cent of those crossing. Asylum was granted to 62 per cent of all those who came by small boat. “Around 36,000 people arrived by small boat in the year ending 31 May 2026, 13 per cent less than in the same period the year before,” it said. The fall in arrivals has been much steeper over the first five months of this calendar year. Only 9000 crossed in that period, down 38 per cent on the same period last year. The data is likely to change because boat arrivals generally increase over the northern summer. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

The former broadcaster has emphatically denied wrongdoing, and Bashir said on Monday that the credibility and reliability of the complainants’ evidence would be tested.

“Rivalry, treachery, double-dealing, money, hatred, desperation, opportunism and more are all at the heart of this case,” Bashir said in her opening remarks to the court.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: Making the hospo industry safer: Good Food calls for Cultural Change Champion nominees
World.content:
Awarded by The Age and Sydney Morning Herald Good Food Guides, the accolade shines a light on initiatives and programs that foster positive and empowering work cultures.

For the third year, Good Food is shining a light on the people and organisations making the Australian hospitality industry a better place to work by calling nominations for its Cultural Change Champion award.

The Good Food Guide award was introduced in 2024 following investigations by this masthead that revealed the workplace culture of a number of high-profile Australian hospitality businesses were putting women at risk, with allegations of sexual assault, harassment, drug use and misogyny. Further investigations last year revealed more claims, including the underpayment and exploitation of vulnerable workers.

The Cultural Change Champion award – presented by The Age and Sydney Morning Herald Good Food Guides in October 2026 – is about highlighting the exceptional Victorian, NSW and ACT business operators, organisations, not-for-profits, voluntary groups and networks transforming the industry, and trying to make it a more safe and respectful industry.

Jamie Bucirde won The Age’s first Cultural Change Champion award. Carmen Zammit

Former hospitality worker Jamie Bucirde, who was behind the Instagram account Not So Hospitable, was the inaugural Victorian winner. It sparked a nationwide reckoning and brought the systemic, largely sidelined issue to the surface. She consolidated her findings into an academic report with the University of Melbourne to galvanise the movement into meaningful change.

World.title: Police injured as protesters descend on homes for asylum seekers in England
World.content:
WorldEuropeImmigration Police injured as protesters descend on homes for asylum seekers in England David Crowe Updated August 7, 2026 — 9:22am ,first published 4:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Thetford: Angry residents have turned on police in a clash over asylum seekers in an English town where homes have been used to house migrants, with some protesters trying to break into a property to force the new arrivals to leave. A crowd of about 100 residents gathered in the Norfolk town of Thetford over two nights to try to stop local homes from being used to offer emergency accommodation for asylum seekers, including many who cross the English Channel by boat. View post on X Authorities had to evacuate at least five of the migrants when the protest turned violent on Wednesday night, the second night of the protests, as residents threw eggs and rocks at the house as well as the police. The town was calmer on Thursday night (early on Friday, AEST) after police applied public safety powers to require people to remove balaclavas and other face coverings or risk being arrested.



While dozens of people gathered on the third night of protests, police issued 10 dispersal notices to prevent any violence. The unrest is the latest example of violence over migration after years of growing anger at the arrival of thousands of asylum seekers, many of whom are housed in hotels or homes in residential areas. Around 36,000 people arrived by small boat over the year to the end of May, straining the government’s capacity to house them despite plans to turn former military bases into asylum seeker camps. An image of the disturbance on Wednesday night posted by Reform UK councillor Scott Hussey. X Tempers in Thetford, halfway between Cambridge and Norwich, were already raw over government plans to house about 1000 migrants at an air base south of the town. Opponents are planning a public rally against the plan later this month.



The angry scenes over the past few nights included men in black balaclavas confronting police in the apparent belief that the authorities were protecting the asylum seekers rather than the community. While the gatherings were largely peaceful on Tuesday night, they turned violent on Wednesday night when police stopped the protesters trying to break into the ground floor of a home with asylum seekers living upstairs. “As police intervened, members of the group became physically aggressive towards officers,” the Norfolk Police said. “Two were taken to hospital after a male officer was struck with a rock and a female officer was seriously bitten, breaking the skin. A third officer was also spat at.”



Related Article Immigration ‘Impenetrable border’: Farage claims Australian plan can stop the boats to Britain Police said one man, 68, a resident of Thetford, was charged with possession of an offensive weapon – a wooden bat – on Wednesday night. He was released on bail and is due to appear in court on August 25. Another man, aged in his 30s, was arrested after the first night of unrest on suspicion of a public order offence, but was released and issued with a conditional caution. Two men, both in their 40s, were arrested on the third night of the protests. One was detained on suspicion of inciting racial hatred the previous evening. The second was arrested on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly. Assistant Chief Constable Julie Dean said the police supported the right to peaceful protest but would act against violence, intimidation or criminal behaviour.



“Our role is to keep people safe. We have a duty to protect everyone in our communities, maintain public order and prevent harm,” she said on Thursday afternoon, local time (about 10.30pm AEST). “We will not stand by and allow violence to take place, whether that is directed towards members of the public, local residents or police officers carrying out their duties.” Related Article Northern Ireland Reading the riots: Belfast reveals a nation at boiling point One protester drew a direct link with recent violence in Belfast when local residents burned homes being used to house asylum seekers, according to the Eastern Daily Press. “They got them out, kicked them out, and the ones that didn’t go, they burned the house down,” the woman told the local newspaper.



“I’m not saying that we would do it, I’m not an arsonist. “At the end of the day, we got them removed.” View post on X A video shared on TikTok showed dozens of police escorting the small group of asylum seekers while protesters jeered, with some yelling: “Get them out.” Related Article Analysis

Immigration How the storming of Ceuta shifts Europe to the right



Reform UK councillor Scott Hussey, a cabinet member at Norfolk County Council, highlighted the scale of the police response in a post on X that said “half of Norfolk police” were guarding the house with migrants. A key issue in public debate is how a residential property can be converted into a “house of multiple occupancy” (HMO) where each room can be rented under a separate tenancy. Companies including Serco have used HMO properties to provide housing services to the Home Office to help with the arrival of asylum seekers, but this is controversial in residential areas where local people oppose the new arrivals in their neighbourhoods. The Labour MP for South West Norfolk, Terry Jermy, condemned the violence and said some local residents told him they feared for their safety. Jermy, a former mayor Thetford, said he opposed the plan to turn the air force base at nearby Barnham into a camp for asylum seekers.



About 193,000 people crossed in small boats to reach the UK over the seven years to 2025, according to the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford. An anti-immigration “Unite the Kingdom” rally in central London in September. Getty Citizens of six countries – Iran, Afghanistan, Iraq, Albania, Syria and Eritrea – made up 65 per cent of those crossing. Asylum was granted to 62 per cent of all those who came by small boat. “Around 36,000 people arrived by small boat in the year ending 31 May 2026, 13 per cent less than in the same period the year before,” it said. The fall in arrivals has been much steeper over the first five months of this calendar year. Only 9000 crossed in that period, down 38 per cent on the same period last year. The data is likely to change because boat arrivals generally increase over the northern summer. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: 'It's a shock': Kaitāia's Northland Mill closes down two weeks early
World.content:
It's a shock and a disappointment that Kaitāia's Northland Mill will close down today - two weeks ahead of schedule, a union organiser says.

Marcus Coverdale, of Workers First Union, said he only found out about the decision late on Wednesday.

About 60 people had been employed at the mill, which produced wood veneer and was owned by Juken NZ.

The company still owned the neighbouring Triboard Mill, with 140 jobs, but the future of that plant was also uncertain.

Earlier this year, the company said it wanted to exit Kaitāia and put both mills on the market.

Coverdale said a skeleton crew had committed to keeping the Northland Mill operating until 21 August.

"So obviously it's a shock, but the workers themselves are a bit relieved that they don't have to carry on sweeping the floor and opening and closing the gates for the last times," he said.

A buyer is yet be found for Kaitāia's Northland Mill - but only for the site and machinery, not the mill itself or its 60 workers. RNZ / Peter de Graaf

"The mood was quite sombre. People are just ready to move on and start the new chapters in their life, moving next door or moving on to other opportunities."

There was some good news, with 10 older workers at the Triboard Mill opting for voluntary redundancy, opening up jobs for younger workers laid off at the Northland Mill.

Some still had 20 years of working life ahead of them, so they were "really grateful" for the opportunity.

Juken NZ had committed to paying staff out in lieu of notice, Coverdale said.

Workers would also receive a wage increase and backpay in their final pay calculations.

He was still hopeful a buyer could be found for the Northland Mill site.

"There's been rumblings there is an interested party looking to buy the site. It comes with the council consents, some of the materials and the machinery. But not attached to the workers or the employment."

Juken NZ said 19 workers from the Northland Mill had accepted jobs at the neighbouring Triboard Mill (pictured). RNZ / Peter de Graaf

Meanwhile, Coverdale said another interested party was due to tour the neighbouring Triboard Mill site on Friday - but it was not known if it was a serious buyer.

The Triboard Mill produced a manufactured wood product used in the construction industry and was one of the biggest employers in Kaitāia.

The flow-on effects of the Northland Mill closure would be felt in Northland long after the gates closed for the last time, he said.

"It's not just the 40-odd workers that are out on the street. It's the flow-on effect of those wages not being spent in the local community anymore. And also the smaller businesses that provided support, a lot of transport and maintenance companies are going to feel the pinch as well."

Juken NZ director Yasufumi Tsuchiya said redundancy payments for the Northland Mill workers were being made this week, with final pay, including entitlements through to 21 August, to be paid out next week.

He said 28 employees had secured ongoing employment with Juken NZ through redeployment and retention opportunities.

This included 19 staff who had accepted roles at the Triboard Mill.

A further six had agreed to remain temporarily to help with site maintenance and closure, with three of those likely to be redeployed into ongoing positions.

That left a total of 44 employees retiring or seeking new jobs.

Tsuchiya said employees continued to have access to help from the Ministry of Social Development, the Employee Assistance Programme, employment services and wellbeing support.

The company would host a job fair in coming weeks to help connect affected workers with potential employers.

While manufacturing had ended at the Northland Mill, Juken NZ was still exploring opportunities for the future of the site, including selling the land and associated assets.

The company was also continuing to explore selling the Triboard Mill as a going concern.

"Discussions remain ongoing, however no buyer has been identified to date," he said.

World.title: CNMI: Tinian mayor welcomes US military training approval
World.content:
The US Navy and Marine Corps have finalised a plan to conduct distributed operations training on Tinian in the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands.

Tinian mayor Edwin Aldan has welcomed the US Department of the Navy's decision to approve expanded joint military training on the island, but said residents should have been better informed about the contents of the final decision.

The comments came after the navy issued a Record of Decision, signed on 23 July by Assistant Secretary of the Navy (Energy, Installations and Environment) Brendan Rogers, formally approving Alternative 1 under the CNMI Joint Military Training project.

The decision allows expanded land-based military training and associated infrastructure on Tinian following more than a decade of environmental review and public consultation.

"These things should have been pushed out in public," Aldan said.

"Our people should be aware of what are the contents of this record of decision."

Under the approved alternative, military training on Tinian will increase by about 15 percent over previously approved activities and include two live-fire ranges, landing zones, ammunition holding areas, radar towers, biosecurity facilities and other supporting infrastructure.

The US Navy said the project is intended to improve US military readiness in the Indo-Pacific while incorporating mitigation measures to reduce environmental and community impacts.

Aldan said the decision also provides greater certainty about what will be built and how the project could benefit Tinian's economy.

"Environment is an issue for us and should be compliant with EPA," he said, adding that the proposed development would attract interest from people outside Tinian and create economic opportunities for the island.

He also said Tinian has long played an important role in US defence.

"I'm just proud to be a part of the military movement that is happening in our region," Aldan said.

World.title: Coalition still in position to form government in new Taxpayers' Union Curia poll
World.content:
National has gone up and the coalition is still in a position to form a government, but only by the slimmest margin, in a new Taxpayers' Union Curia poll on Friday.

The Opportunity Party would enter parliament on this poll with 6.1 percent, but would form part of the Opposition after National ruled out working with the party last week.

National is up 0.5 points to 31 percent - making it the most popular party in Parliament - while Labour has taken a decent drop of 3.7 points to 27.8 percent.

The Greens are down ever so slightly to 10.1 while New Zealand First also dropped, down 1.7 points to 9.1 percent.

Act gained slightly to 7.3 percent while Te Pati Maori has recorded its worst result since March 2023 with just 1.5 percent - down 1.9 points.

The coalition parties - National, Act, and New Zealand First - would be able to form a government with 61 seats if this poll was replicated on election day.

The Opposition - including the Opportunity Party - would have just 59 seats - not enough to govern.

On this poll result Labour would lose five seats.

In the preferred prime minister polling National's Christopher Luxon is out ahead on 23.2 percent - up 4.1 points - compared to Labour's Chris Hipkins who is down slightly to 19.8 percent.

The poll surveyed 1000 respondents between Saturday and Tuesday and has a margin of error +/- 3.1 percent.

Curia is a long-running and established pollster in New Zealand. In 2024 it resigned its membership from the Research Association New Zealand (RANZ) industry body.

World.title: 'A perfect storm': Teachers forced outside subjects of expertise as shortage bites
World.content:
Secondary school teacher shortage hitting Nine To Noon Download MP3 12m

A current shortage of qualified high school teachers is a "perfect storm", the University of Waikato's pro vice-chancellor of education says.

The Ministry of Education's most recent forecast predicted secondary schools will have a national shortfall of 710 teachers this year.

Pro vice-chancellor of education Claire McLachlan told Nine to Noon the problem has long been signalled as baby boomers retire and student numbers increase.

"I think you've kind of at the moment got the perfect storm, you know, you did have quite a big, steep growth in immigration 10 or more years ago and you've also got baby boomers retiring."

She said one of the impacts was an increase in teachers teaching subjects outside of their expertise.

McLaughlin said Australia has been doing a lot of research on "out of field teaching", and New Zealand has been seeing a similar pattern.

While this practice was problematic at upper levels, she said at lower levels a good teacher could "understand what the curriculum's asking of them" and then do an "okay" job.

The shortage was also an issue for McLaughlin's own student teachers who were having difficulties to find placements in classrooms.

"We know that the load of carrying those placements is not evenly shared across the country."

She said in a 2024 report by the Ministry of Education Workforce Division, it was clear that Auckland and Hamilton are training most teachers with Canterbury carrying the bulk of training in the South Island.

There are also nine new subjects being rolled out next year as part of the new curriculum, including energy and infrastructure, engineering technology and tourism.

McLaughlin said not all schools will have teachers whose expertise overlap with the new subjects.

"I would imagine there's probably going to be a little bit of shuffling of the chessboard within schools to see who can do what.

"Then trying to identify people within local communities who could work possibly initially under limited authority to teach and then qualify through something like Waikato's alternative entry pathway to teaching."

She said it would take same time and there is a possibility that at the beginning only the bigger schools will be able to offer some of those vocational pathways.

McLaughlin said the idea that teachers are not being retained in the profession may be an "urban myth".

She said in the last report around teacher shortages the retention rate was around the 90 percent mark.

"The bigger issues, I think, are in our regional areas in New Zealand ... there are some areas which really struggle to get the sort of teachers in the subjects that are needed."

World.title: Northern Marianas tennis player Carol Lee stuns top seed in Poland
World.content:
Northern Marianas tennis player Carol Young Suh Lee has upset the top seed at the Warsaw Open in Poland on her way to the tournament's quarterfinals.

The Saipan-born player defeated top-seeded Elsa Jacquemot 6-4, 6-4 in the opening round before recovering from a set down to beat Aliona Falei 2-6, 6-3, 6-1 in the Round of 16.

Lee, 24, told Marianas Press she went into the match against Jacquemot believing she was capable of pulling off the upset.

"I wouldn't say I was surprised because I believed I was capable of winning the match. At the same time, I knew Elsa was the top seed for a reason and that I would need to play at a very high level," Lee said.

"I went onto the court with a plan and focused on being aggressive, trusting my shots and competing for every point."

Lee produced five aces and won 71 percent of her first-serve points against Jacquemot, while converting four of eight break-point opportunities.

Her next match required a comeback after Falei took the opening set 6-2.

Lee responded by winning the second set 6-3 and then ran away with the deciding set 6-1.

She converted five of seven break-point opportunities and won 72 percent of her first-serve points during the three-set victory.

"It was a very difficult match. Aliona is a strong competitor, and there were many challenging moments when I had to stay mentally tough," Lee said.

"I had to keep adjusting, remain patient and accept that the momentum could change during the match. I'm proud of the way I handled the pressure and continued fighting until the end."

Lee said reaching the final eight was particularly satisfying after being tested in different ways in her first two matches.

"It feels great to move into the quarterfinals. I'm really happy with the way I have competed throughout the tournament so far," she said.

Lee was scheduled to face Poland's Weronika Falkowska in the quarterfinals.

World.title: Shearer Dylan Manthey sentenced for inflicting 'extreme violence' on lambs
World.content:
This story discusses violence towards sheep which some readers might find distressing.

A shearer caught on film violently abusing three lambs was at the time of his offending drinking too much as he struggled to cope with the death of his father.

While he was part of a shearing gang working in Canterbury in January 2024, Dylan Manthey was filmed throwing one lamb against a shearing platform, one into swing doors and one over a metre-high fence.

The Palmerston North District Court heard on Friday that the video of this was obtained by an animal rights group that passed the footage to the Ministry for Primary Industries, which laid charges.

RNZ had previously reported the group was PETA and that other shearers were also facing charges.

Manthey has admitted three charges of ill-treating animals and was sentenced to six months' community detention at a Palmerston North property. He will have a curfew for 12 hours on Friday nights and from Saturday nights until Monday mornings.

Lambs thrown in frustration

As Manthey stared at the ground, Judge Mark Callaghan read a summary of the offending.

It started on 27 January, 2024, when Manthey was working on a Pleasant Point farm in South Canterbury.

Manthey grew frustrated with a lamb, which was struggling with him, so dropped his equipment, picked up the lamb and threw it head first into a hard wooden shearing platform.

Manthey then picked up the lamb and continued shearing.

Frustrated with another lamb on the same day, he picked the animal up, swung it around and threw it over a metre-high wall into a pen of sheep. The impact of the fall could be heard on the video.

The following day at a Hunter Hills farm he threw another struggling lamb into a set of swinging doors. The lamb fell to the floor before scrambling through the doors.

Judge Callaghan said a vet had examined the footage.

"The opinion says each lamb would have suffered unnecessary pain and distress and impact because of your actions," the judge told Manthey.

"You used what is considered to be extreme violence towards the animals."

Impulsive, not sadistic - judge

MPI prosecutor Jaclyn Field-Turner said Manthey's offending was extremely violent and repetitive.

"There's simply no excuse for the offending against the sheep."

She asked for Manthey to be disqualified from owning animals for two years, but the judge didn't impose this.

Judge Callaghan said Manthey had struggled with the death of his father and a medical problem, so had turned to alcohol. Manthey saw his father as his rock, especially after his mother had died when he was young.

Manthey has since given up drinking, has sought help and was working in a different industry.

He had also admitted two drink-driving charges from September and October 2025, in Palmerston North. Both times Manthey was seen swerving across the road.

The judge said Manthey was in a dark place and alcohol was "a main contributing factor" to his offending.

"I accept that your offending is not something which shows you have any sadistic intent," Judge Callaghan told Manthey about the ill-treatment charges.

"Your offending appears to be impulsive and reactive behaviour which was, obviously, disproportionate, emotional and violent."

World.title: Fiji Rugby defends scheduling after women's test match put between school games
World.content:
The Fiji Rugby Union (FRU) has defended its scheduling of the Fijiana XV's Test match against Springbok Women.

The test match for the Ubuntu-Bula Trophy kicks off at 2pm on Saturday at HFC Bank Stadium, with school games before and after.

Under-14, under-15 and under-18 Raluve games will all be played Saturday morning before the test, with two under-18 Deans Trophy games to follow after.

FBC reported the union saying it acknowledged public discussion surrounding the schedule, but it was designed to showcase rugby from grassroots to the international level.

FRU chief executive Koli Sewabu said the Fijiana XV are not only representing Fiji this weekend, but also inspiring the next generation of young girls and boys who dream of wearing the white jersey.

"We wanted our school players to witness what international rugby looks like, and we wanted our Fijiana players to know that an entire generation is watching and drawing inspiration from them."

Former Fijiana sevens coach Saiasi Fuli wrote on Facebook that earning a cap in a test match is the ultimate career validation for players.

"The same test value that was given to the Flying Fijians must be given to the Fijiana XV, not a curtain-raiser to schools rugby," he wrote.

"A rugby test match represents the absolute pinnacle of international competition."

The Fijiana captain says they are expecting a physical battle with South Africa on Saturday 8 August. Fiji Rugby

The Fijiana have named their team for the match.

Two debutants have been named by coach Wille Walker - Ruth Raketekete at inside centre, and Adi Vani Buleki on the wing.

Kolora Lomani will captain the side from halfback, with prop Bitila Tawake named vice-captain.

The Fijiana captain said they are expecting a physical battle, and they have worked on preparing to come up against the strength in the South African side.

"We know they're a physical team," she said.

"We've worked on this week what we need to do, to be able to come up against that strong side of them.

"They come out with a fighting heart."

World.title: Le Court wins Tour de France Femmes stage as Reusser keeps overall lead
World.content:
Kimberley Le Court of Mauritius overcame earlier difficulties to emerge victorious in a reduced sprint and win stage six of the Tour de France Femmes, as Swiss rider Marlen Reusser held on to the overall lead with three stages remaining.

Le Court joined a small breakaway group 10 kilometres from the finish, launched her sprint with 300 metres to go and held off French rider Cedrine Kerbaol on the line, with Puck Pieterse of the Netherlands coming in third.

The 30-year-old Le Court suffered a mechanical before the final climb and had to change bikes, but, thanks to her teammates, made it back in time to launch her telling move.

"They brought me back slowly but surely to the bunch, and I got back on top of the last climb, which was a really big effort," Le Court said.

"Then I just tried to stay patient, try to recover from this big effort. Riejanne Markus and I bridged to the breakaway, and we got to the front."

There was no change at the top of the standings after the 153.4km ride from Montbrison to Tournon-sur-Rhone, with Reusser holding a 12-second lead over Dutch rider Demi Vollering. Poland's Katarzyna Niewiadoma-Phinney is third, 1:17 off the leader.

A group of three riders built an early lead of over two minutes but were brought back with 54km remaining.

World champion Magdeleine Vallieres set a blistering pace at the front on the penultimate climb of Col de Lalouvesc, which split the peloton, leaving a reduced bunch of about 30 riders to go for the stage win.

A group of six then got away, before they were joined by Le Court and Markus. The breakaway managed to hold off the chasing pack, and Markus made a move with one kilometre left.

The Dutch rider was unable to make her attack count, and it was left to Le Court to claim an almost carbon copy victory of her stage win last year when she outfought Vollering and Niewiadoma-Phinney in a seven-rider sprint to the line.

World.title: NRL and AFL 'saturated' with gambling and alcohol sponsors, report finds
World.content:
All NRL and AFL clubs have an alcohol sponsor this season, while every NRL and five AFL clubs are sponsored by gambling companies, a new report has found.

The findings from the Foundation for Alcohol Research and Education (FARE) also show that both leagues have deals worth tens of millions of dollars each year with sports betting companies, which see them make money on every bet placed on their games.

The deals reportedly amount to $50 million per year for the NRL and $30 to $40 million per year for the AFL, FARE said.

SportsBet is a major sponsor of both codes as well, under deals worth about $10 million per year to the NRL and between $8 million and $10 million per year to the AFL.

With alcohol and gambling ads also becoming more prevalent in the leagues' women's competitions, FARE said its research showed these sponsorships were "deeply embedded across every level" of Australia's two largest sporting codes.

It comes as Labor's proposed crackdown on gambling advertising draws criticism from all sides of politics, with the Coalition, Greens, crossbenchers and some of its own party calling for stronger reforms during a Senate inquiry on the issue this week.

Labor's plan would limit gambling ads on TV to three per hour between 6pm and 8:30pm, on radio during school pick-up and drop-off, and ban logos on player jerseys or promotions in stadiums.

Labor MPs call for tougher gambling reforms The Albanese government faces internal pressure to strengthen its gambling reforms, with more MPs calling for sweeping amendments.

Alcohol ads cannot be shown on television until after 8:30pm when the media watchdog's designated children's viewing hours end, but an exemption exists for sporting matches.

However, the Australian Communications and Media Authority is currently reviewing that rule and is due to hand down a decision in the coming weeks.

FARE's State of Play report found that seven NRL clubs have gambling branding on their official playing uniforms this season — one more than the previous season — while betting advertising is part of 10 clubs' match-day promotions and across 12 clubs' digital channels.

Gambling sponsors are not on any AFL jerseys this season, but four clubs have digital gambling advertising and four clubs show betting ads at stadiums during matches.

Every AFL club advertises alcohol brands at stadiums during matches and through their digital channels, while five NRL clubs have alcohol logos on their jerseys and most clubs show alcohol ads in stadiums.

Every NRL club promotes alcohol brands through their digital channels.

Across the women's competitions, there are nine confirmed alcohol sponsorships for AFLW teams in this year's season and four for the NRLW, the report found.

Three AFLW clubs and seven NRLW clubs have gambling sponsors in the 2026 season.

FARE's research also found the volume of alcohol and betting ads during NRL and AFL broadcasts grew this year, with Seven and Nine both increasing their number of sponsors.

FARE chief executive Ayla Chorley said the report showed alcohol ads "saturate every part" of the sports and called on ACMA to take action.

Independent senator David Pocock, one of parliament's most vocal critics of Labor's planned reforms, has been calling for the government to implement all 31 recommendations of the Murphy Review — which includes a full ban on gambling advertising.

The Canterbury-Bankstown Bulldogs have an alcohol sponsor on their playing jerseys. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

"We need a full gambling advertising ban — not some ineffective partial one that has been approved by the gambling industry, an end to harmful inducements and a national regulator to enforce the rules," he told the ABC.

Ex-NRL player alleges gambling staff offered drugs as he lost thousands Luke Bateman says gambling company employees unofficially offered him illicit drugs.

"Research shows that gambling and alcohol are huge accelerants to family and domestic violence.

"With 43 women murdered already this year, we should be doing everything possible to reduce and bring an end to this violence and the factors that exacerbate it."

Alcohol and Drug Foundation chief executive Erin Lalor said alcohol ads during sports broadcasting and at games influenced children and young people's attitudes towards drinking.

"Despite the significant harms that alcohol causes to individuals, families and communities, the alcohol industry continues to use sport to promote their unhealthy products," she said.

"That's why it's important to reduce children and young people's exposure to alcohol advertising, especially in the activities they love, like sport."

The NRL and AFL have been contacted for comment.

World.title: Richmond is facing a rebuild riddle — can it afford to stay the course?
World.content:
It's one of the most dreaded words in football: rebuild.

It's what's led Carlton into a search for its fifth senior coach in twelve seasons. It's why North Melbourne have been flirting with a seventh consecutive bottom-six finish and it's where Richmond finds itself six years after its drought-breaking dynasty.

The Tigers win over West Coast on Sunday was their 10th in their last 67 games. You could see how much it meant to former pick one Sam Lalor when he smashed through the sealer late at the MCG, whilst Willem Duursma's tears showed how devastating perennial losses can be.

Triple premiership-winning defender Nathan Broad, who announced his retirement this week, told ABC Sport's Alexia Pesce he was proud of the victory.

"It's reward for effort … the boys are working so hard, they have not thrown the towel in," he said.

" We're trying to win, we're not trying to get pick one. We're trying to build a winning culture. "

The 2017 grand final triumph broke a 37-year premiership drought. (AAP: Julian Smith)

Despite the win, Richmond will walk into the Adelaide Oval on Saturday night with a big decision looming.

If they're unable to salvage a win against Adelaide, St Kilda or Geelong in the final month, they'll finish their third season under coach Adem Yze with their worst record in history across three campaigns; surpassing the 1959-61 Tigers who managed 11 victories.

No-one in the AFL era has kept their job after winning fewer than 10 games over three seasons. Most, like David Noble in 2022 and Mark Neeld in 2013, exited during their second year of a disappointing run.

Brendon Bolton was given a fourth term at Carlton after a 14-41 start but managed just one win from his next 11 games and was sacked.

Justin Leppitsch departed Brisbane after just 14 wins across 2014-2016, whilst Stuart Dew survived an 11-61 record in the inaugural years of the Gold Coast Suns but was sacked three years later.

Richmond is at a fork in the road.

Their three flags across four years was only six years ago, and was built off a steely move to stick with coach Damien Hardwick when former players and Tiger identities were calling for change.

A disappointing 2016 campaign saw them finish 13th in Hardwick's seventh season, which followed three consecutive elimination final losses.

President Peggy O'Neal and CEO Brendon Gale backed their man and immediately found success in 2017 defeating Adelaide to snap a 37-year drought.

In 2017, the Tigers were flying high — but the three premierships in four years now feel like a distant memory. (AAP: Julian Smith)

The win sent their opponents, the Crows, spiralling out of their premiership window.

Once heavy flag favourites, Adelaide missed finals in consecutive campaigns and senior coach Don Pyke resigned.

'Two years into a significant rebuild'

Ironically the Crows, who face Richmond this weekend, found themselves in a similar situation to the 2026 Tigers. They signed a first-time coach in Matthew Nicks and were 0-13 to start his tenure.

Disconsolate Crows stars Taylor Walker and Rory Sloane in the immediate aftermath of the 2017 grand final. (AAP: Julian Smith)

They had progressed to 18-39 after three seasons and after narrowly missing finals in 2023, re-signed their figurehead twice in the space of two years, culminating in a minor premiership in 2025 and a potential return to the top four this season.

So should Richmond stick by Adem Yze who has the worst record of any coach in history after 67 games?

President John O'Rourke was emphatic Monday morning on 774 ABC Melbourne that the question isn't even being contemplated.

"He will coach to 100 games, I can assure you of that," he said.

"We're less than two years into a significant rebuild … [and] if you look at four of the top six teams they've all done a similar thing and they've taken four or five years to get back into contention so we do have to be a bit patient.

"We won't make judgement calls on where we sit until we see that through."

Richmond president John O'Rourke has spoken candidly about his side's form and fortunes. (AAP: James Ross)

The Tigers extended Yze's contract by another two years until 2028 in November last season after rising from two wins to five in 2025 and have shown some improvement statistically in 2026.

Richmond has risen from 17th to 12th for clearance differential; moving the delisted Thomson Dow's midfield minutes into first round pick Sam Cumming and rising star Jack Ross.

They've had small jumps with inside 50 differential as a result and scores from stoppage differential; but defensively are leaking 104 points per game compared to 95 last season.

Crisis or all is fair in footy? Pundits and fans alike talk about the AFL being an uneven competition — but does the data support that concern?

There has been a significant injury crisis that's likely to have played a role. Richmond have used a league-high 40 players this season with only one player, Seth Campbell, featuring in all 20 games.

Senior figures like spearhead Tom Lynch (12 games), captain Toby Nankervis (9 games) and midfielder Jacob Hopper (12 games) have barely featured; and young stars like Josh Smillie, Harry Armstrong, Taj Hotton, Josh Gibcus and Sam Lalor have managed just 21 games combined this campaign.

In football it's often believed rising stars find their rhythm around the 50-game mark. But of the Tigers nine first round picks in the last two years, only three have managed 18 matches or more out of a possible 43.

Former Richmond premiership player and Australian Football Hall of Famer Mick Malthouse, whom you can hear on AFL Saturday 12am AEST on ABC Sport, doesn't believe there's a universal number to development.

"The simple fact is, the more you play, the more experience you get and you become more aware of the game around you," he said.

"Is there a magical number? I've seen players 80 to 90 games in and they're as naive as they started and others have been street smart after 20 days.

" Today's football it's about whether you can keep the group together. I judge coaches on how their players improve. "

Mick Malthouse says player improvement should be the yardstick of coaching. (ABC Grandstand: Damien Peck)

Richmond's crippling injury toll led to an extensive internal review leading to the departure of high-performance manager Ben Serpell in July after two years in the role.

But will it be the only change at Punt Road following 2026? Or will the Tigers lean into their past success and their opponent Adelaide's current trajectory and stand by their embattled senior coach?

Richmond has a habit of upsetting Adelaide this decade, particularly at the Adelaide Oval where the 17th-placed Tigers jagged their second win of the season in Round 13, 2024, and in 2023 when they shocked the Crows with a 32-point win in Round 2.

Could another surprise be brewing Saturday night? Adem Yze will certainly be hoping so.

ABC Sport will be broadcasting Adelaide v Richmond live from Adelaide from 7pm AEST on Saturday, August 8, via ABC Listen.

World.title: UEFA doubles down on FIFA boycott threat as Infantino pressure grows
World.content:
European football's governing body has retained its threat to boycott FIFA competitions despite FIFA apologising for its failed plan to sell stakes in the World Cup.

UEFA reiterated that it had lost confidence in FIFA president Gianni Infantino and said conditions to withdraw its boycott threat had not been met.

"UEFA's associations were very clear about the conditions attached to the non participation in FIFA competitions," it said in a statement.

"First, the proposals to sell off the major competitions had to be withdrawn and secondly, assurances have to be made that such attempts to disfigure the game in this way will never be made again.

"These conditions have not been met. In addition, UEFA made it abundantly clear in its statement on Saturday that it has lost confidence in Gianni Infantino's presidency. That position holds."

Gianni Infantino retains the support of FIFA, but is losing sway with the continental bodies. (Reuters: Dylan Martinez)

It was another bruising day for Infantino, with global football players union FIFPRO accusing him of "a profound abuse of presidential power".

"No institution can restore confidence in a presidency that has itself dismantled the conditions upon which confidence depends," the FIFPRO statement read.

"Trust cannot simply be demanded. Authority cannot merely be asserted. Legitimacy cannot be proclaimed. Each must be earned. Each can be lost."

The English Football Association has also withdrawn its support for Infantino's re-election.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Even Amnesty International said the "current crisis spotlights the need for governance reforms".

FIFA and Infantino tried to present a united front following a high-level summit in Morocco on Wednesday when the organisation announced the president had the full support of top staff in attendance.

The world governing body also apologised for errors made over its controversial plan to sell profits in the World Cup through a commercial subsidiary and committed to "ensure they do not happen again".

FIFA said it hoped its meeting would "help restore confidence" in the organisation after the turbulence created by Infantino's now abandoned project, which provoked widespread condemnation.

UEFA voted to abandon FIFA competitions if it went ahead. And even after Infantino's hasty climbdown, Europe's governing body said it had lost confidence in FIFA's leadership, paving the way for a challenge to his presidency.

In its defiant statement, UEFA made it clear its position still held.

"Yesterday's announcement that some people employed by the FIFA president (and whose careers depend on his favour) agree with him changes nothing," it said.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.
