World.title: St Kilda drafted a 27yo who couldn’t kick. She ended up as captain
World.content:
In late October 2019, 27-year-old Hannah Priest was getting a range of her Year 12 classes ready for their South Australian Certificate of Education (SACE) exams.

She went into her school's principal's office and asked if she could have the following day off as she needed to fly to Melbourne.

"I said 'I might get drafted or I might not, but if you're okay just to give me a day off to give it a crack?' and he said, 'Absolutely, Hannah, go for it,'" Priest told ABC Sport.

Her hopes eventuated when St Kilda chose her with pick No.41.

Hannah Priest was elected co-captain in 2021, and took the reins in a solo capacity in the first season of 2022. (Getty: Daniel Pockett/Getty Images))

"I returned the next day, and all the kids were like, 'Miss Priest, what? You got drafted? What is this? We didn't even know you played football,'" she said.

"I finished up the year there and then moved over to Melbourne, not knowing if I'd ever play a game for the Saints. And lucky enough to have played every game since."

Priest's career trajectory reflects a lot of the growth of the early days of AFLW, and how it's grown in such a short period of time.

The now 34-year-old grew up playing netball, a centre wing attack, and despite watching footy all her life, only tried her hand with the Sherrin when AFLW was introduced in 2017.

Had Priest been a few years older, she likely would have missed the boat entirely to play AFLW. Her mum, for example, never got the chance to try, which she says would have "given it a real good crack".

Had she been younger, she would have had a far less disrupted pathway into high-level football, like many of her peers.

St Kilda made their maiden finals appearance last year. (Getty: Daniel Pockett/Getty Images)

Priest was drafted alongside Georgia Patrikios, Nicola Zenos, Olivia Vesely and Molly McDonald, who were all 18 or 19 at the time.

"I think it was in the first season; I just remember the Saints said, 'You can't really kick, but we think you can learn,'" she said.

"In those first few years we had several different athletes that had come across from different sports. We had athletes in those first few years from swimming and basketball and volleyball," she said, herself from netball.

"I think the thing that stands out now is the professionalism and the actual athletic profile of our young talent coming through there. They've been in a pathway now where their bodies are really ready [when they are drafted]."

Stadiums still major AFLW bugbear The AFL has introduced four double-headers this season, meaning games will be played at bigger venues, while the league remains steadfast on boutique grounds for standalone matches.

Just a year after her 2020 debut season, Priest was elevated to co-captain and then sole captain in 2022. She held that role for six seasons before handing the reins over to Serene Watson this year.

It meant she went from a high school teacher in Adelaide, her hands learning to manage the shape of a Sherrin, to leading a club within a few short years.

When she arrived at Moorabbin, Jarryd Roughead was a development coach there, someone she had idolised as a kid. Being a Hawthorn supporter, growing up, he jostled for her favouritism with Buddy Franklin.

"He's sort of sending me photos and videos of his daughter saying, "Go, Hannah, go Saints. And my family are like, "Han, what is your life now?' This has just changed," she said.

This weekend, Priest will help lead the Saints out to the club's first AFLW game at Docklands Stadium, although without the official title now.

St Kilda play in a double header with Carlton for Spud's game, which will also open the women's season.

Loading Instagram content

Priest said the team were excited and nervous to play at a bigger venue, with more eyes on them and for a very special occasion.

"As the AFL's marquee mental health match, it's much more than just a game of footy this weekend. Danny Frawley is obviously a legendary figure of our club, and it's so important for all of us at the club to honour his legacy," Priest said.

"Throughout the week, we're just really encouraging people to check in on themselves, and not just this week but every single week and every single day and look out for their family and mates.

"As footballers we have a really strong responsibility to role model this sort of thing.

"I always say you can't pour from an empty cup, so you've got to make sure that you're looking after yourself first, and whatever you need to do to make yourself feel mentally fit and physically fit, it's just as important."

World.title: Broadcasting veteran Charlie King retires after 32 years with the ABC
World.content:
When British heavyweight boxer Anthony Joshua won gold at the Olympic Games in London, Charlie King sat in the Australian commentary box and pinched himself.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article includes the name and image of an Indigenous person who has died, used with the permission of their family.

It was 2012, and the ABC broadcaster was making history himself as the first Indigenous broadcaster to commentate his second Olympics in a row.

"I was happy to announce that he won a gold medal — it was a big moment for me," Charlie says.

As he announced the athlete's win, Charlie had a "flashback" to his childhood, when he'd sit on father's feet and listen to the boxing on the wireless radio.

It's where his passion for sports commentating began.

Charlie King developed a passion for sports commentating at a young age. (Supplied)

"He would talk to the radio and say things like, 'What happened to him? Is he going to be okay?' and then he'd try telling me what he was talking about; I loved it," Charlie says.

"Watching Anthony Joshua walk out and stand in the middle of the ring as the gold medallist, I went back to that happening with dad and thought, 'Wow this is such a good moment, pinch yourself,' and I did."

The well-known ABC Sport and Grandstand broadcaster retired in May after more than 32 years with the public broadcaster in the Northern Territory.

During his time working across radio and television, the 75-year-old has commentated more than 600 matches for the NT Football League (NTFL), as well as broadcast two Olympic Games and two Commonwealth Games.

A premiership player with NTFL team Wanderers, Charlie also played a key role in coaching the NT's pioneering female footballers to their first national competition in 1990.

"They desperately wanted to play, and they weren't getting the support they needed back then — they couldn't even get an oval," he says.

Charlie King became involved in sports commentating after calling fictitious games for his friends. (Supplied)

'Tough area' of family violence advocacy

Everywhere Charlie goes in the Northern Territory, he is recognised and stopped for a chat.

He has used his large profile in the media to speak up on challenging issues, including the NT's scourge of family violence with the No More campaign.

"It was a tough area to work in because it's hard to measure success … you're also working with people who are violent, and they're angry and threatening," he says.

Charlie King founded the No More campaign, which advocates for the prevention of domestic violence. (ABC News: Isabella Tolhurst)

He credits his weekend work with the ABC for giving him the time to focus on his advocacy work during the week — a movement that would grow to see footballers link arms against violence.

For instance, he says he would suggest an outside broadcast at Nhulunbuy, and while he was there, he could engage with locals.

"I got to know people in those communities and the work I was doing in the No More campaign gave me an opportunity to talk to those people about things like family violence," he says.

Push for DV background checks of NT football players Long-time anti-domestic violence campaigner Charlie King is among those calling for sporting codes to take a tougher stance on the issue.

The Gurindji man has received many accolades for his public-facing work, including an Order of Australia medal (OAM) and being named the NT's Senior Australian of the Year in 2019.

But it's been his advocacy behind the scenes with the ABC's Bonner Committee, which works with senior leaders at the public broadcaster to shape culture and recruitment of Indigenous staff, where he has felt his greatest responsibility.

"I wanted to say to Aboriginal people, 'I can do this, you can too'," he says.

" There are so many Aboriginal stories to be told.

"There's been important work to increase employment of Aboriginal staff, but the ABC still has more work to do — that's an observation, not a criticism."

'Be better, not bitter'

Charlie credits his mother's experience of being removed from her family at Limbunya Station near Kalkarindji during the era of the Stolen Generations for giving him a strong sense of social justice.

Born in Alice Springs in 1951, as the third of 11 children, Charlie has described feeling the sting of racism growing up, and says it was his mother who helped him push back on it.

Charlie King with his twin sister Cheryl Scott and mother Ruby Ningardi King. (Supplied)

"People don't know the damage of racism; it's a horrible thing," he says.

" She would say 'don't get bitter, get better', and I'd go and deal with it front-on and make a difference. "

His one regret during his long broadcasting career was never getting the chance to hear his mother's full story about her childhood or to interview her before she died in 1984.

"I'm so sad to say that we got so close to having a sit-down conversation, which we didn't have," Charlie recalls.

"I called in to see her one day, on a Saturday … she walked with me to the car and she said, 'When are we going to have the talk?' and I said, 'I'll be back out on Sunday," and she passed away on the Saturday — I missed it."

Charlie King was awarded an Order of Australia medal in 2015 for his service to broadcast media and the Indigenous community. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Parkinson's disease Charlie's new challenge

As Charlie embarks on retirement, he faces his greatest challenge yet as he manages life with Parkinson's disease.

Diagnosed in 2025, Charlie says the condition has slowed down his movement somewhat, but not his drive to make a difference.

"I love people, I simply love people, I get on well with people, I need people," he says.

He credits his partner Jayne Lloyd and daughter Emma King for being his greatest supporters, and says patience is the number one gift a person can give to someone living with the disease.

Charlie says his partner Jayne Lloyd has been one of his biggest supporters. (Supplied)

"I'll be sitting in a conversation with three people, say, and they are talking and I want to make a comment," he explains.

"By the time I figure out in my mind what my comment is going to be, they have already moved on to two or three other topics, so you've got to be patient."

Charlie remains focused on the silver linings that retirement offers: weekends at home with family, saying yes to watching his grandchildren play footy and more hours in the day for his advocacy work.

"It's a slow disease, you know; it doesn't end your life quickly, it's very slow, so I still have a lot of time left and things to do," he says.

Charlie King says more time with family, including with his daughter Emma, will be one of the benefits of retirement. (Supplied)

He signs off the ABC airwaves with a simple message to his huge following: live your best life.

"Every day counts — if you want to do something good, do it, don't wait until it's too late," he says.

"Don't wait until you pick up some disease that's going to strike you down quickly.

" Be a good person and stand strong and say no more to family violence. "

World.title: Resting or tanking? Why your AFL club may not win before finals
World.content:
For some, to lose sometimes is better than winning — especially if the loss is a late season dead rubber and the win is a premiership.

Tension between the present and the future exists throughout society. Buy now, pay later deals are peddled readily. Conversely, saving for the future has been a staple of financial advice for generations, even if it means being more parsimonious in the short term.

Football is no different. Not all wins are the same. For some, winning now can even be an obstacle for winning later.

These thoughts came to a head last Thursday night on AFL Nation when host Gerard Whateley asked AFL executive general manager football performance Greg Swann a pointed question; whether the AFL had a policy to prevent a team mass resting players if they were locked into position for finals.

Swann's response — after a pregnant pause — was short.

"Yeah … I think we do. I'd have to go [check]." Swann said, later elaborating that "there's obligations to put your best team out there."

Greg Swann says teams have an obligation to try their best. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Michael Willson)

On Monday the AFL attempted to provide more clarity, sending a memo to all 18 league clubs to remind them to "perform to their merits". As per Fox Footy, the memo referred clubs to league rules about performance and trying.

"Please be reminded of the obligation in the AFL Rules on Clubs to "perform on one's merits", meaning that Clubs must perform honestly and to the best of their ability," the memo read.

"While legitimate management of player fatigue and injuries is permitted, the AFL will scrutinise Club team selection decisions in the lead-up to the AFL Finals in the context of this Rule."

This memo caused a mild uproar across clubs, coaches and fans, hijacking much of the conversation of the week.

"I think the main consideration for the teams who might be certainties to play a wildcard game is the fact that the six teams above seventh all have a week off," Western Bulldogs coach Luke Beveridge told Fox Footy on Monday.

Luke Beveridge will not be swayed on his selection choices. (Getty Images: Graham Denholm)

One of his potential finals rivals, Melbourne coach Steven King, also weighed in strongly.

"I'm the coach of the Melbourne footy club. I'll make any decision that's best for our football club and best for the management of our players," King said.

AFL clubs double down on resting players The AFL warns clubs they risk being sanctioned should they rest players in round 24, but several coaches say they will not be paying attention to the memo.

While much of the focus of the memo this season appears to be on sides that are preparing for finals, the rule also applies to those set to take a long September sojourn.

The spectre of tanking and strategic resting in football was once rife, with unproven allegations that several clubs performed to less than their merits in order to earn better (and more) draft picks.

The removal of clear guidelines around priority picks quietened this chat, but it has never fully gone away. Likewise, the mass-resting of players by North Melbourne and Fremantle about a decade ago spurred the AFL to institute a pre-finals bye.

Changes to the AFL's finals structure and to the draft compensation awarded to the league's weakest teams, may have renewed motivation to stretch the AFL's rules — and the patience of its fans — to its limits.

What's merit got to do with it

Teams are being encouraged to perform to their merits, whatever that entails. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

To find out what the AFL means by "performing on one's merits" you first need to crack out one of the core documents that governs the league — the AFL Rules. The Rules — not to be confused with the Laws of the Game — sets out how the AFL administers the league across 191 breezy pages.

It's in the middle of the definitions section that the league defines what they actually mean:

Perform on one's Merits: at all times to perform honestly and to the best of one's ability in the pursuit only of legitimate competitive objectives. For the avoidance of doubt "legitimate competitive objective" includes the development of the team or players or management of player fatigue or injuries but does not include improving a Club's draft position, improving a Club's position with respect to a potential Player exchange or manipulating a Club's position on the ladder for the purpose of improving its draw within the Finals Series.

The definition is both broad and narrow, vague and specific. The league puts that definition into action in two different sections of the Rules — Rule 29 and Rule 32.

Most of the time it's rule 29 that is considered when looking at sides performing to their merits. That rule relates to the operations of the draft, and more specifically "conduct prejudicial to the Draft". In real, non-lawyer speak that means tanking and tanking adjacent decisions. Rule 29 has a set series of penalties and procedures, and has been called into action previously — more on that later.

But it's rule 32 that's more interesting. That rule — called "Gambling" — looks at acts that are prohibited in the bookmaking space. That includes ensuring that:

In relation to any Match, aspect of a Match, or pre-Match planning and tactics, a Player, Coach or member of the Match Committee must at all times Perform on their Merits.

This section is even broader to its operations, with penalties handed out by the AFL Commission or General Counsel as they see fit. Rule 32 is more concerned with bulk resting before finals rather than sheer tanking, but more broadly ensures that the game is fair to uphold the obligations the league has to gambling markets.

So a team has to perform to their merits, unless their players are hurt or tired. Finding a better match in finals isn't a valid reason for failing to meet those standards, nor is securing a better draft pick.

But more broadly, does tanking, and resting up, stack up as strategy?

Tank commanders

The Houston Rockets potentially tanked in 1983/1984 to take Hakeem Olajuwon (right) with the number one draft pick. Chicago claimed Michael Jordan (left) with the third pick. (Getty Images)

Tanking is not a new concept to the league, nor to sports that utilise drafts. But it's also not always successful — either in the short term or the long term.

It is generally believed that the first instance of tanking in sport occurred in the 1983/1984 NBA season.

In that season the Houston Rockets had eyes on Hakeem Olajuwon, a young Nigerian centre from the nearby University of Houston.

The team started the season strongly before fading late, making some questionable decisions along the way.

That stretch of futility afforded the Rockets with a coin flip to secure the top pick — one which landed their way.

The Rockets got their man, with The Dream eventually leading Houston to two titles and a brief stint as the best basketball player in the world on his way to the Basketball Hall of Fame.

However, Olajuwon didn't end up as the best player in that draft.

Two picks later the Chicago Bulls tabbed a 6'6" guard named Michael Jordan, who had a handy career of his own.

Sides in all four of the major US sports have tanked their way to title winning stars and cores — but not all sides have succeeded. While rumours of tanking abounded for years, it took some time for the phenomenon to firmly hit these shores.

In the AFL, tanking isn't just about securing the number one pick.

The number one pick is rarely the best player in the draft, or even often better than the second overall pick. The floor is higher than almost every other selection, but it's hard to pick who will be the single best player from looking at kids aged 17 or younger.

The most commonly cited examples of AFL tanking coincide with the era of defined priority draft picks.

Between the years of 1992 and 2012 teams received a draft pick at the start of the first round if they won very few games — five or less before 2005, and four or less in two consecutive seasons before between 2006 and 2012.

Not all the teams who received priority picks did so via tanking, but there are a small subset who have faced closer scrutiny.

In 2012 former Melbourne player Brock McLean gave an interview alleging that Melbourne made decisions around the selection and positioning of players that lessened the chances of victory for the club in 2009.

"Well, they don't call it tanking — we were calling it experimenting or whatever it was — and it just went against everything I was taught as a kid, taught as a footballer, as a person," McLean told Fox Footy's On The Couch.

Brock McLean says Melbourne did not tank, but "experimented". (Getty Images: Ryan Pierse)

After the interview the AFL opened a seven-month investigation. While the league cleared the club of tanking, it found the Demons had acted in a manner "prejudicial to the interests of the AFL".

The club was fined $500,000, with former staffers Chris Connolly and Dean Bailey serving suspensions from AFL duties.

The Demons were far from the only club to raise eyebrows for how closely to their merits they were performing.

Former Brownlow medallist and Carlton assistant coach Tony Liberatore alleged that Carlton had also considered future draft picks when making experimental late season selections in 2007.

In 2010 West Coast coach John Worsfold was clear that experimenting with selecting young players in unfamiliar positions was not tanking.

Neither side was sanctioned by the league. Both received priority picks. Rumours have existed about how closely to their merits other sides have performed in recent years, but no known formal action has been taken.

But one part of the equation is far more clear.

Priority picks were worth their weight in gold

The allure of a priority pick was worthy of extreme action. Despite Melbourne tabbing Tom Scully and Jack Trengove ahead of Dustin Martin in that fateful 2009 draft, other clubs have used those picks to kickstart a swift rise up the ladder.

The gains from a coveted priority pick have been enormous at times — think Hawthorn securing a bonus Lance Franklin at pick five in addition to taking Jarryd Roughead at two, or Collingwood adding Scott Pendlebury to go with Dale Thomas.

Of the 17 occasions in which a club has earned very high priority picks, the majority made finals in the next few years.

Three teams won flags within five years, with the Judd/Sampi, Roughhead/Franklin and Pendlebury/Thomas pick combinations featuring prominently in multiple grand finals and premiership success.

Some second round priority picks, such as Alex Rance and Jack Darling, also proved critical to premiership pushes.

After 2012 the league changed the criteria for awarding priority picks, making them discretionary.

Since then, the Suns, Lions and Roos have been awarded assistance packages, with two of those three rising to finals shortly after gaining assistance.

While the priority pick rules haven't changed for 2026, another rule has been introduced that may further induce the need to experiment late in the year.

Dale Thomas and Scott Pendlebury made a dynamic pairing for Collingwood. (Getty Images: Robert Prezioso)

Experiment away

At the start of the year the AFL introduced a series of draft reforms designed to make the draft — and distribution of young talent across the league — fairer.

Matching bids for father-son and academy talents has got harder for clubs.

At the same time, clubs holding high draft picks at the top end of the draft now receive compensation (at the start of the second round) for club-tied players bid on (and matched) early.

Clubs holding their natural draft picks whose picks are pushed down the order now receive a compensation selection at the start of the second round of the draft, if they go on to pick a player with their original selection.

While this is not as generous as the previous priority pick regime, an extra pick could incentivise finishing 14th over 13th if finals are off the table.

A fresh, early second round pick is more likely to be worthy of a tank than the mere difference between pick one and two.

While many have raised North Melbourne's late season win in 2023 that cost the club the chance to select Harley Reid, the young Eagle has yet to fully cement himself as the most valuable player of that draft class.

Indeed, heading into that draft, some clubs tabbed Jed Walter as the most talented player in the class, albeit one that was firmly off limits due to his ties to the Suns.

The race for the fifth pick appears to be heading down to the wire, with the Suns, Roos and Giants all in the mix for the last choice.

If the Suns finish fifth, no compensation pick will be generated due to the pick already being traded to Melbourne.

Jed Walter was always tied to the Suns through the 2023 draft class. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Russell Freeman)

There's now also a stronger incentive for clubs with tied talent to ensure they have enough points to match any bid — or to sneak a pick in before a bid comes in.

For example, Carlton's late season surge has made the battle to get likely top three draft pick Cody Walker to the club harder.

If the Blues finish inside the top 10 they will not receive a discount on matching a potential bid, alongside having a worse hand to match with.

Time will tell if these sides — and others — experiment more in the last three weeks of the season.

Resting before finals

Then there's what many people noted as the original intent of the AFL's memo — the locked-in finals teams.

While the finals have expanded and the bye week before finals removed, the week off is still functionally there for the top six sides, with the top four eyeing two weeks off in a three week period.

As a result it's the sides placed 7 through 10 with reasons to make sure their players are rested for a deep run in finals. Wildcard teams face the prospect of winning five straight games to win a long shot premiership, and can only be expected to eke out every little advantage facing such a gauntlet.

A week off isn't automatically an advantage for football teams — statistics show no advantage for teams coming off a bye in the middle of the year.

It's likely that team circumstances vary too much for planned byes to have consistent influence.

One club may benefit from a rest, extra player rehab, and renewed energy to help them reset and succeed, while another may find the danger of upsetting their rhythm and getting a bit rusty.

However, later in the year, when teams are banged up and facing the step up to finals level intensity, a week without football is more likely to appear as a boon for many players.

Why now?

Players are dropping down with injuries during this longest AFL season ever. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Russell Freeman)

Even considering all of these factors, many will be asking why the AFL released this memo now.

The risks outlined above aren't down to changes made in the last week or month, or unforeseen circumstances.

The 2026 season is one of the longest on record. By the end of the year, most players will be battling niggles, injuries or fatigue.

As per the AFL Rules, these are valid reasons for players to be rested. In addition, the rules encouraging players, staffers and teams to "perform to one's merits" have rarely been tested, if ever.

For many clubs and fans, the concept of acceptable losses and tanking runs contrary to the entire concept of sport.

This is similar to the teachings of Canadian philosopher Shorsey, who exalted that the most important thing is not that players don't love to win, but that they hate to lose.

The tears shed by West Coast's Willem Duursma speaks to this anguish at loss, and what drives the best to the next level.

Instead, the memo appears to be an AFL attempt to control a developing media cycle.

Rather than quietening discontent, it seemed to accelerate the uncertainty — including amongst the coaching cohort.

A clearer initial answer from the league may have headed the conversation off at the pass.

In the end, the only added dimension may be fans now trying to guess the ultimate intentions of teams with ground to gain at the margins — regardless of whether they are trying to do so or not.

World.title: Legend's first try in 1,426 days inspires Cowboys turnaround
World.content:
North Queensland hit back from last week's debacle to re-enter the NRL's top eight with a 30-8 win over Gold Coast, as playmaker Jaxon Purdue turned from villain to hero.

When the Cowboys lost 82-12 to Sydney Roosters in their previous outing in Townsville there were huge doubts they could bounce back from the most points conceded in a premiership match in 91 years.

At Robina, in front of 11,740 fans, the Cowboys got the response coach Todd Payten wanted after he labelled last week the club's "darkest day".

Scott Drinkwater, Jason Taumalolo, Heilum Luki and Purdue — four of their biggest stars — came up with key plays at the right time on Thursday to ensure the rout by the Roosters would not derail their season.

This was a test of character, which the Cowboys passed. It wasn't pretty, but it was enough to secure their 12th win of the year and move temporarily to seventh on the ladder. One more win may be enough to play finals.

"I'm really proud of their efforts and that we held our nerve," said Cowboys coach Todd Payten.

"I have no doubt about who we are and what we can be.

"I stressed this on Monday, one game doesn't define who we are.

"I'd take a win any way it comes, but we played with a fair bit of control and I didn't think the game was in doubt after 18-4. We stuck at it.

"We had to do it the hard way, defending our line in the first half and with the sin bin in the second half."

The turning point came in the second half when the Cowboys led 18-8. Purdue had been sin-binned for a professional foul and two minutes after returning he raced 70m from dummy-half to score an individual try for the ages.

Veteran prop Taumalolo set the scene in the fifth minute when he broke a 69-game try drought with a barnstorming charge after a scintillating 40/20 by fullback Drinkwater, his third of the season.

The Cowboys legend's previous try was week one of the finals series in 2022.

Purdue put his halves partner Jake Clifford through a gaping hole for a 12-0 lead after 13 minutes.

But the visitors didn't put their foot on the throat and the Titans found a way back into it.

Winger Phil Sami's 84th try for the club put him one behind Titans all-time record holder Anthony Don, courtesy of a slick Jaylan De Groot pass.

Shocking errors and defence by the Titans all but handed Cowboys second-rower Luki a try on the cusp of halftime.

Sami equalled "The Don" after halftime with his second try of the night after Purdue's infringement.

The Titans could not make the most of the advantage. After Purdue's magic, Luki scored his second try of the night to secure a crucial win.

AAP

Tech.title: Trevor Noah is hosting Google’s Pixel 11 launch event
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google is set to host its next live Made by Google hardware launch event on August 12th, and the company says in a new video that comedian Trevor Noah will be hosting the show.

The video indicates that the event will feature other celebrities and influencers as well, including Call Her Daddy host Alex Cooper (who was at the 2025 event), Indian cricketer Shubman Gill (who has starred in Pixel ads), Japanese actress Ayami Nakajo (who has also starred in Pixel ads), and NBA star / Google Performance Advisor Stephen Curry. (Cooper and Noah are also bringing shows to YouTube.)

Jimmy Fallon hosted the show last year, an event that my colleague Victoria Song described as more like “a live taping of The Tonight Show with Jimmy Fallon” than a traditional tech launch event. Given the celebrity faces set to appear at this year’s event, it seems that Google is once again aiming to reach a more mainstream audience. It’s also airing right at the end of the ET workday: the event, which takes place in New York City, starts at 6PM ET.

As for the gadgets you can expect, Google’s event teaser video features brief glimpses of a new phone and smartwatch, and the company has previously shown teases of the Pixel 11 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro Fold. There are a bunch of leaked images and specs of the upcoming hardware floating around, too. However, if you’re thinking about picking up one of Google’s new gadgets, you should be prepared for a higher price tag.

Tech.title: Jony Ive’s first OpenAI gadget is reportedly a hockey puck-sized smart speaker
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The AI device OpenAI is developing with former Apple designer Jony Ive is “essentially a smart speaker without a display” that’s battery-powered, doughnut-shaped and roughly the size of a hockey puck, according to Bloomberg reporter Mark Gurman. The device, expected to launch in 2027 for a price over $300, reportedly “will have a unique look, complete with moving parts,” including some that will move on their own to show when the device is responding or interacting with the user, along with lights, a camera system, and other sensors.

Gurman’s sources also say the “battery-powered” device is designed to be “easy to carry around the home with one hand,”similar to Amazon’s now-discontinued Tap speaker. Gurman says it will “work similarly to the company’s ChatGPT voice mode on smartphone apps, but with more advanced models for humanlike interactivity” but look and feel nothing like an Apple product — despite their ongoing lawsuit.

The speaker / pocket personal assistant could be the first in a “family of devices” OpenAI has planned, but we’ll probably hear a lot more about all of them before it eventually arrives.

Tech.title: The AirPods Pro are $60 off, their best price since late June
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Best Buy kicked off a sale on Apple products with discounts on its latest smartwatches to phones. Another deal that caught our eye is on the latest AirPods Pro, Apple’s flagship wireless earbuds, which are down to $189.99 ($60 off), with retailers like Amazon and Walmart matching the price. That’s their lowest price since Prime Day in late June, and just $20 shy of their all-time low.

The AirPods Pro are our favorite wireless earbuds to recommend for iPhone owners because they offer better sound quality than Apple’s entry-level AirPods. Our A/V reviewer John Higgins uses them more often than other pairs because of their, praising their excellent audio, best-in-class active noise cancellation, and just how easy they are to use. They also provide a tighter fit, making them more comfortable for some people, especially during workouts.

Beyond how good they sound, they offer a number of perks for Apple users. They can automatically sync with other Apple devices you’re signed in on, so you can move from taking a call on your iPhone to watching a show on your iPad. They also feature a built-in heart rate sensor that works with more than 50 workout types in Apple’s Fitness app, so you can use them as a fitness tracker of sorts.

Tech.title: The Zelda movie’s Ganondorf casting hints at more movies
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Deadline reported Thursday that the upcoming The Legend of Zelda movie will feature Australian actor Uli Latukefu as the villain Ganondorf, and the publication notes that “We hear Latukefu inked a multi-picture deal.”

Nintendo or Sony haven’t formally confirmed that there’s more than one movie in the works, though it’s been rumored that Nintendo and Sony might be planning a trilogy. Still, it’s not exactly unexpected that more Zelda movies might be on the way, especially given the huge success of the recent Super Mario films at the box office.

Nintendo initially announced the live-action Zelda movie, which it’s making with Sony Pictures Entertainment, back in 2023, with Wes Ball directing with Shigeru Miyamoto and Avi Arad producing. Last year, Nintendo announced that Bo Bragason and Benjamin Evan Ainsworth had been cast as Princess Zelda and Link, respectively. The movie is set to release on April 30th, 2027, and filming has officially wrapped.

In a separate report published later on Thursday, Deadline says that Dichen Lachman, Yvonne Strahovski, and the late Sam Neill will be in the Zelda movie as well. Neill’s role is unclear, but the article says Lachman plays Impa while Strahovski has been cast as “a queen character.”

Nintendo is also preparing a big new Zelda game: the company has announced a Switch 2 remake of Ocarina of Time that’s set to launch sometime in 2026.

Update, August 6th: Adds new casting details from another Deadline report.

Tech.title: Suno shares plans to combat spammy AI music
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Suno announced plans to implement a new watermarking technology and download policy to limit the spread of spammy AI tracks and increase transparency. In a lengthy blog post, CEO and co-founder Mikey Shulman laid out the company’s principles and the next steps for the company as it seeks legitimacy.

The company is rolling out new transparency tools, along with new watermarking and fingerprinting tech. Shulman says it aligns with “emerging industry standards” that will make it easier to identify Suno-generated content. He also says the company is aiming to partner with “distribution platforms on combatting fraud and misuse.”

Last year, the company also announced it would change its download policy following a settlement with Warner Music Group (WMG), and in the wake of a similar settlement between WMG and Udio that ended downloads of outputs from that platform entirely. The company hasn’t offered specifics yet, but at the time it announced the plan last year, it said that downloads would be limited to paying subscribers, and users would be limited to a certain number of downloads each month.

Shulman’s post repeatedly mentions the company’s dedication to transparency, respect for rights holders, and the importance of human-made art. But he’s also careful to say it’s not Suno’s place to “pass judgment” on the value of individual pieces of art, and that it’s ultimately up to artists and platforms to decide whether they want to disclose the use of AI tools.

Suno didn’t immediately respond to a request for specifics about the new policies and technology.

Tech.title: Brendan Carr officially unleashes broadcast consolidation
Tech.content:
is a senior policy reporter at The Verge, covering the intersection of Silicon Valley and Capitol Hill. She spent 5 years covering tech policy at CNBC, writing about antitrust, privacy, and content moderation reform.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The era of set broadcast ownership limits is officially over, after the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) voted Thursday to end the national ownership cap rule.

The agency’s two Republicans, Chair Brendan Carr and Commissioner Olivia Trusty, voted to end the ownership cap, which restricts broadcast owners from holding stations that reach a combined more than 39 percent of US TV households, while Democratic Commissioner Anna Gomez dissented. It formalizes a policy Carr has long criticized, and which he announced last month that he would seek to end at Thursday’s open FCC meeting. In place of a set limit, the FCC says, there will now be “granular, case-by-case review” to determine if broadcast consolidation is in the public interest. That will let the agency avoid having to “show special circumstances that would justify a waiver of a rule that no longer serves the public interest,” according to an FCC press release.

In place of a set limit, the FCC says, there will now be “granular, case-by-case review”

Carr has often criticized the rule as an artificial limit that restrains broadcast owners from competing with social media and streamers that can reach “100 percent of the country” without accessing broadcast licenses. This is happening at the same time Carr and President Donald Trump have threatened broadcasters for coverage they view as unfair. For example, the FCC demanded early renewal of ABC’s broadcast licenses shortly after Trump criticized the network for late night host Jimmy Kimmel’s joke about his wife. The agency said its decision was connected to an investigation into the company’s diversity, equity, and inclusivity (DEI) policies.

Those who oppose ending the ownership cap, including Gomez, say that allowing broadcast owners to gobble up as many stations as they can buy will disincentivize local reporting on public airwaves and drive up consumer costs. They also say that only Congress has the power to lift the ownership cap, since the figure was written into a 2004 law, leaving it open to legal scrutiny.

Still, the FCC under Carr has already found ways to work around the rule, even before voting it off the books. Carr agreed to waive the cap to approve the $6.2 billion merger of broadcasters Nexstar and Tegna. A federal judge has paused the merger pending a challenge by a group of state attorneys general.

Tech.title: OpenAI is giving ChatGPT free users unlimited text chats
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

OpenAI is making a big change for ChatGPT users on its free and Go tiers: Starting next week, users on those tiers will be able to have unlimited text chats with the chatbot, according to OpenAI. Right now, you may run into rate limits if you do too many text chats on those tiers, but those limits, just for text, will be going away soon. Messages that include things like file uploads and images will continue to have limits.

Next week, OpenAI is also adding a “Think” button for free and Go users that they can use to “access higher reasoning for harder questions.” This week, for those users, the company is additionally upgrading ChatGPT’s default AI model to the recently released GPT-5.6 Luna.

The “Think” button for free and Go subscribers. Image: OpenAI

For Plus and Pro subscribers, GPT-5.6 Sol in ChatGPT is being updated to be “more reliable with facts,” OpenAI says. “The new GPT‑5.6 Sol is designed to make fewer mistakes — especially when answers depend on dates, numbers, sources, rules, or assumptions — by better using the sources it finds to answer your question.” The updated GPT-5.6 Sol will also give you “more direct responses” with “tighter formatting,” and OpenAI says ChatGPT will “avoid extra detail when it does not help.”

Plus and Pro subscribers can also use a new slider to decide “how much thought ChatGPT puts into an answer.” Both the updated GPT-5.6 Sol and the slider will be available starting Thursday.

ChatGPT’s new slider. Image: OpenAI

Tech.title: TikTok blames ‘moderator error’ on slow response to Perez Hilton livestream
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

TikTok says a “moderator error” delayed the removal of a livestream that appeared to show blogger Perez Hilton harming himself, as reported earlier by Wired. Jamie Favazza, a spokesperson for TikTok US, tells The Verge that the platform notified law enforcement about the situation and banned Hilton’s account for violating its community guidelines.

Hilton, or Mario Armando Lavandeira Jr., is known for the celebrity gossip blog he started in 2004, where he often posted photos of stars featuring his own often obscene or cruel drawings layered on top.

Though some users claimed Perez’s livestream aired for more than 30 minutes, Favazza disputes this, saying it lasted around 15 minutes. Favazza adds that TikTok’s automated content moderation team flagged the video “within minutes” and routed it to US moderation teams. TikTok also took down the subsequent livestreams started by Hilton within 90 seconds. Screenshots and clips from the livestream are still floating around on some platforms like X.

The livestream aired on Tuesday night, with the Miami-Dade Sheriff’s Office responding to Hilton’s home after saying they received “multiple calls regarding an individual who was livestreaming acts of self-harm on social media,” according to CNN. The authorities transported Hilton to a local hospital.

The slow response to Hilton’s livestream has raised concerns about moderation on TikTok, which some creators have found to be unevenly applied. TikTok’s policies strictly prohibit content that “shows, promotes, or provides instructions for suicide or self-harm,” along with “extremely graphic, violent, or disturbing content.” On Wednesday, The New York Times reported that TikTok US is laying off 250 employees and shutting down its Nashville office, where part of its content moderation team is based.

If you or someone you know is considering suicide or is anxious, depressed, upset, or needs to talk, there are people who want to help. In the US: Crisis Text Line: Text HOME to 741-741 from anywhere in the US, at any time, about any type of crisis. 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline: Call or text 988 (formerly known as the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline). The original phone number, 1-800-273-TALK (8255), is available as well. The Trevor Project: Text START to 678-678 or call 1-866-488-7386 at any time to speak to a trained counselor. Outside the US: The International Association for Suicide Prevention lists a number of suicide hotlines by country. Click here to find them. Befrienders Worldwide has a network of crisis helplines active in 48 countries. Click here to find them.

Tech.title: OpenAI’s new AI smart speaker will reportedly sell for between $300 and $400
Tech.content:
In Brief

More details continue to trickle out about OpenAI’s mysterious new hardware device — described previously as an AI-fueled smart speaker that will be the “physical manifestation” of ChatGPT.

Bloomberg now reports that the device will be “donut-shaped,” designed thusly to allow users to carry it around their home and place it in different locations, like a bedside table or a kitchen counter.

It will be constructed from “high-quality metal,” have a “premium look,” and (in a detail that mystifies) will have distinct “moving parts,” sources told Bloomberg.

It also could be slightly more expensive than your average smart speaker, perhaps $300 to $400 per unit, according to this report. For comparison, most of Amazon’s smart home speakers range in price from $40 on the low end to $240 on the high end.

So, to sum up: an expensive talking AI donut that has … moving parts? OpenAI releasing a smart home device has a certain logic to it, in that it would further integrate ChatGPT into users’ lives. However, historically speaking, smart speakers have not always been profitable and may prove a difficult market to break into. The potentially high price point also might not help.

The device, which is being developed in partnership with LoveFrom, the design studio founded by famous former Apple developer Jony Ive, will likely be released at some point in 2027, Bloomberg writes.

The company’s attempt to enter the hardware market has not gone off without a hitch. OpenAI is being sued by the current king of hardware, Apple, which has accused the AI lab of stealing trade secrets. OpenAI has denied wrongdoing.

Tech.title: Vogue just gave another nod of approval to the tech world
Tech.content:
Vogue World is coming to San Francisco next year — perhaps another indication that tech billionaires have become leaders in the fashion zeitgeist.

Of course, the announcement of the enormous fashion/art/music event doesn’t say that. Instead, Anna Wintour wrote that Vogue believes in celebrating cities and “San Francisco is a city like none other.”

“It’s a place of diverse communities living side by side, a place that loves the arts, loves creativity, and isn’t afraid of change.” She also noted the city’s history of rebelliousness and innovation.

“I love that San Francisco has always stood up for values and the things it believes in,” Wintour wrote. “Vogue World will support San Francisco’s creative minds and strengthen the entire ecosystem — and it will offer another opportunity to show San Francisco is on the rise.”

There were rumors that Vogue World would head to San Francisco after Winter was seen having meetings with the city’s mayor, Daniel Lurie.

Plus, in the past year, Wintour has cozied up to the most powerful names in tech, culminating in this year’s Met Gala, which saw Jeff Bezos and his wife, Lauren Sanchez, serve as lead sponsors for the event. Google’s Sergey Brin and Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg were also spotted at the event (the latter’s first, that is). In fact, OpenAI bought a table, as did Meta and Snap (for $350,000 a pop). It’s true that TikTok, Apple, and Instagram previously sponsored the event, but the presence of the tech crowd was so considerable that the Met Gala this year was dubbed the “tech gala” in some places.

Last year, Vogue put Lauren Sanchez on the cover of the magazine after her wedding to the Amazon founder. To the fashion world, this was Wintour’s stamp of approval — not just for Sanchez’s ascent into the fashion world, but that tech and its leaders were worthy of cultural recognition.

Though Bezos and Sanchez reportedly live in Florida (and Amazon is, of course, headquartered in the Seattle area), there is no city more associated with tech than San Francisco. By locating Vogue World there, this is another indication of Wintour’s approval.

Vogue, as a media publication, is always following the money, and as a cultural bible, is always looking for ways to stay relevant. Turning toward the worldwide headquarters of AI, good or bad, is brilliant for business (and Wintour is nothing if not brilliant).

But Vogue World was previously held in New York, London, Paris, and this year, Milan. Maybe because I live in an East Coast bubble, but I’ve not heard anyone in recent years refer to San Francisco as a beacon of style to rank alongside these other cities.

While the city has a reputation as the land of the free-spirited bohemian, tech and its workers have a reputation for hoodies, Patagonia vests, and expensive athletic shoes, if they even dress up that much.

For instance, billionaire Alexandr Wang, who is now running Meta’s all-important Superintelligence Labs, just did an interview with Y Combinator’s Garry Tan in front of a packed stadium wearing a faded Nintendo T-shirt and what looked like a pair of Crocs. Comfy? Yes. High fashion? Decidedly no.

But maybe that’s changing. Wang’s boss, Mark Zuckerberg, who once always appeared in a plain gray T-shirt and jeans, has made efforts in recent years to become more fashionable. Zuck and his wife Priscilla Chan were spotted front row at a Prada show this season. The new campaign for Meta Glasses has a slew of celeb ambassadors and looks like it could be a Saint Laurent or Balenciaga ad.

OpenAI and Palantir have recently released merch collabs, playing on the minimalist style of tech workers (the merch line of the latter, I would argue, looks inspired by Virgil Abloh’s Off-White).

I concede that creatively there is much to be done with the understated, Northern California style. Surrounded by beautiful nature and cooler temperatures, plenty of fashion designers could be motivated by San Francisco’s tech industry. I look forward to seeing Claude-inspired terra cotta-colored gowns and Vogue-emblazoned quarter-zips soon.
